questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A media company prepares a dataset of 5 million news articles to fine-tune a model for headline generation. An AWS Glue visual ETL job writes the data into an Amazon S3 training bucket.
Every record must meet three standards. The headline column must not be null. The body_text column must hold at least 300 characters. The sentiment_score must fall between -1.0 and 1.0.
Records that fail any standard must land in a separate quarantine prefix. The job must keep running and must still write the passing records. The team wants the least custom coding.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A media company prepares a dataset of 5 million news articles to fine-tune a model for headline generation. An AWS Glue visual ETL job writes the data into an Amazon S3 training bucket.
Every record must meet three standards. The headline column must not be null. The body_text column must hold at least 300 characters. The sentiment_score must fall between -1.0 and 1.0.
Records that fail any standard must land in a separate quarantine prefix. The job must keep running and must still write the passing records. The team wants the least custom coding.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the Evaluate Data Quality node to output original data with the error columns, then add a Conditional Router transform that splits rows on the evaluation result.
Define the DQDL ruleset with IsComplete, ColumnLength, and ColumnValues rules, then enable Fail job when data quality fails so failing records never reach the training bucket.
Attach the DQDL ruleset to the Data Catalog table and schedule recurring evaluation runs, so the job writes only the records that pass those scheduled checks.
Set the Evaluate Data Quality node to output original data with the error columns, then run a downstream Python shell job that reads them and drops failed rows.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the Evaluate Data Quality node to output original data with the error columns, then add a Conditional Router transform that splits rows on the evaluation result.
Choosing Original data and enabling the new columns option adds a rowLevelOutcomes node carrying DataQualityRulesPass, DataQualityRulesFail, DataQualityRulesSkip, and DataQualityEvaluationResult, and those column values let you filter rows and act on them. The Conditional Router transform evaluates each incoming row against group conditions and sends it to the matching output group. Both are visual transforms, so the team writes no code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.1: "Create comprehensive data validation workflows to ensure data meets quality standards for FM consumption"
Example: "AWS Glue Data Quality"

Sources:

  • Evaluating data quality for ETL jobs in AWS Glue Studio

  • Creating a Conditional Router transformation

INCORRECT: Define the DQDL ruleset with IsComplete, ColumnLength, and ColumnValues rules, then enable Fail job when data quality fails so failing records never reach the training bucket.
The three rule types match the three standards, so the ruleset part of this option is right. The action is the problem. With a fail option on ruleset failure, the whole job fails when a rule fails, and the job saves no data. One bad article among five million stops the run, so no passing records reach the training bucket and no failed records reach the quarantine prefix. The team needs each record sorted while the job keeps running.

INCORRECT: Attach the DQDL ruleset to the Data Catalog table and schedule recurring evaluation runs, so the job writes only the records that pass those scheduled checks.
AWS Glue Data Quality can also run a ruleset on a table in the Data Catalog, on demand or on a schedule. Such a run is a separate task that checks data that is already in the table, so it fits regular audits of stored data. It does not run inside the ETL job, so it cannot stop or move single rows while the job writes them. The failed records would reach the training bucket first, and a later run would only report them.

INCORRECT: Set the Evaluate Data Quality node to output original data with the error columns, then run a downstream Python shell job that reads them and drops failed rows.
This option uses the same error columns as the key, and a separate job can read them and remove the failed rows. It breaks the need for the least custom coding. A Python shell job is code that the team must write, test and maintain, and it adds a second job run. This option also drops the failed rows, while the team must keep them in a quarantine prefix. The Conditional Router splits the rows inside the visual job with no code.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare startup is aggregating patient feedback logs from multiple sources to build a RAG-based chatbot. The data includes unstructured text and metadata (timestamps, clinic IDs). The data science team needs to perform an initial visual quality assessment to identify outliers and missing values without writing pandas code. Additionally, once the ingestion pipeline is running, the operations team needs to be alerted immediately if the percentage of incoming records with missing clinic_id values exceeds 5% in any 5-minute interval. The number of incoming records changes a lot during the day.
Which combination of tools meets these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A healthcare startup is aggregating patient feedback logs from multiple sources to build a RAG-based chatbot. The data includes unstructured text and metadata (timestamps, clinic IDs). The data science team needs to perform an initial visual quality assessment to identify outliers and missing values without writing pandas code. Additionally, once the ingestion pipeline is running, the operations team needs to be alerted immediately if the percentage of incoming records with missing clinic_id values exceeds 5% in any 5-minute interval. The number of incoming records changes a lot during the day.
Which combination of tools meets these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Import the raw dataset into Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler and create a Data Quality and Insights Report that shows missing values, outliers and column distributions.
Publish custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics for null clinic_id records and for all records, and alarm on a metric math ratio of the two with a 5-minute period and a 5% threshold.
Publish custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics for null clinic_id records and for all records, and alarm on a metric math ratio of the two with a 5-minute period and anomaly detection.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter that counts null clinic_id values in the pipeline logs, and alarm on that count with a 5-minute period and a fixed threshold.
Run an Amazon SageMaker Processing job with a pandas script that counts missing values and outliers in each column and writes the results to Amazon S3.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Import the raw dataset into Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler and create a Data Quality and Insights Report that shows missing values, outliers and column distributions.
SageMaker Data Wrangler builds the Data Quality and Insights Report from a few choices in its interface, so the data science team writes no code. The report shows missing values, invalid values, feature types and outlier counts, and it adds high severity warnings that point to likely problems in the data. The team can build it on the interactive sample of the data flow or on the full dataset. For the full dataset, SageMaker AI runs a Processing job in the background. Either way, the team gets a visual first look at the feedback logs.

CORRECT: Publish custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics for null clinic_id records and for all records, and alarm on a metric math ratio of the two with a 5-minute period and a 5% threshold.
The requirement is a rate, not a count: records with a missing clinic_id as a share of all records. The pipeline publishes one custom metric for null clinic_id records and one for all records. A metric math expression divides the first by the second, and a CloudWatch alarm watches the result with a 5-minute period and a 5% threshold. When the rate in a 5-minute period goes above 5%, the alarm changes state, and its alarm action can notify the operations team. The rate stays correct when the number of records rises or falls during the day.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.1: "Create comprehensive data validation workflows to ensure data meets quality standards for FM consumption"
Example: "SageMaker Data Wrangler"

Sources:

  • Perform exploratory data analysis (EDA)
  • Create a CloudWatch alarm based on a metric math expression

INCORRECT: Publish custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics for null clinic_id records and for all records, and alarm on a metric math ratio of the two with a 5-minute period and anomaly detection.
The two metrics and the ratio are right. The difference is the threshold. Anomaly detection learns the normal hourly, daily and weekly pattern of a metric, and it alarms when the value leaves a band of expected values. It also works on a metric math expression. This fits a team that has no fixed limit and wants to find unusual behavior. Here the operations team has a fixed limit of 5%. An anomaly band follows past behavior, not that limit, so it can alarm below 5% or stay in the OK state above 5%.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter that counts null clinic_id values in the pipeline logs, and alarm on that count with a 5-minute period and a fixed threshold.
A metric filter turns log lines that match a pattern into a CloudWatch metric, so the team can count null clinic_id values from the pipeline logs and alarm on the count. A fixed count works when the volume is steady, because then a count stands for a known share of the records. Here the number of records changes a lot during the day. At a busy time, a count above the threshold can still be less than 5% of the records. At a quiet time, the rate can pass 5% while the count stays below the threshold.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon SageMaker Processing job with a pandas script that counts missing values and outliers in each column and writes the results to Amazon S3.
A Processing job runs a script on managed compute, and a pandas profiling script is a common way to check data in a repeatable pipeline. This team must do its first check without writing pandas code, and it wants a visual assessment. This option needs a pandas script, and it writes a results file, not a visual report.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A media company maintains a massive archive of unlabeled raw video footage. They want to build a "smart search" application that allows editors to find clips using natural language queries like "show me the segment where the reporter talks about climate change while standing in a forest." The search index must account for both the visual context of the video and the spoken content.
Which combination of processing steps should the GenAI Developer use to ingest this data for the search application?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A media company maintains a massive archive of unlabeled raw video footage. They want to build a "smart search" application that allows editors to find clips using natural language queries like "show me the segment where the reporter talks about climate change while standing in a forest." The search index must account for both the visual context of the video and the spoken content.
Which combination of processing steps should the GenAI Developer use to ingest this data for the search application?
Select TWO.

options.text: Use Amazon Transcribe to generate a text transcript of the video's audio track. Chunk the transcript by time segment and generate text embeddings to index the spoken content for semantic search.

Extract representative frames from the video at regular intervals. Use an Amazon Bedrock multimodal model to generate detailed text descriptions of the visual scene in each frame, then embed those descriptions for indexing.
Run Amazon Rekognition label detection on extracted video frames. Embed the returned object tags to represent each frame's visual content.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings to ingest the raw video files directly. Rely on the unified embedding model to handle both visual and spoken content retrieval without a separate Transcribe step.

Use Amazon Transcribe to generate a transcript with speaker diarization enabled. Feed the raw transcript directly into an Amazon Bedrock FM as a single prompt to generate one summary embedding representing the entire video.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use Amazon Transcribe to generate a text transcript of the video's audio track. Chunk the transcript by time segment and generate text embeddings to index the spoken content for semantic search.
Amazon Transcribe turns the audio track into text. The transcript gives a start time and an end time for every word, so the team can cut it into time segments that match parts of the video. Each segment gets its own text embedding. A query about what the reporter says, such as climate change, then finds the segment where those words were spoken, and the times point the editor to the right clip.

CORRECT: Extract representative frames from the video at regular intervals. Use an Amazon Bedrock multimodal model to generate detailed text descriptions of the visual scene in each frame, then embed those descriptions for indexing.
An Amazon Bedrock multimodal model can read an image and answer questions about it or summarize it. The pipeline takes frames from the video at fixed times and asks the model to describe the scene in each frame in text, for example a reporter who stands among trees. An embedding model then turns each description into a vector for the index. A query about a reporter in a forest then finds the frames that show that scene. The transcript cannot do this, because the reporter may never say the word forest.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "advanced multimodal pipeline architectures"

Sources:

  • Choosing your multimodal processing approach
  • Data input and output (Amazon Transcribe Developer Guide)
  • Image understanding (Amazon Nova User Guide)

INCORRECT: Run Amazon Rekognition label detection on extracted video frames. Embed the returned object tags to represent each frame's visual content.
Amazon Rekognition label detection returns labels for the objects, events and concepts that it finds in an image, such as tree, person or outdoors, each with a confidence score. Labels are useful to tag and filter a large photo library. They do not describe what happens in the scene. A list of labels cannot tell a reporter who speaks in a forest from a person who walks past some trees, so embeddings of the labels match a detailed natural language query poorly.

INCORRECT: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings to ingest the raw video files directly. Rely on the unified embedding model to handle both visual and spoken content retrieval without a separate Transcribe step.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings can embed video files directly, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can use it to search visual content. It cannot reliably search the speech in audio or video, so spoken words are not searchable this way. The editors search for what the reporter talks about. For that, the speech must become text first, and this option removes the step that does it.

INCORRECT: Use Amazon Transcribe to generate a transcript with speaker diarization enabled. Feed the raw transcript directly into an Amazon Bedrock FM as a single prompt to generate one summary embedding representing the entire video.
Speaker diarization labels which speaker says each part of the transcript, so the first step is sound. The problem is the second step. One embedding for the whole video mixes every topic into a single vector. A search can at best return the whole video, not the segment where the reporter talks about climate change, and it can miss the video when that topic fills only a small part of it.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company fine-tuned an open-weight model and serves it from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint in one AWS Region. Client apps call a custom domain name that points to a Regional REST API in Amazon API Gateway, and the API sends each request to the endpoint. Company policy says the model must run only on SageMaker AI in the company's account.
Last month, an outage in that Region stopped the service for hours. The team now wants traffic to move to a second Region within minutes and with no manual steps. The second Region will run a smaller standby endpoint, so it must receive traffic only while the first Region is down.
Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company fine-tuned an open-weight model and serves it from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint in one AWS Region. Client apps call a custom domain name that points to a Regional REST API in Amazon API Gateway, and the API sends each request to the endpoint. Company policy says the model must run only on SageMaker AI in the company's account.
Last month, an outage in that Region stopped the service for hours. The team now wants traffic to move to a second Region within minutes and with no manual steps. The second Region will run a smaller standby endpoint, so it must receive traffic only while the first Region is down.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Replicate the model files to the second Region with Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication, and have the on-call engineer create the endpoint and the API there when an outage starts.
Deploy the model to a standby endpoint and a Regional API in the second Region with the same custom domain name, and create Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks.

Replicate the model files to the second Region with Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication, run a copy of the endpoint and the API there, and have the on-call engineer change the DNS records in an outage.
Move the model calls to an Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock selects a Region of the profile for each request, with no endpoints to run.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Deploy the model to a standby endpoint and a Regional API in the second Region with the same custom domain name, and create Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks.
The model now runs in two Regions: the main endpoint in the first Region and a smaller standby endpoint in the second. Each Region has its own Regional API with the same custom domain name, so client apps keep one address. Route 53 failover records send all traffic to the primary record while its health check passes. When the health check fails, Route 53 answers with the secondary record, and traffic moves to the second Region with no person involved. While the first Region is healthy, the standby gets no traffic. SageMaker AI needs the model files in Amazon S3 and the container image in the same Region as the endpoint, so the team copies both to the second Region before it creates the standby endpoint.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.3: "Design resilient AI systems to ensure continuous operation during service disruptions"
Example: "cross-Region model deployment"

Sources:

  • Configure custom health checks for DNS failover for an API Gateway API

  • Failover routing (Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide)

  • ContainerDefinition (Amazon SageMaker API Reference)

INCORRECT: Replicate the model files to the second Region with Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication, and have the on-call engineer create the endpoint and the API there when an outage starts.
S3 Cross-Region Replication copies new model files to a bucket in the second Region automatically, so the files wait there until they are needed. A plan where an engineer builds the endpoint and the API after an outage starts fits a service that can be down for some hours, and it costs little because nothing runs in the second Region. This team wants traffic to move within minutes and with no manual steps. Here a person must create the endpoint and the API during the outage, and the service stays down until that work ends.

INCORRECT: Replicate the model files to the second Region with Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication, run a copy of the endpoint and the API there, and have the on-call engineer change the DNS records in an outage.
This design keeps a running copy of the endpoint and the API in the second Region, so the service can move quickly once someone acts. A manual switch fits a team that wants a person to decide each failover, for example after a check that the first Region is really down. This team wants the move to happen with no manual steps. The service stays down until the on-call engineer notices the outage and changes the DNS records.

INCORRECT: Move the model calls to an Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock selects a Region of the profile for each request, with no endpoints to run.
An inference profile names a foundation model and the Regions that can serve it, and Amazon Bedrock selects the Region for each request. It fits a company that calls a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock and wants help with traffic bursts or a Region problem. This company's model is its own fine-tuned open-weight model, and company policy says the model must run only on SageMaker AI in the company's account. The model cannot move to Amazon Bedrock, so no inference profile can serve it.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A financial services firm processes thousands of unstructured PDF earnings reports daily. The engineering team uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock to extract specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and populate a downstream SQL database.
Users have reported that while the model handles narrative text well, it consistently hallucinates values when processing financial tables that span multiple pages or contain complex nested headers. The raw text ingested from the OCR pipeline often arrives with broken formatting, missing whitespace, and merged columns. The damage differs from report to report. The team must keep its Claude Sonnet extraction step and its prompts unchanged.
Which strategy should the GenAI Developer implement to enhance the input data quality and resolve the extraction errors?
questions.promptText:
A financial services firm processes thousands of unstructured PDF earnings reports daily. The engineering team uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock to extract specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and populate a downstream SQL database.
Users have reported that while the model handles narrative text well, it consistently hallucinates values when processing financial tables that span multiple pages or contain complex nested headers. The raw text ingested from the OCR pipeline often arrives with broken formatting, missing whitespace, and merged columns. The damage differs from report to report. The team must keep its Claude Sonnet extraction step and its prompts unchanged.
Which strategy should the GenAI Developer implement to enhance the input data quality and resolve the extraction errors?

options.text: Add a step before extraction that calls the Converse API with a smaller model to rewrite the OCR text as Markdown tables, and pass that text to Claude Sonnet.
Add a step before extraction that runs a Lambda function with fixed rules to restore missing spaces and split merged columns, and pass that text to Claude Sonnet.
Add examples of damaged tables and their correct KPI values to the Claude Sonnet extraction prompt, so that the model learns to read the broken layout.
Send the PDF files to Amazon Bedrock Data Automation with a custom blueprint that holds the KPI fields and a table field, and load its JSON output into the database.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a step before extraction that calls the Converse API with a smaller model to rewrite the OCR text as Markdown tables, and pass that text to Claude Sonnet.
The errors start before extraction. The OCR text reaches Claude Sonnet with broken spacing and merged columns, so the model cannot see which value belongs to which row and header, and it guesses. A first call with the Converse API sends the raw text to a smaller, faster model on Amazon Bedrock and asks it to rewrite the text as Markdown tables. A model reads the meaning of the text, so it can repair damage that looks different in every report. Claude Sonnet then reads clean rows and columns, and the extraction step and its prompts stay as they are.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.4: "Enhance input data quality to improve FM response quality and consistency"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock to reformat text"

Sources:

  • Inference using Converse API
  • Blueprints (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)
  • Design a prompt (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)

INCORRECT: Add a step before extraction that runs a Lambda function with fixed rules to restore missing spaces and split merged columns, and pass that text to Claude Sonnet.
A Lambda function that normalizes text is a good first step when the same errors repeat, for example when one character always replaces a space. Fixed rules work only for damage that follows a known pattern. Here the damage differs from report to report, so rules written for one report miss the errors in the next one, and many tables still reach Claude Sonnet broken.

INCORRECT: Add examples of damaged tables and their correct KPI values to the Claude Sonnet extraction prompt, so that the model learns to read the broken layout.
Examples in a prompt can improve a model's answers, and they help most when they look like the real input. This option changes the extraction prompt, and the team must keep its prompts unchanged. It also leaves the broken text as it is, so the model still has to guess which value sits under which header.

INCORRECT: Send the PDF files to Amazon Bedrock Data Automation with a custom blueprint that holds the KPI fields and a table field, and load its JSON output into the database.
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation extracts the fields that a blueprint lists, and a blueprint can hold table fields with named columns. For a new project that extracts KPIs from PDF files, this is a strong choice. In this design, its JSON output goes straight into the database, so Data Automation takes the place of the Claude Sonnet extraction step. The team must keep that step and its prompts.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A manufacturing company has deployed a RAG-based maintenance assistant for its field technicians. The system ingests thousands of technical manuals and uses an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for retrieval. Technicians report that when they ask about specific proprietary components (e.g., "How do I reset the Turbo-Encabulator V2?"), the system frequently retrieves irrelevant content related to similarly named but distinct parts (e.g., "Turbo-Encabulator V1" or "Retro-Encabulator"). The standard semantic search is failing to distinguish between these specific proprietary terms.
How should the GenAI Developer enhance the data ingestion pipeline to resolve this retrieval ambiguity?
questions.promptText:
A manufacturing company has deployed a RAG-based maintenance assistant for its field technicians. The system ingests thousands of technical manuals and uses an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for retrieval. Technicians report that when they ask about specific proprietary components (e.g., "How do I reset the Turbo-Encabulator V2?"), the system frequently retrieves irrelevant content related to similarly named but distinct parts (e.g., "Turbo-Encabulator V1" or "Retro-Encabulator"). The standard semantic search is failing to distinguish between these specific proprietary terms.
How should the GenAI Developer enhance the data ingestion pipeline to resolve this retrieval ambiguity?

options.text: Train an Amazon Comprehend Custom Entity Recognizer on the proprietary component name list. Update the ingestion pipeline to extract component names and store them as metadata fields in the Knowledge Base for precise retrieval filtering.

Use the Amazon Comprehend DetectEntities API in the ingestion pipeline. Map identified COMMERCIAL_ITEM entities to a metadata field in the Knowledge Base and configure retrieval queries to filter on matching component names.

Train an Amazon Comprehend Custom Classifier to categorize each document by component family during ingestion. Store the predicted component category as a metadata field in the Knowledge Base and filter retrieval results by category.

Configure the Amazon Comprehend Custom Entity Recognizer to run in real-time detection mode during retrieval. Use the detected entity from the technician's query to dynamically construct a metadata filter before the Knowledge Base similarity search executes.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Train an Amazon Comprehend Custom Entity Recognizer on the proprietary component name list. Update the ingestion pipeline to extract component names and store them as metadata fields in the Knowledge Base for precise retrieval filtering.
Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition finds entity types that the built-in types do not cover, such as a company's own product codes. The team trains a recognizer with its list of component names and a set of manuals that contain them. During ingestion, the recognizer finds every component name in each manual, and the pipeline writes those names into the document's metadata in the Knowledge Base. At query time, a metadata filter on the exact name, such as Turbo-Encabulator V2, returns only chunks from manuals tagged with that name. Semantic search alone sees V1 and V2 as almost the same text; the filter keeps them apart.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.2: "Develop comprehensive metadata frameworks to improve search precision and context awareness for FM interactions"

Sources:

  • Custom entity recognition
  • Configure and customize queries and response generation
  • Preparing classifier training data

INCORRECT: Use the Amazon Comprehend DetectEntities API in the ingestion pipeline. Map identified COMMERCIAL_ITEM entities to a metadata field in the Knowledge Base and configure retrieval queries to filter on matching component names.
The DetectEntities API finds built-in entity types such as PERSON, ORGANIZATION and COMMERCIAL_ITEM. COMMERCIAL_ITEM means a branded product, and it fits well-known product names in general text. No built-in type stands for a company's internal part names, so the service has no way to learn that Turbo-Encabulator V1 and V2 are two different components. A custom recognizer trained on the company's own list does that.

INCORRECT: Train an Amazon Comprehend Custom Classifier to categorize each document by component family during ingestion. Store the predicted component category as a metadata field in the Knowledge Base and filter retrieval results by category.
A custom classifier sorts documents into classes, and in multi-label mode one document can get several classes. Classes by component family help when users search a broad area, such as hydraulics. This option labels each manual by component family. Turbo-Encabulator V1 and V2 belong to the same family, so a filter on the family still returns manuals for both parts, and the answers about the wrong version stay.

INCORRECT: Configure the Amazon Comprehend Custom Entity Recognizer to run in real-time detection mode during retrieval. Use the detected entity from the technician's query to dynamically construct a metadata filter before the Knowledge Base similarity search executes.
Running the custom recognizer on the technician's question does find the component name, and it is a useful step to build a filter at query time. But a filter needs a metadata field on the stored chunks to match against. This option adds no metadata during ingestion, so the Knowledge Base has no component field, and the filter has nothing to match.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A retail company is building a product search engine using a RAG architecture. The application must support hybrid search (combining semantic relevance with keyword matching) to handle specific product model numbers accurately. Currently, the ingestion process uses a complex AWS Lambda function to send product descriptions to Amazon Bedrock for embedding generation, waits for the response, and then indexes the vectors into Amazon OpenSearch Service.
The development team wants to simplify this architecture by removing the custom middleware code while ensuring that embedding generation remains automated for both ingestion and search queries. The team must keep its existing OpenSearch Service domain and index.
Which architectural change achieves this goal?
questions.promptText:
A retail company is building a product search engine using a RAG architecture. The application must support hybrid search (combining semantic relevance with keyword matching) to handle specific product model numbers accurately. Currently, the ingestion process uses a complex AWS Lambda function to send product descriptions to Amazon Bedrock for embedding generation, waits for the response, and then indexes the vectors into Amazon OpenSearch Service.
The development team wants to simplify this architecture by removing the custom middleware code while ensuring that embedding generation remains automated for both ingestion and search queries. The team must keep its existing OpenSearch Service domain and index.
Which architectural change achieves this goal?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock connector and an ingest pipeline with a text_embedding processor, and send hybrid queries with a neural clause through a search pipeline with a normalization processor.
Register the Amazon Bedrock embedding model through an ML connector, embed documents at ingestion with a text_embedding processor, and search with neural queries that have no keyword clause.

Move the index to an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection with an Amazon Bedrock connector, a text_embedding ingest pipeline, and hybrid queries with a neural clause and a normalization search pipeline.
Send product data through Amazon Data Firehose with a Lambda transformation that calls Amazon Bedrock for each embedding before Firehose delivers the records to the index.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock connector and an ingest pipeline with a text_embedding processor, and send hybrid queries with a neural clause through a search pipeline with a normalization processor.
Neural search moves the embedding calls into OpenSearch Service itself. The connector lets the domain call the embedding model on Amazon Bedrock. In the ingest pipeline, the text_embedding processor creates the vector for each product description when the document is indexed, so the Lambda function is no longer needed. At search time, the neural clause sends the query text to the same model, so OpenSearch creates the query vector too. The hybrid query also holds a keyword clause that matches model numbers exactly. The normalization processor in the search pipeline puts the keyword scores and the vector scores on one scale before it combines them. All of this runs in the existing domain and index.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.1: "Create advanced vector database architectures specifically for FM augmentation to enable efficient semantic retrieval beyond traditional search capabilities"

Sources:

  • Amazon OpenSearch Service ML connectors for AWS services
  • Configure Neural Search and Hybrid Search on OpenSearch Serverless

INCORRECT: Register the Amazon Bedrock embedding model through an ML connector, embed documents at ingestion with a text_embedding processor, and search with neural queries that have no keyword clause.
The ingestion side of this option is right, and a neural query alone gives pure semantic search. That fits a catalog where shoppers describe what they want in their own words. It has no keyword clause, so an exact model number counts only as much as its meaning in the vector, and similar model numbers look almost the same. The application must support hybrid search to match model numbers accurately, and this option drops the keyword side.

INCORRECT: Move the index to an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection with an Amazon Bedrock connector, a text_embedding ingest pipeline, and hybrid queries with a neural clause and a normalization search pipeline.
OpenSearch Serverless supports neural search with remote models through connectors, and hybrid search with a normalization processor, so this design works for a new project. An OpenSearch Serverless collection is a group of indexes in a separate deployment option. The team would have to create a new index in the collection and load all the product data again. Here the team must keep its existing OpenSearch Service domain and index.

INCORRECT: Send product data through Amazon Data Firehose with a Lambda transformation that calls Amazon Bedrock for each embedding before Firehose delivers the records to the index.
Amazon Data Firehose can call a Lambda function to transform records before it delivers them, which fits a streaming pipeline that needs custom changes to each record. Here the Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock is still custom code that the team writes and maintains, and that code is what the team wants to remove. Firehose also works only on the ingestion side, so search queries would still need their own embedding code.

3. Single Datastore: The operations team wants to avoid managing a separate specialized vector database.
Which vector store architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a BEFORE INSERT trigger that uses the aws_ml extension.

Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a Lambda function that a trigger invokes asynchronously through aws_lambda.
Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a Lambda function that reads new row IDs from an Amazon SQS queue.
Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a pg_cron job that runs every minute for rows with no vector.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a BEFORE INSERT trigger that uses the aws_ml extension.
A BEFORE INSERT trigger runs as part of the insert, inside the same database transaction. The aws_ml extension lets SQL code call an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock, so the trigger creates the vector and sets the vector column before the row is written. The vector is created at the moment the row is written, so the row and its vector are always in sync. Because the vector sits in the same table as the amount, date and merchant category, one SQL query can filter on those columns and order the rows by vector distance, in one datastore. The cost is a slower insert, because each write waits for the model call.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.3: "Deploy and configure vector search solutions to enable semantic search capabilities for FM augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Aurora with the pgvector extension"

Sources:

  • Automating vector embedding generation in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with Amazon Bedrock

  • Using Amazon Aurora machine learning with Aurora PostgreSQL

  • AWS Lambda function and parameter reference

INCORRECT: Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a Lambda function that a trigger invokes asynchronously through aws_lambda.
The aws_lambda extension can invoke a Lambda function with the Event type, which is asynchronous and returns at once. Inserts stay fast, so this fits a busy system where write speed matters more than having each vector right away. The function writes the vector later, in its own transaction. Until then, the new transaction has no vector, and if the function fails, the vector may never be written. The question says the vectors must always stay in sync with the transaction data.

INCORRECT: Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a Lambda function that reads new row IDs from an Amazon SQS queue.
A queue with a Lambda function that works in batches handles high volume well and retries failed messages, so it suits production systems that need strong error handling at scale. The vectors still arrive after the rows commit. For a short time after each insert, the row exists with no vector, and a search in that time can miss it. That breaks the rule that the vectors always stay in sync with the transaction data.

INCORRECT: Store the vectors in a pgvector column of the transactions table in Aurora PostgreSQL, and create each vector with Amazon Bedrock in a pg_cron job that runs every minute for rows with no vector.
The pg_cron extension runs SQL on a schedule inside Aurora PostgreSQL, and a job that fills missing vectors in batches is simple to run. It fits a search where a short delay is acceptable. Here every transaction written between two runs has no vector until the next run, so the vectors are not always in sync with the transaction data.

The reports describe in detail how attackers broke into systems. Since the passages were added, many normal questions get the guardrail's blocked message, and tests show the passages cause it. The security team trusts the reports. Every analyst question must still be checked with the same filters and strength, and harmful questions must still be blocked. The team also wants the guardrail to process less text.
Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Change the prompt strength of the Misconduct content filter in the guardrail from HIGH to LOW, so the attack details in the passages pass and the other categories stay at HIGH.
Switch the content filters of the guardrail to detect mode for prompts, so the guardrail notes its findings in the trace and lets each request through.
Put the analyst's question in a guardContent block and the passages in a plain text block of the same message, so the guardrail checks the question and skips the passages.
Change the prompt strength of the Misconduct content filter in the guardrail from HIGH to NONE, so the attack details in the passages pass and the other categories stay at HIGH.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Put the analyst's question in a guardContent block and the passages in a plain text block of the same message, so the guardrail checks the question and skips the passages.
In a Converse request, a guardContent block marks the text that the guardrail must check. Once a guardContent block appears anywhere in the messages, the content filters check only the text inside guardContent blocks and skip the other content blocks. With the question inside guardContent, every analyst question still goes through the same filters at HIGH strength, and a harmful question is still blocked. The passages still reach the model, but the content filters no longer check them, so they stop causing blocks. The guardrail also processes less text on each request, which lowers its cost.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.1: "Develop comprehensive content safety systems to protect against harmful user inputs to FMs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content"

Sources:

  • Include a guardrail with the Converse API

  • GENCOST03-BP04 Annotate user input to enable cost-aware content filtering

  • Options for handling harmful content detected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

INCORRECT: Change the prompt strength of the Misconduct content filter in the guardrail from HIGH to LOW, so the attack details in the passages pass and the other categories stay at HIGH.
The Misconduct filter looks for text that seeks or gives information about criminal activity, and detailed reports on break-ins can match it. A lower strength for one category fits an app where normal user questions often match that category and a weaker check on every prompt is acceptable, for example a tool for lawyers who ask about criminal cases. But a filter's strength applies to all the prompt text that the guardrail checks, not to the passages alone. The analyst questions would get the weaker Misconduct check too, while the team must keep the same filters and strength for every question. The guardrail also still processes every passage.

INCORRECT: Switch the content filters of the guardrail to detect mode for prompts, so the guardrail notes its findings in the trace and lets each request through.
Detect mode takes no action on a finding. The guardrail lets the request through and returns what it found in the trace. Teams use it to test a new guardrail and to study false matches before they turn blocking on. Here harmful questions must still be blocked, and in detect mode the guardrail blocks nothing. It also keeps processing every passage, so the amount of text stays the same.

INCORRECT: Change the prompt strength of the Misconduct content filter in the guardrail from HIGH to NONE, so the attack details in the passages pass and the other categories stay at HIGH.
A strength of NONE turns off the Misconduct filter for prompts, and the filter's setting for model responses can stay as it is. This fits an app where the team does not need that category checked in user input, because the filter still checks the model's answers. Here the filter would stop checking the analyst questions for criminal activity, so a harmful question in that category would pass. The team wants every question checked with the same filters and strength, and it wants harmful questions blocked. The passages also stay in the text that the guardrail processes.

questions.promptHtml:
A research organization uses Amazon OpenSearch Service with the k-NN plugin to store embeddings for a massive dataset of scientific journals (100 million vectors). The current architecture relies on a single monolithic index with 5 primary shards running on 3 Data nodes. The search latency has increased to over 3 seconds, and the Data nodes frequently crash with OutOfMemory (OOM) exceptions due to the size of the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs.
Each question is about only one research area. New papers arrive every day. Each shard must keep one replica. Tests showed that compressed vectors lower recall for this collection.
Which architectural changes should the GenAI Developer implement to resolve these performance and stability issues?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A research organization uses Amazon OpenSearch Service with the k-NN plugin to store embeddings for a massive dataset of scientific journals (100 million vectors). The current architecture relies on a single monolithic index with 5 primary shards running on 3 Data nodes. The search latency has increased to over 3 seconds, and the Data nodes frequently crash with OutOfMemory (OOM) exceptions due to the size of the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs.
Each question is about only one research area. New papers arrive every day. Each shard must keep one replica. Tests showed that compressed vectors lower recall for this collection.
Which architectural changes should the GenAI Developer implement to resolve these performance and stability issues?
Select TWO.

options.text: Split the collection into separate indexes by scientific field, so each index has smaller HNSW graphs, and search only the index that matches each question's field.
Add data nodes, and reindex into a new index with more primary shards, so the HNSW graphs on each node fit in the memory that k-NN can use.
Move the vector index to UltraWarm storage, so the index data sits in Amazon S3 and the hot data nodes no longer hold its HNSW graphs.
Reindex into a new index that uses FP16 quantization for the vectors, so the HNSW graphs on each node need less memory.
Set the number of replicas on the index to zero, so each data node holds fewer copies of the HNSW graphs in its memory.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Split the collection into separate indexes by scientific field, so each index has smaller HNSW graphs, and search only the index that matches each question's field.
A multi-index design splits one large collection into smaller indexes, here one for each scientific field. When a question belongs to one field, the application searches only that index. Each query then searches a much smaller set of vectors, not all 100 million, so the search has less work to do. Each index also has its own, smaller HNSW graphs. Together with more shards on more data nodes, this change fixes both the slow searches and the crashes.

CORRECT: Add data nodes, and reindex into a new index with more primary shards, so the HNSW graphs on each node fit in the memory that k-NN can use.
The k-NN plugin keeps HNSW graphs in memory outside the Java heap. OpenSearch Service gives half of an instance's RAM to the heap, up to a heap of 32 GiB, and by default k-NN uses up to half of the other half. Here five large shards on three nodes hold graphs that do not fit, so the nodes run out of memory and crash. More data nodes add memory. More primary shards split the graphs into smaller parts that spread across those nodes. You cannot easily change the number of primary shards of an existing index, so the team reindexes into a new one. This fix keeps full-precision vectors and the replica on every shard.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.3: "Implement high-performance vector database architectures to optimize semantic search performance at scale for FM retrieval"
Example: "OpenSearch sharding strategies"

Sources:

  • k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) search in Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • UltraWarm storage for Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • Cost optimization techniques for Amazon OpenSearch Service

INCORRECT: Move the vector index to UltraWarm storage, so the index data sits in Amazon S3 and the hot data nodes no longer hold its HNSW graphs.
UltraWarm keeps index data in Amazon S3 and serves it from warm nodes at a lower cost per GiB. From version 2.17, an approximate k-NN index can move to warm storage, so this fits a vector index that users query less and no longer change. But warm indexes are read-only: you can query them and delete them, but you cannot add, update or delete documents. New papers arrive every day, so this index must stay writable in hot storage.

INCORRECT: Reindex into a new index that uses FP16 quantization for the vectors, so the HNSW graphs on each node need less memory.
FP16 quantization stores each vector value in 16 bits instead of 32, which makes the stored vectors half their size. It is a common way to fit a large vector index into less memory. Compression can lower recall, which means some of the true nearest neighbors no longer appear in the results. The organization's tests showed this loss for this collection, so compressed vectors are not an option here.

INCORRECT: Set the number of replicas on the index to zero, so each data node holds fewer copies of the HNSW graphs in its memory.
Every replica holds its own copy of the HNSW graphs, so the memory need grows with each replica. Setting replicas to zero is a real practice during a heavy bulk load, and the team turns them back on when the load ends. Here each shard must keep one replica. A replica takes over when a primary shard becomes unavailable, so with no replica, one node failure makes part of the collection unavailable.

Account numbers also appear in full, although the guardrail's sensitive information filter masks them.

questions.promptText:
A bank's assistant streams answers from a model in Amazon Bedrock to staff. An AWS Lambda function calls the ConverseStream API with a guardrail. Last month, a developer changed one guardrail setting in the request so that the first words appear sooner. Since then, a user saw two sentences of a violent reply before the answer stopped. Account numbers also appear in full, although the guardrail's sensitive information filter masks them.
The bank wants no harmful text on any screen, and account numbers masked in answers that staff still read. Text must still appear while the model writes it, but a short wait is acceptable. The team wants no new code in the function.
Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the guardrail stream processing mode to synchronous, and keep the sensitive information filter in the guardrail that masks account numbers in answers.
Set the guardrail stream processing mode to synchronous, and have the function find account numbers in each chunk with Amazon Comprehend and replace them.
Keep the guardrail stream processing mode asynchronous, and change the sensitive information filter in the guardrail to block answers that hold account numbers.
Keep the guardrail stream processing mode asynchronous, and have the function find account numbers in each chunk with Amazon Comprehend and replace them.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the guardrail stream processing mode to synchronous, and keep the sensitive information filter in the guardrail that masks account numbers in answers.
A guardrail on a streamed response works in one of two modes. In the default synchronous mode, the guardrail buffers one or more chunks and applies its policies before it sends them to the user. Each chunk waits a little longer, but no chunk reaches the screen before the guardrail scans it. Synchronous mode also supports the masking of sensitive information, so the filter that masks account numbers works again. Staff still see the answer arrive in parts while the model writes it. The change is one setting in the guardrail configuration of the ConverseStream request, so the function needs no new code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.2: "Create content safety frameworks to prevent harmful outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter responses"

Sources:

  • Configure streaming response behavior to filter content

  • GuardrailStreamConfiguration (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Detecting PII entities

INCORRECT: Set the guardrail stream processing mode to synchronous, and have the function find account numbers in each chunk with Amazon Comprehend and replace them.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection finds entities such as bank account numbers in text, and the application can then replace them. This is a good design when an application has no guardrail, or needs an entity type that its guardrail does not cover. Here synchronous mode already brings back the guardrail's own masking of account numbers. A Comprehend call on each chunk is new code in the Lambda function, and the team wants none.

INCORRECT: Keep the guardrail stream processing mode asynchronous, and change the sensitive information filter in the guardrail to block answers that hold account numbers.
In asynchronous mode, the guardrail sends each chunk as soon as it is ready and scans it in the background. It fits an app where fast first words matter more than a short exposure to unsafe text. Chunks can reach the user before the scan ends, and the guardrail blocks only the chunks after it finds a problem. That is how a user saw two violent sentences. Blocking also removes the answers that hold account numbers, but staff must still read those answers with the numbers masked.

INCORRECT: Keep the guardrail stream processing mode asynchronous, and have the function find account numbers in each chunk with Amazon Comprehend and replace them.
This keeps the mode that caused the violent sentences. Chunks can still reach the screen before the guardrail scans them, so harmful text can still appear. A team that accepts that risk for speed could hide account numbers with its own Comprehend step, because the guardrail cannot mask them in this mode. Here the bank wants no harmful text on any screen, and the Comprehend step is new code in the Lambda function.

The catalog is highly dynamic, with thousands of price updates, new product additions, and discontinued item removals occurring daily. A Generative AI shopping assistant uses Amazon OpenSearch Service to store vector embeddings of the product descriptions for semantic retrieval. Users are complaining that the assistant frequently recommends products that were removed from the catalog hours ago or fails to find newly added items. Which data maintenance system should the GenAI Developer deploy to ensure the vector store remains in sync with the catalog in near real-time?
questions.promptText:
An e-commerce company stores its product catalog in Amazon DynamoDB. The catalog is highly dynamic, with thousands of price updates, new product additions, and discontinued item removals occurring daily. A Generative AI shopping assistant uses Amazon OpenSearch Service to store vector embeddings of the product descriptions for semantic retrieval. Users are complaining that the assistant frequently recommends products that were removed from the catalog hours ago or fails to find newly added items. The current architecture relies on a nightly batch job to re-index the entire catalog. The team wants no job that runs all the time.
Which data maintenance system should the GenAI Developer deploy to ensure the vector store remains in sync with the catalog in near real-time?

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the table, and have a Lambda function embed and upsert items from INSERT and MODIFY records and delete documents for REMOVE records.
Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the table, have a Lambda function embed and upsert items from INSERT and MODIFY records, and let the nightly job remove deleted products.
Turn on Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB on the table, and have an AWS Glue streaming ETL job embed changed items and delete documents for removed items.
Keep the nightly job, and have the assistant's Lambda function check each retrieved product in DynamoDB and drop any product that no longer exists.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the table, and have a Lambda function embed and upsert items from INSERT and MODIFY records and delete documents for REMOVE records.
DynamoDB Streams records each change to an item in the table. Every stream record has an event name: INSERT for a new item, MODIFY for a changed item and REMOVE for a deleted item. With a Lambda trigger, the function receives the new records soon after each change. For INSERT and MODIFY, it creates a new embedding in Amazon Bedrock and upserts the document in OpenSearch Service. For REMOVE, it deletes the matching document. New products become searchable within moments, and removed products stop appearing in answers. The function runs only when new records arrive, so no job runs all the time.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.5: "Design and deploy data maintenance systems to ensure that vector stores contain current and accurate information for FM augmentation"
Example: "real-time change detection systems"

Sources:

  • DynamoDB Streams and AWS Lambda triggers

  • Record (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference)

  • Change data capture with Amazon DynamoDB

INCORRECT: Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the table, have a Lambda function embed and upsert items from INSERT and MODIFY records, and let the nightly job remove deleted products.
This design keeps new and changed products current in near real time, and the nightly job, which re-indexes the whole catalog, removes deleted products once a day. It fits a catalog where a removed item may stay visible until the next night. Here users complain that the assistant recommends products that were removed hours ago. Each deletion creates a REMOVE record, but this function does nothing with it, so the old vector stays in the index for up to a day.

INCORRECT: Turn on Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB on the table, and have an AWS Glue streaming ETL job embed changed items and delete documents for removed items.
Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB copies each item change, including deletes, to a Kinesis data stream in near real time, and AWS Glue streaming ETL jobs can read from Kinesis Data Streams. With a delete step in the job, this pipeline keeps the index current for new, changed and removed products. It suits a team that already runs streaming jobs with heavy transforms on high-volume data. But a Glue streaming ETL job runs continuously, and the team wants no job that runs all the time.

INCORRECT: Keep the nightly job, and have the assistant's Lambda function check each retrieved product in DynamoDB and drop any product that no longer exists.
A check against the source table at query time is a real way to hide stale results, and it can help when the index changes rarely. It adds a database lookup to every answer, and it only removes items. New products still reach the index only after the nightly job, so users still cannot find items that were added during the day.

Each file is divided into short Articles, and the header of each Article names the agreement type, such as vendor or client. The data source uses fixed-size chunks of 512 tokens. The search finds the right clause, but the chunk often lacks the Article header, so the model cannot say which agreement the clause belongs to. In a test, the model answered correctly when it received about 1,500 tokens of text around the clause, including the Article header. With larger fixed-size chunks, the search found the right clause less often.
What should the firm change in the knowledge base?

options.text: Create a new data source with hierarchical chunking, with small child chunks and parent chunks of up to 1,500 tokens, so each match returns its parent.
Create a new data source with fixed-size chunks of 1,500 tokens, so each match gives the model about 1,500 tokens of contract text.
Keep the current data source, and add a reranker model to the retrieval settings, so the chunks that best match each question rank first.
Keep the current data source, and add a metadata file with the agreement type for each contract file, so the search can filter chunks by agreement type.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a new data source with hierarchical chunking, with small child chunks and parent chunks of up to 1,500 tokens, so each match returns its parent.
Hierarchical chunking splits each document into parent chunks and smaller child chunks, with a maximum token size for each level. The search compares the question with the small child chunks, so the search still finds the right clause.

The knowledge base then replaces each matching child chunk with its parent chunk. With parents of up to 1,500 tokens, the model receives about the same amount of text around the clause as in the test. The firm can choose the chunking strategy only when it connects a data source, so this change needs a new data source.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.1: "Develop effective document segmentation approaches to optimize retrieval performance for FM context augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock chunking capabilities"

Sources:

  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases

  • Customize ingestion for a data source

INCORRECT: Create a new data source with fixed-size chunks of 1,500 tokens, so each match gives the model about 1,500 tokens of contract text.
Fixed-size chunking cuts each document into chunks of about the same number of tokens. Larger chunks give the model more text with each match, so this setting fits documents where most questions need a long passage. Here the firm already tried larger fixed-size chunks, and the search found the right clause less often. A chunk of 1,500 tokens mixes the clause with many other clauses, so a question about one clause matches that chunk less well.

INCORRECT: Keep the current data source, and add a reranker model to the retrieval settings, so the chunks that best match each question rank first.
A reranker model scores each retrieved chunk against the question and puts the most relevant chunks first. This helps when the search finds the right chunk but ranks that chunk too low. Here the search already finds the right clause. The problem is the missing Article header, and a new order cannot add text that a chunk does not contain.

INCORRECT: Keep the current data source, and add a metadata file with the agreement type for each contract file, so the search can filter chunks by agreement type.
A metadata file adds fields to one source document, and the fields apply to every chunk of that document, so a query can filter on them. This fits a value that describes the whole document, such as a year or a region. In this firm, one contract file can contain several agreements, and the header of each Article names the agreement type. One value for the whole file cannot tell the model which agreement a clause belongs to.

questions.promptText:
A media company is aggregating data for a new "Market Intelligence" RAG chatbot. The dataset consists of two distinct data types:
1. Financial News Articles: Long-form, narrative text with complex sentence structures and varying paragraph lengths.
2. Stock Ticker Logs: Structured, line-delimited text files where each line contains a timestamp, ticker symbol, and price.
Each article covers several topics. Each log line stands alone. The logs grow fast, so the team wants no model cost to chunk them.
The GenAI Developer must configure the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base ingestion to optimize retrieval relevance for both data types.
Which combination of chunking strategies should the developer apply?
Select TWO.

options.text: For the news articles, choose semantic chunking, so a foundation model sets chunk boundaries between sentences where the meaning changes, within a maximum token size.
For the ticker logs, choose fixed-size chunking with a small number of tokens per chunk, so each chunk holds only a few lines of prices.
For the news articles, choose no chunking, so each article becomes one chunk and every result gives the model the complete story.
For the ticker logs, choose hierarchical chunking, so each small child chunk that matches a question returns a larger parent chunk of log lines.
For the ticker logs, choose semantic chunking, so a foundation model sets chunk boundaries between lines where the meaning changes, within a maximum token size.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: For the news articles, choose semantic chunking, so a foundation model sets chunk boundaries between sentences where the meaning changes, within a maximum token size.
Semantic chunking splits text by meaning. It compares nearby sentences and starts a new chunk where they differ most, and it keeps each chunk under a maximum token size without cutting a sentence. The news articles are long narrative text, and each one covers several topics, so each chunk keeps one topic together. Semantic chunking uses a foundation model, so it has an extra cost. The team wants to avoid that cost only for the logs, so the news can use it.

CORRECT: For the ticker logs, choose fixed-size chunking with a small number of tokens per chunk, so each chunk holds only a few lines of prices.
Fixed-size chunking cuts text into chunks of a set number of tokens, with an overlap percentage that the team chooses. With a small size, each chunk holds only a few log lines, so a question about one ticker matches a small piece of text. Default chunking keeps whole sentences in each chunk, but fixed-size chunking gives no such promise, so the team should not expect every line to stay whole at a chunk edge. It uses no foundation model, so it adds no model cost for the large, fast-growing logs.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.1: "Develop effective document segmentation approaches to optimize retrieval performance for FM context augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock chunking capabilities"

Sources:

  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases
  • SemanticChunkingConfiguration

INCORRECT: For the news articles, choose no chunking, so each article becomes one chunk and every result gives the model the complete story.
No chunking treats each document as one chunk. It fits short documents that each cover one topic. These articles are long, and each covers several topics. One vector for a whole article matches a question about one of those topics poorly, and each result sends the whole article to the model.

INCORRECT: For the ticker logs, choose hierarchical chunking, so each small child chunk that matches a question returns a larger parent chunk of log lines.
Hierarchical chunking matches small child chunks and then replaces them with their larger parent chunks, so the model gets more context. It helps with long, structured documents where a passage needs the text around it, such as manuals or contracts. Here each log line stands alone. A parent chunk adds many lines about other tickers and other times, which gives the model more text but no more useful facts.

INCORRECT: For the ticker logs, choose semantic chunking, so a foundation model sets chunk boundaries between lines where the meaning changes, within a maximum token size.
Semantic chunking fits narrative text where the topic shifts between sentences. It uses a foundation model to find those shifts, and that model use adds a cost that depends on the amount of data. The ticker logs grow fast, and the team wants no model cost to chunk them.
