questions.promptText:
A startup is building a document search engine for a repository of 50 million legal briefs. The team plans to use Amazon OpenSearch Service as the vector store. The standard 1,536-dimensional vectors produced by their current model are driving up storage costs and increasing k-NN search latency beyond the acceptable 200ms threshold. The GenAI Developer needs to switch to a new embedding solution that reduces the vector size to 512 dimensions to optimize storage and speed, while maintaining high semantic accuracy for English text.
Which solution meets these requirements natively?

options.text: Switch to the Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 model. In the InvokeModel API call, set the dimensions parameter to 512.
Switch to the Cohere Embed English v3 model. In the InvokeModel API call, configure the truncation parameter to END to automatically shorten the vector output.

Continue using the Amazon Titan Embeddings G1 - Text model. Implement an AWS Lambda function to post-process the embeddings using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality to 512 before indexing.
Switch to the Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 model. In the InvokeModel API call, set embeddingConfig.outputEmbeddingLength to 512 to produce compact text embeddings for the legal brief corpus.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Switch to the Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 model. In the InvokeModel API call, set the dimensions parameter to 512.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 has a dimensions parameter in the InvokeModel request. It accepts 1,024, which is the default, 512 or 256. With the parameter set to 512, the model returns vectors with 512 values, so the index stores smaller vectors and each k-NN search compares fewer values. The model makes the smaller vectors itself, so the team adds no step after embedding and keeps a managed model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.2: "Select and configure optimal embedding solutions to create efficient vector representations for semantic search"
Example: "Amazon Titan embeddings based on dimensionality and domain fit"

Sources:

  • Amazon Titan Embeddings G1, Text
  • Cohere Embed v3
  • Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1

INCORRECT: Switch to the Cohere Embed English v3 model. In the InvokeModel API call, configure the truncation parameter to END to automatically shorten the vector output.
Cohere Embed English v3 is a real English embedding model on Amazon Bedrock. Its truncate setting controls what happens when an input text is longer than the model accepts: END drops the end of the text, START drops the start, and NONE returns an error. The setting changes the input, not the vector. Embed English v3 returns vectors with 1,024 values, so this setting cannot give the 512-dimension vectors that the team needs.

INCORRECT: Continue using the Amazon Titan Embeddings G1 - Text model. Implement an AWS Lambda function to post-process the embeddings using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality to 512 before indexing.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a real math method that reduces the number of dimensions in a set of vectors. Here the team would have to build the PCA model, run it in a custom Lambda function on every vector, and keep the model current as the data changes. That adds latency and upkeep. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 already returns 512-dimension vectors when the team sets one parameter, so the extra step is not needed.

INCORRECT: Switch to the Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 model. In the InvokeModel API call, set embeddingConfig.outputEmbeddingLength to 512 to produce compact text embeddings for the legal brief corpus.
Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 embeds text, images or both, and its outputEmbeddingLength setting picks the vector size. The accepted values are 256, 384 and 1,024, with 1,024 as the default. 512 is not one of them, so this request cannot return the vectors that the team needs. The model fits search across images and text. For this text-only repository, Titan Text Embeddings V2 gives 512 dimensions with one parameter.

questions.promptHtml:
An insurance company builds a claims assistant on a model in Amazon Bedrock. An AWS Lambda function sends each claim note to the model, and the model drafts a letter to the customer. Company policy says that customer names and policy numbers must never reach the model.
The claims agent who sends the letter must see the real name and policy number in the draft. A quality team reads every draft in a log and must never learn who the customer is. Any data that links a customer to a draft must be encrypted with a key that the company controls.
Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company builds a claims assistant on a model in Amazon Bedrock. An AWS Lambda function sends each claim note to the model, and the model drafts a letter to the customer. Company policy says that customer names and policy numbers must never reach the model.
The claims agent who sends the letter must see the real name and policy number in the draft. A quality team reads every draft in a log and must never learn who the customer is. Any data that links a customer to a draft must be encrypted with a key that the company controls.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: A Lambda function swaps each name and policy number for a random token, stores the token map in DynamoDB under a customer managed KMS key, and restores values only for the agent.
A Lambda function swaps each name and policy number for a salted SHA-256 hash, stores the hashed notes in DynamoDB under a customer managed KMS key, and sends each draft to both.
A guardrail masks each name and policy number in the note before the model call, and the function sends the same masked draft to the agent and to the log.
The function sends the note unchanged, passes the model's draft to the agent, and masks each name and policy number in the log copy with the ApplyGuardrail API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A Lambda function swaps each name and policy number for a random token, stores the token map in DynamoDB under a customer managed KMS key, and restores values only for the agent.
This is reversible pseudonymization, also called tokenization. Before the model call, the function replaces each name and policy number with a random token, so the model never receives the real values. The token map is the only link between a token and a customer. The function keeps it in a DynamoDB table that is encrypted with a customer managed key in AWS KMS, a key that the company creates, owns and controls. The log keeps the draft with tokens, so the quality team never learns who the customer is. For the agent's copy, the function looks up each token and puts the real values back, so the letter is ready to send.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.3: "Create privacy-focused AI systems to protect user privacy while maintaining FM utility and effectiveness"
Example: "anonymization strategies for sensitive information"

Sources:

  • Integrate tokenization with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for secure data handling

  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters

  • DynamoDB encryption at rest

INCORRECT: A Lambda function swaps each name and policy number for a salted SHA-256 hash, stores the hashed notes in DynamoDB under a customer managed KMS key, and sends each draft to both.
A salted hash turns each value into a fixed string that nobody can turn back into the original value. It is a good choice when analysts need a stable pseudonym to count or join records but must never learn who the customer is. Here the claims agent must see the real name and policy number in the draft. A one-way hash cannot give those values back, so the agent's letter would hold hash strings instead of the customer's details.

INCORRECT: A guardrail masks each name and policy number in the note before the model call, and the function sends the same masked draft to the agent and to the log.
A sensitive information filter with the mask action replaces each detected value with its type, such as {NAME}, before the model sees it, and a regular expression filter can catch policy numbers. This fits an app where nobody needs the real values later. The masked note holds only the placeholder, so the model can only write {NAME} into the draft. The agent would get a draft full of placeholders, not a letter with the customer's name and policy number.

INCORRECT: The function sends the note unchanged, passes the model's draft to the agent, and masks each name and policy number in the log copy with the ApplyGuardrail API.
The ApplyGuardrail API checks any text against a guardrail without calling a model, so it can mask a copy of the draft for the log. This is a real pattern when the model may see personal data but a second audience must not. The agent gets the real values, and the quality team does not. But company policy says names and policy numbers must never reach the model, and this design sends them in every call.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A technical support chatbot uses a RAG architecture with Amazon OpenSearch Service as the vector store. Users frequently ask queries containing specific error codes and product model numbers (e.g., "How to fix Error 523 on the AC-900 unit?"). The current system uses pure semantic search (k-NN). It often retrieves documents describing "generic connection errors" or manuals for the wrong device model (e.g., "AC-800") because they are semantically similar to the query. The GenAI Developer needs to modify the retrieval architecture to prioritize exact matches for the specific codes while maintaining the semantic understanding of the problem description.
Which architectural update should the developer implement?
questions.promptText:
A technical support chatbot uses a RAG architecture with Amazon OpenSearch Service as the vector store. Users frequently ask queries containing specific error codes and product model numbers (e.g., "How to fix Error 523 on the AC-900 unit?"). The current system uses pure semantic search (k-NN). It often retrieves documents describing "generic connection errors" or manuals for the wrong device model (e.g., "AC-800") because they are semantically similar to the query. The GenAI Developer needs to modify the retrieval architecture to prioritize exact matches for the specific codes while maintaining the semantic understanding of the problem description.
Which architectural update should the developer implement?

options.text: Configure the OpenSearch index for Hybrid Search by combining the k-NN vector score with a BM25 keyword score. Then apply an Amazon Bedrock Rerank model to re-score the retrieved candidate documents.
Upgrade to Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and set the dimensions parameter to 1,024 to capture more granular semantic nuances of the product codes and error identifiers before re-indexing.

Implement Query Expansion using an Amazon Bedrock LLM. Prompt the model to generate five variations of the user's query (e.g., "AC-900 troubleshooting"), retrieve vectors for all variations, and aggregate the results.

Use Amazon Comprehend to extract the "Product Code" entities from the user's query. Rewrite the OpenSearch query to use a strictly boolean term filter for the product code, disabling vector search for queries that contain numbers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Configure the OpenSearch index for Hybrid Search by combining the k-NN vector score with a BM25 keyword score. Then apply an Amazon Bedrock Rerank model to re-score the retrieved candidate documents.
Hybrid search runs a keyword query and a vector query together. OpenSearch Service scores the keyword query with BM25, normalizes both sets of scores in a search pipeline, and combines them. The keyword part rewards documents that contain the exact terms in the question, such as "523" and "AC-900", and the vector part still matches the meaning of "how to fix". A reranker model in Amazon Bedrock then scores each retrieved document against the question and reorders the list, so the most relevant manual section comes first.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.4: "Create advanced search architectures to improve the relevance and accuracy of retrieved information for FM context"
Example: "hybrid search that combines keywords and vectors"

Sources:

  • Hybrid Search with Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • Improve the relevance of query responses with a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Upgrade to Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and set the dimensions parameter to 1,024 to capture more granular semantic nuances of the product codes and error identifiers before re-indexing.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 returns 1,024 dimensions at most, so this change only picks the model's largest size. More dimensions do not change what an embedding does: it places texts with similar meaning close together. "AC-900" and "AC-800" are similar product names in similar manuals, so their vectors stay close. Only keyword matching rewards the exact code that the user typed.

INCORRECT: Implement Query Expansion using an Amazon Bedrock LLM. Prompt the model to generate five variations of the user's query (e.g., "AC-900 troubleshooting"), retrieve vectors for all variations, and aggregate the results.
Query expansion asks a model to write several versions of the user's question, and the search runs each version and combines the results. It helps when the right document uses other words than the user, so a single query misses it. Here the search already finds documents, but the wrong ones: manuals for the AC-800 instead of the AC-900. Each new version still runs as a semantic search, so it can bring back more manuals for similar models instead of the exact code.

INCORRECT: Use Amazon Comprehend to extract the "Product Code" entities from the user's query. Rewrite the OpenSearch query to use a strictly boolean term filter for the product code, disabling vector search for queries that contain numbers.
Amazon Comprehend has no built-in entity type for a product code. Its built-in types include COMMERCIAL_ITEM, a branded product, so the team would need to train a custom entity recognizer to extract codes such as "AC-900". A term filter on the product code is a good way to force exact matches. But this option also turns off vector search for every question that contains a number, so the search loses the meaning of the symptom. The user might get the AC-900 manual, but not the section about Error 523.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare startup operates a patient support chatbot using a RAG architecture with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. Patients frequently submit complex, multi-part queries such as: "What are the common side effects of Lisinopril, and is it safe to take with the Ibuprofen I use for my arthritis?" The current system performs a single semantic search, which often retrieves documents about "Lisinopril side effects" but fails to retrieve specific documents regarding "Drug Interactions" or "Ibuprofen contraindications," leading to incomplete safety warnings. The top 50 results hold no interaction document. The documents use clinical terms, while patients use everyday words.
Which advanced query handling strategies should the GenAI Developer implement to ensure comprehensive retrieval for such queries?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A healthcare startup operates a patient support chatbot using a RAG architecture with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. Patients frequently submit complex, multi-part queries such as: "What are the common side effects of Lisinopril, and is it safe to take with the Ibuprofen I use for my arthritis?" The current system performs a single semantic search, which often retrieves documents about "Lisinopril side effects" but fails to retrieve specific documents regarding "Drug Interactions" or "Ibuprofen contraindications," leading to incomplete safety warnings. The top 50 results hold no interaction document. The documents use clinical terms, while patients use everyday words.
Which advanced query handling strategies should the GenAI Developer implement to ensure comprehensive retrieval for such queries?
Select TWO.

options.text: Use a model in Amazon Bedrock to split each patient question into separate sub-questions, run one search for each sub-question, and merge the retrieved chunks.
Use a model in Amazon Bedrock to add clinical terms and synonyms to the words of each patient question, and run the search with both sets of terms.
Use a model in Amazon Bedrock to rewrite each patient question as one clear query that holds both intents, and run one search with that query.
Send the results of the single search to a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock, so the chunks that best match each patient question reach the prompt first.
Raise the number of results that the single search returns, so more chunks from more documents reach the prompt for each patient question.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use a model in Amazon Bedrock to split each patient question into separate sub-questions, run one search for each sub-question, and merge the retrieved chunks.
This is query decomposition. The patient asks two things in one message: the side effects of one drug, and whether two drugs are safe together. A single search turns the whole message into one vector, and that vector is most similar to the side effects documents. A model in Amazon Bedrock splits the message into sub-questions, and each sub-question gets its own search. The interaction question then finds the interaction documents. The application merges the chunks from all the searches into one context for the answer.

CORRECT: Use a model in Amazon Bedrock to add clinical terms and synonyms to the words of each patient question, and run the search with both sets of terms.
This is query expansion. The documents use clinical terms such as NSAIDs and osteoarthritis, but patients write ibuprofen and arthritis. Before the search, a model in Amazon Bedrock adds the clinical terms and close synonyms to the patient's own words. The search then also matches the words that the documents use, so a document that names only the drug class can appear in the results.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.5: "Develop sophisticated query handling systems to improve the retrieval effectiveness and result quality for FM augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock for query expansion"

Sources:

  • Configure and customize queries and response generation
  • Improve the relevance of query responses with a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Use a model in Amazon Bedrock to rewrite each patient question as one clear query that holds both intents, and run one search with that query.
Query rewriting turns a vague or chatty message into one clear query. It works well when the patient asks one thing in unclear words. This message holds two separate needs. One rewritten query still becomes one vector, and that one vector is still most similar to only one of the two topics. The interaction documents stay out of the results, as they do today.

INCORRECT: Send the results of the single search to a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock, so the chunks that best match each patient question reach the prompt first.
A reranker model scores each retrieved chunk against the question and puts the best chunks first. It helps when the right chunks are in the results but sit too low in the list. Here, even the top 50 results hold no interaction document. A reranker can only reorder what the search returns. It cannot add documents that the search never found.

INCORRECT: Raise the number of results that the single search returns, so more chunks from more documents reach the prompt for each patient question.
More results help when the right chunks rank just below the cutoff. The question says that even the top 50 results hold no interaction document. The one search vector is most similar to the side effects documents, so more results from the same search bring more chunks on that topic. They do not bring the interaction documents.

questions.promptHtml:

1. The agent must autonomously decide whether to use a Vector Search (for general market trends) or a Keyword Search (for specific stock tickers).
2. The agent must be able to apply dynamic date filters (e.g., "reports from last week") based on the user's natural language query.
3. The developer wants to avoid complex "Prompt Engineering" to parse these parameters and instead use a structured interface supported natively by the model.
Which integration pattern meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A financial services company is building a "Research Assistant" agent using Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The agent needs to retrieve information from a secure Amazon OpenSearch Service vector store. However, the search requirements are complex:
1. The agent must autonomously decide whether to use a Vector Search (for general market trends) or a Keyword Search (for specific stock tickers).
2. The agent must be able to apply dynamic date filters (e.g., "reports from last week") based on the user's natural language query.
3. The developer wants to avoid complex "Prompt Engineering" to parse these parameters and instead use a structured interface supported natively by the model.
Which integration pattern meets these requirements?

options.text: Define a search tool in the Converse toolConfig with inputs for the query, a vector or keyword search type and a date range, and run each tool request on OpenSearch Service.
Run an MCP server on AWS Lambda with one search tool whose single input is the query text, and let the server choose vector or keyword search from the words in each query.
Tell the model in the system prompt to write an OpenSearch query in JSON, and have the application send the returned text to the index as the search request.
Move the reports into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and have the application add a date filter to each Retrieve call with a fixed rule in its own code.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Define a search tool in the Converse toolConfig with inputs for the query, a vector or keyword search type and a date range, and run each tool request on OpenSearch Service.
Tool use gives the model a structured way to ask for a search. The tool definition in toolConfig holds a JSON schema with three inputs: the query text, a search type with two allowed values, and a date range. The model reads the user's question and fills these inputs, so the model itself chooses between vector and keyword search and turns "last week" into dates. The model then stops with the tool_use stop reason. The application runs the search on OpenSearch Service and returns the results to the model in a toolResult block, so no free text needs parsing.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.6: "Create consistent access mechanisms to enable seamless integration with FMs"
Example: "function calling interfaces for vector search"

Sources:

  • Call a tool with the Converse API
  • Configure and customize queries and response generation

INCORRECT: Run an MCP server on AWS Lambda with one search tool whose single input is the query text, and let the server choose vector or keyword search from the words in each query.
An MCP server on AWS Lambda is a good way to give many agents the same search tool. This tool has one input, the query text, and the server's own code picks the search type. The first requirement says that the agent must make that choice. The model never sees a search type here, so the server code, not the model, decides between vector and keyword search.

INCORRECT: Tell the model in the system prompt to write an OpenSearch query in JSON, and have the application send the returned text to the index as the search request.
Asking a model to write a search query in JSON is a real text-to-query practice, and it can work for a quick prototype. The developer here wants to avoid prompt work that parses parameters, and wants a structured interface that the model supports natively. With this design, the application must check and parse free text from the model before it can run any search.

INCORRECT: Move the reports into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and have the application add a date filter to each Retrieve call with a fixed rule in its own code.
A metadata filter on a Retrieve call fits an application that knows the right dates in advance, for example "only reports from this quarter". Here the dates come from the user's own words, and the agent must set them. The fixed rule in the application code also leaves the model with no way to choose between vector and keyword search for each question.

The compliance team wants these questions checked outside the model. Each week, the product team, which has no engineers, changes the assistant's persona and output format. The product team must test each change on the model and read the answers before users see the change. Which TWO actions meet these requirements?

Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A financial technology company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock for a spending assistant in its banking app. The company has no license to give tax or legal advice, so the assistant must refuse questions about tax advice and legal liability. The compliance team wants these questions checked outside the model. Each week, the product team, which has no engineers, changes the assistant's persona and output format. The product team must test each change on the model and read the answers before users see the change. The application reads the prompt version from a setting that the product team can change, so a weekly change needs no new code.
Which TWO actions meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create a guardrail in Amazon Bedrock with denied topics for tax advice and legal liability, and apply it to the user questions and the model answers.
Keep the persona and output format in a Prompt Management prompt, let the product team test each draft in the console, and create a new version.
Keep the persona and output format in a freeform profile in AWS AppConfig, and let the product team edit and deploy each new version from the console.
Add a rule to the Prompt Management prompt that tells the model to refuse tax and legal questions, and keep that rule in every new version.
Create a guardrail in Amazon Bedrock with a word filter for tax and legal phrases, and apply it to the user questions and the model answers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a guardrail in Amazon Bedrock with denied topics for tax advice and legal liability, and apply it to the user questions and the model answers.
A denied topic has a name, a short definition in plain language, and optional sample phrases. The guardrail checks both the user's prompt and the model's response against each denied topic, and it returns a blocked message when it detects one. The guardrail judges the meaning of the text against the definition, not a list of exact words. So it can block a question about tax or legal matters even when the user writes none of the words in the definition. A clear and precise definition helps the guardrail detect more of these questions. A guardrail can still miss a new or unusual wording, so the team tests the variations of these questions that it expects users to ask.

CORRECT: Keep the persona and output format in a Prompt Management prompt, let the product team test each draft in the console, and create a new version.
Prompt Management keeps the persona and the output format in a prompt outside the application code. In the console, the product team runs each draft against the model in the test window and reads the answers. When the answers are right, the team creates a version, which is a fixed snapshot of the prompt. The application calls the model with the ARN of a prompt version, and the application reads that ARN from the setting. So the product team puts the new version in the setting, and no engineer deploys new code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.1: "Create effective model instruction frameworks to control FM behavior and outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce responsible AI guidelines"

Sources:

  • Block denied topics to help remove harmful content

  • Test a prompt using Prompt management

  • Remove a specific list of words and phrases from conversations with word filters

INCORRECT: Keep the persona and output format in a freeform profile in AWS AppConfig, and let the product team edit and deploy each new version from the console.
AWS AppConfig can store text such as a prompt in a freeform configuration profile, and the application reads the new value at run time without a code deployment. This fits a team that only needs to change and release the wording safely. Here the product team must test each change on the model and read the answers before users see the change. AppConfig stores, validates and deploys the text, but AppConfig does not run the text against a model.

INCORRECT: Add a rule to the Prompt Management prompt that tells the model to refuse tax and legal questions, and keep that rule in every new version.
An instruction in the prompt that tells the model to refuse a subject is a common first step for low-risk subjects. The model follows the instruction most of the time, but nothing outside the model checks the question or the answer. So this option gives the compliance team no check outside the model. The product team also changes this prompt every week, and one edit can weaken or drop the rule.

INCORRECT: Create a guardrail in Amazon Bedrock with a word filter for tax and legal phrases, and apply it to the user questions and the model answers.
Word filters in a guardrail block exact words and phrases in prompts and responses. They fit a fixed list, such as competitor names or banned terms. The assistant must refuse questions about tax advice and legal liability, and users can ask such questions in many different words. A question such as "how much will I owe the government this year" contains none of the listed phrases, so the filter lets it through.

The chatbot must decide from the customer's first message whether the claim is Auto, Home, or Life, before it asks anything else. A message such as "Water came through my kitchen ceiling last night" names no claim type. The company keeps 20,000 past customer messages, each labeled with its claim type. Each claim type has a fixed checklist of questions, for example about the date of the incident and the policy number. The chatbot must ask these questions one at a time, and customers can take hours to reply. The design must track which details each customer has already given.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Label each message with an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier, and run an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that branches by claim type and waits for each reply with a task token.
Label each message with an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier, and run an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that branches by claim type and uses a Wait state before it reads each reply.
Label each message with an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier, and run an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that branches by claim type and asks for all missing details in one message.
Keep the collected claim fields in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and have an AWS Lambda function ask a model in Amazon Bedrock which missing detail to request in each turn.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Label each message with an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier, and run an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that branches by claim type and waits for each reply with a task token.
Amazon Comprehend custom classification trains a model, called a classifier, on example documents for each class. Here the company trains the classifier on its 20,000 past messages, each labeled with its claim type. The classifier then gives each first message a claim type, such as Home for the message about the kitchen ceiling. A Choice state in the workflow branches by that type, so each type follows its own checklist. For each question, a task uses the waitForTaskToken pattern: the workflow sends one question and pauses until the application returns the token with SendTaskSuccess after the customer replies. The workflow state keeps the details collected so far, with no servers to manage.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.2: "Build interactive AI systems to maintain context and improve user interactions with FMs"
Example: "Step Functions for clarification workflows"

Sources:

  • Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions

  • Custom classification

  • Choice workflow state

INCORRECT: Label each message with an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier, and run an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that branches by claim type and uses a Wait state before it reads each reply.
A Wait state pauses a workflow for a set number of seconds or until a set time. It fits a step that must wait a known period, such as a delay before a reminder. Customers here can take hours to reply, and nobody knows the time in advance. A fixed wait either ends before the reply arrives or keeps a fast customer waiting. The workflow must pause until the reply itself arrives.

INCORRECT: Label each message with an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier, and run an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that branches by claim type and asks for all missing details in one message.
A single message that asks for every missing detail suits a short web form, where the customer sees all fields at once. This design still classifies the claim and branches by type. But the chatbot must ask the checklist questions one at a time, and one message with every question breaks that requirement.

INCORRECT: Keep the collected claim fields in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and have an AWS Lambda function ask a model in Amazon Bedrock which missing detail to request in each turn.
A DynamoDB table that keeps the collected fields, with a model that picks the next question, is a flexible design for open conversations. Here each claim type has a fixed checklist of questions. When a model decides what to ask next, the order and the wording can change from one conversation to the next, so nothing makes the chatbot follow the checklist. A Choice state in Step Functions applies the same rule every time.

A large banking institution is scaling its use of Generative AI across multiple departments (Marketing, Fraud, Customer Support). The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) has identified two critical governance gaps:
1. Inconsistency: Different teams are using slightly different versions of the "Standard Banking Tone" system prompt, leading to brand misalignment.
2. Lack of Oversight: There is no audit trail to determine who modified a prompt or which specific prompt version was used to generate a loan denial explanation on a specific date.
The bank already keeps an AWS CloudTrail trail of all management events in every account.
Which combination of actions should the GenAI Developer take to implement a robust governance system?
Select TWO.

options.text: Keep the banking tone in one Prompt Management prompt, and have every team call the ARN of the same published version of that prompt.
Keep a copy of the banking tone in a Prompt Management prompt for each team, and have each team call the ARN of its own published version.
Keep the banking tone in one Prompt Management prompt, and have every team use its working draft so each team gets the newest text at once.
Turn on model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs with a retention period, and send the prompt version ARN in the requestMetadata of each call.
Create a new CloudTrail trail for the Amazon Bedrock management events, and keep its log files in Amazon S3 for the full audit period.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Keep the banking tone in one Prompt Management prompt, and have every team call the ARN of the same published version of that prompt.
Prompt Management stores the banking tone as one prompt. A published version is a fixed snapshot that later edits do not change. When every team passes the ARN of the same version as the modelId of its Converse call, every department sends the same approved text, and the tone stays consistent. The bank's existing CloudTrail trail records the Amazon Bedrock API calls that change or publish a prompt as management events, which shows who modified a prompt and when.

CORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs with a retention period, and send the prompt version ARN in the requestMetadata of each call.
Model invocation logging writes one entry for each call, with the time, the caller's identity, the request body and the model's response. The requestMetadata field adds the caller's own key-value pairs to that entry, and the application sets one pair to the prompt version ARN. For any loan denial explanation, the bank finds the entry by date, reads the text that the model wrote, and sees which prompt version produced it. A retention period on the log group keeps the entries for the whole audit cycle.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.3: "Implement comprehensive prompt management and governance systems to ensure consistency and oversight of FM operations"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create parameterized templates and approval workflows"

Sources:

  • Converse
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail

INCORRECT: Keep a copy of the banking tone in a Prompt Management prompt for each team, and have each team call the ARN of its own published version.
A separate prompt for each team fits departments that need different instructions, for example a formal tone for Fraud and a friendly tone for Marketing. Here the gap is that teams already use slightly different versions of one standard tone. Separate copies keep that drift, because each team can edit and publish its own copy, and the texts move apart again.

INCORRECT: Keep the banking tone in one Prompt Management prompt, and have every team use its working draft so each team gets the newest text at once.
The working draft is where a team edits and tests a prompt in the console before it creates a version. It changes with every edit and keeps no snapshot. Teams that use the draft at different times get different text, so the inconsistency returns. The bank also cannot show what the draft said on the date of a past loan denial.

INCORRECT: Create a new CloudTrail trail for the Amazon Bedrock management events, and keep its log files in Amazon S3 for the full audit period.
A CloudTrail trail records who called which AWS API and when, and it is the first step for an audit in an account that has none. This bank already keeps a trail of all management events in every account, and that trail already records the Amazon Bedrock calls. A new trail repeats the same records. It adds no link between a loan denial explanation and the prompt version that wrote it.

The engineer is writing a Python client application using boto3 to generate text responses from this endpoint. The client already puts each user message into the Llama chat template as one text string.
When calling the invoke_endpoint API, which request body works for this endpoint?

options.text: A JSON body with an inputs key that holds the templated text, and a parameters object with max_new_tokens and temperature, sent as application/json.
A JSON body with a prompt key that holds the templated text, and top-level max_gen_len and temperature fields, sent as application/json.
A JSON body with a messages list of role and content blocks, and an inferenceConfig object with maxTokens and temperature, sent as application/json.
A CSV body with one row of comma-separated feature values for each record, in the training order, sent as text/csv.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A JSON body with an inputs key that holds the templated text, and a parameters object with max_new_tokens and temperature, sent as application/json.
JumpStart deploys Meta Llama models with a request format that takes an inputs string and an optional parameters object. The inputs string holds the prompt, here the text that the client already put into the Llama chat template. The parameters object holds generation settings such as max_new_tokens, temperature and top_p. The client passes this body to invoke_endpoint with the application/json content type.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.3: "Format input data for FM inference according to model-specific requirements"
Example: "structured data preparation for SageMaker AI endpoints"

Sources:

  • Llama 3.1 models are now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
  • Common data formats for inference
  • Meta Llama models

INCORRECT: A JSON body with a prompt key that holds the templated text, and top-level max_gen_len and temperature fields, sent as application/json.
This is the request body for Meta Llama models when an application calls InvokeModel on Amazon Bedrock. There, prompt holds the text and max_gen_len sets the longest output. This engineer calls invoke_endpoint on a SageMaker AI endpoint that JumpStart deployed, and that endpoint reads the inputs and parameters keys.

INCORRECT: A JSON body with a messages list of role and content blocks, and an inferenceConfig object with maxTokens and temperature, sent as application/json.
This is the shape of a Converse request on Amazon Bedrock: a list of messages with roles and content blocks, and inferenceConfig for settings such as maxTokens. Converse is an Amazon Bedrock API. The engineer calls a SageMaker AI endpoint with invoke_endpoint, and the client already holds one templated text string, not a list of messages.

INCORRECT: A CSV body with one row of comma-separated feature values for each record, in the training order, sent as text/csv.
The text/csv format is the request format of many SageMaker AI built-in algorithms, such as XGBoost, where each row holds the feature values of one record. It fits a tabular model that predicts from numbers. A text generation model needs the prompt text and its generation settings in a JSON body.

Recruiters still find ads that link a role to one age group or gender, such as "a young and energetic team" or "he will lead the sales team". Most of these phrases praise a group and attack or insult no one, and the wording changes with each prompt version. No staff can read ads for this check.
What should the team change?
questions.promptText:
A recruiting company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write job ads from short notes that hiring managers enter. Every week, before a new prompt version goes live, the team runs an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job with a judge model on 500 saved notes. The job uses the built-in Harmfulness metric, and every version passes.
Recruiters still find ads that link a role to one age group or gender, such as "a young and energetic team" or "he will lead the sales team". Most of these phrases praise a group and attack or insult no one, and the wording changes with each prompt version. No staff can read ads for this check.
What should the team change?

options.text: Add the built-in Stereotyping metric to the weekly evaluation job, and compare its score for each new prompt version with the score of the current version.
Move the weekly evaluation job to a larger judge model, and keep the Harmfulness metric and the team's passing score for each new prompt version.
Add the phrases that recruiters found to a word filter in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail, and block each ad that contains one of them before it is published.
Set the Hate content filter in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to high strength for model responses, and block each ad that the filter flags before it is published.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the built-in Stereotyping metric to the weekly evaluation job, and compare its score for each new prompt version with the score of the current version.
The built-in Stereotyping metric asks the judge model whether a response contains stereotypes of any kind, positive or negative. That matches phrases such as "a young and energetic team", which praise one age group. The job still runs on the same 500 saved notes with no staff reading the ads, and the judge explains how it scored each response. When the team compares the score of each new prompt version with the score of the current one, it sees before release whether a change makes the ads more or less biased.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.2: "Apply fairness evaluations to ensure unbiased FM outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock with LLM-as-a-judge solutions to perform automated model evaluations"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand model performance
  • Evaluate model performance using another LLM as a judge
  • Block harmful words and conversations with content filters

INCORRECT: Move the weekly evaluation job to a larger judge model, and keep the Harmfulness metric and the team's passing score for each new prompt version.
A stronger judge model helps when the judge misses content that the metric is meant to find. Here the metric itself is the problem. Harmfulness checks whether a response contains harmful content, and most of these phrases praise a group and attack or insult no one. A larger judge that applies the same metric can still rate these ads as harmless, so each version keeps passing.

INCORRECT: Add the phrases that recruiters found to a word filter in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail, and block each ad that contains one of them before it is published.
A word filter blocks exact words and phrases, which fits a fixed list of terms that must never appear. The wording of the ads changes with each prompt version, so next week's ads can link a role to a group in words that are not on the list. The filter also works at run time and gives no score to compare prompt versions before release.

INCORRECT: Set the Hate content filter in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to high strength for model responses, and block each ad that the filter flags before it is published.
The Hate content filter detects text that discriminates against, criticizes, insults, denounces or dehumanizes a person or group because of an identity, such as gender, religion or national origin. A higher strength also blocks text that the filter marks as hate with low confidence, which helps when hateful text gets through at a lower strength. Most of these phrases praise a group and attack or insult no one, so the filter can mark them as harmless and let them pass at any strength. The filter also gives no score to compare one prompt version with the current one.

questions.promptHtml:
A utility company is developing a "Grid Balancing Assistant" to automate decisions on activating backup gas turbines. To make a safe and accurate Go/No-Go decision, the AI must follow a strict multi-step protocol:
1. Retrieve real-time weather forecasts for the region.
2. Calculate expected solar output based on cloud cover data.
3. Query the SCADA system for current battery storage levels.
4. Compare total projected supply against demand to determine if the turbine is needed.
Initial tests using a single prompt reveal that the model frequently hallucinates the solar calculation or ignores the battery storage data entirely.
Which architectural implementations should a GenAI Developer use to enforce structured reasoning and ensure the model accurately executes this complex workflow?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A utility company is developing a "Grid Balancing Assistant" to automate decisions on activating backup gas turbines. To make a safe and accurate Go/No-Go decision, the AI must follow a strict multi-step protocol:
1. Retrieve real-time weather forecasts for the region.
2. Calculate expected solar output based on cloud cover data.
3. Query the SCADA system for current battery storage levels.
4. Compare total projected supply against demand to determine if the turbine is needed.
Initial tests using a single prompt reveal that the model frequently hallucinates the solar calculation or ignores the battery storage data entirely.
Which architectural implementations should a GenAI Developer use to enforce structured reasoning and ensure the model accurately executes this complex workflow?
Select TWO.

options.text: Build an AWS Step Functions state machine with one state for each protocol step, and pass the checked output of each state to the next until the decision state.
Run a ReAct loop where the model writes a thought and a tool call for each step, and the application ends the loop after all four tool results exist.
Run a ReAct loop where the model writes a thought and a tool call for each step, and the application ends the loop when the model stops asking for tools.
Build an Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows flow with four prompt nodes for weather, solar output, battery storage and the decision, each passing its text to the next node.
Sync the SCADA readings and weather data into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and use RetrieveAndGenerate to write the decision from similar past readings.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Build an AWS Step Functions state machine with one state for each protocol step, and pass the checked output of each state to the next until the decision state.
A Step Functions state machine runs each protocol step as its own state, in a fixed order. A Lambda task can call the weather service and the SCADA system, and a task can call InvokeModel on Amazon Bedrock through the optimized integration. The decision state runs only after the earlier states return their output, and a Choice state can end the run when a value is missing. The model cannot skip the battery check, because the state machine, not the model, decides which step runs next.

CORRECT: Run a ReAct loop where the model writes a thought and a tool call for each step, and the application ends the loop after all four tool results exist.
ReAct mixes reasoning with tool calls. The model writes a thought, asks for a tool, reads the tool result as an observation, and continues. Here the application owns the stop rule. It keeps the loop going until the results of all four required tools exist, and only then does it accept a decision. Each observation gives the model real sensor data, so the model does not invent the solar numbers.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.2: "Create advanced problem-solving systems to give FMs the ability to break down and solve complex problems by following structured reasoning steps"
Example: "Step Functions to implement ReAct patterns and chain-of-thought reasoning approaches"

Sources:

  • Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions
  • Choice workflow state
  • Node types for your flow

INCORRECT: Run a ReAct loop where the model writes a thought and a tool call for each step, and the application ends the loop when the model stops asking for tools.
This loop lets the model decide when it has enough information. That works for open research tasks, where the model should stop as soon as it can answer. This protocol is strict and needs all four checks, and tests already show that the model ignores the battery data. The model can stop asking for tools after two checks, and this loop accepts its decision.

INCORRECT: Build an Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows flow with four prompt nodes for weather, solar output, battery storage and the decision, each passing its text to the next node.
A flow with only prompt nodes fits a chain of text steps, such as a draft followed by an edit. A prompt node sends a prompt to a model and passes the answer on. None of these four nodes calls the weather service or the SCADA system, so each model guesses the numbers, which is the problem that the tests found. The flow would need Lambda function nodes to fetch the live data.

INCORRECT: Sync the SCADA readings and weather data into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and use RetrieveAndGenerate to write the decision from similar past readings.
A knowledge base finds stored text that is similar to a question, which fits a search for past incidents or reports. The decision needs today's forecast, the current battery level and a solar calculation. Similar past readings are not current readings, and retrieval does not calculate anything.

A logistics company has deployed an autonomous GenAI agent responsible for rescheduling delayed shipments. The agent uses tools to query driver availability and update delivery routes in a DynamoDB table.
During a recent outage, the agent entered a failure loop: it repeatedly called the "GetDriverAvailability" tool for the same Order ID thousands of times, one call after another, incurring significant API costs. Additionally, the security team is concerned that the agent currently has the ability to modify routes for "Class-A Restricted" government cargo, which should be strictly off-limits to AI automation.
Which combination of mechanisms should the developer implement to safeguard the agent's behavior and enforce these constraints?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A logistics company has deployed an autonomous GenAI agent responsible for rescheduling delayed shipments. The agent uses tools to query driver availability and update delivery routes in a DynamoDB table.
During a recent outage, the agent entered a failure loop: it repeatedly called the "GetDriverAvailability" tool for the same Order ID thousands of times, one call after another, incurring significant API costs. Additionally, the security team is concerned that the agent currently has the ability to modify routes for "Class-A Restricted" government cargo, which should be strictly off-limits to AI automation.
Which combination of mechanisms should the developer implement to safeguard the agent's behavior and enforce these constraints?
Select TWO.

options.text: Run the agent's tool calls through an AWS Step Functions state machine that counts the calls for each Order ID and moves to a Fail state above a set limit.
Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the routes table, and have a Lambda function undo any update that the agent makes to a route for restricted cargo.
Attach an IAM policy to the agent's execution role that allows dynamodb:UpdateItem only on tables tagged cargo_type=standard, and move restricted cargo to a separate table with another tag.
Add a denied topic for Class-A Restricted cargo to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail on the agent, so that the guardrail blocks any request or response about those routes.
Set the reserved concurrency of the tool's Lambda function to 1, so that no more than one call to the driver availability tool can run at the same time.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run the agent's tool calls through an AWS Step Functions state machine that counts the calls for each Order ID and moves to a Fail state above a set limit.
This state machine works as a circuit breaker on the number of calls. It keeps a count of the tool calls for each Order ID, for example in a DynamoDB table. Before each call, a Choice state compares the count with a set limit. When the count goes above the limit, the workflow moves to a Fail state, which stops the execution and marks it as failed. The breaker counts every call for that Order ID, whether the call worked or not, so it also stops a loop of calls that each return without an error. The state machine decides when to stop, so the model cannot keep the loop going.

CORRECT: Attach an IAM policy to the agent's execution role that allows dynamodb:UpdateItem only on tables tagged cargo_type=standard, and move restricted cargo to a separate table with another tag.
An IAM policy can check the tags on a DynamoDB table with the aws:ResourceTag condition key. A tag belongs to a table or an index, never to a single item. So the company moves restricted cargo into its own table with a different tag, and the policy allows UpdateItem only on tables tagged as standard. The agent's role then cannot write a restricted route, whatever the model decides to do. IAM makes the block, not the model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.3: "Develop safeguarded AI workflows to ensure controlled FM behavior"
Example: "IAM policies to enforce resource boundaries"
Example: "circuit breakers to mitigate failures"

Sources:

  • Using attribute-based access control with DynamoDB
  • Circuit breaker pattern
  • How Amazon Bedrock Guardrails works

INCORRECT: Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the routes table, and have a Lambda function undo any update that the agent makes to a route for restricted cargo.
DynamoDB Streams records each change to the items in a table, and a Lambda function can read those records after the write. This fits an audit trail, or work that must react to a change, such as a message after an update. Here restricted routes must stay off-limits to the agent. With a stream, the agent's update is already written before the function sees it, so the agent still changes the route, even if only for a short time.

INCORRECT: Add a denied topic for Class-A Restricted cargo to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail on the agent, so that the guardrail blocks any request or response about those routes.
A guardrail checks user inputs and model responses. A denied topic blocks text about a subject that the company does not allow, which fits a chatbot that must not discuss that subject. Here the risk is a route update that a tool writes to DynamoDB. The guardrail never sees that database write, so it cannot stop it. It also does not limit the repeated tool calls.

INCORRECT: Set the reserved concurrency of the tool's Lambda function to 1, so that no more than one call to the driver availability tool can run at the same time.
Reserved concurrency sets the largest number of instances of a function that can run at the same time. A low value protects a downstream system, such as a database, from too many parallel calls. The agent made its calls one after another, so a limit of 1 does not stop them. Reserved concurrency also does not count the calls for each Order ID, and it does nothing about restricted cargo.

1. Vitals Extraction: Parses simple numerical values (Blood Pressure, Heart Rate) from nurse notes.
2. Medical History Review: Summarizes over 100 pages of attached PDF medical records to identify pre-existing conditions.
3. Diagnostic Reasoning: Analyzes the current symptoms against a complex medical knowledge base to suggest potential rare diseases.
The current prototype uses a single, ultra-large Foundation Model (FM) for all tasks. However, the system is too slow for the simple extraction task and incurs prohibitive costs when processing the large PDF history files.
As a GenAI Developer, which model coordination strategy should you implement to optimize performance and cost?
questions.promptText:
A healthcare startup is building a "Virtual Triage" application. The system performs three distinct functions for every patient interaction:
1. Vitals Extraction: Parses simple numerical values (Blood Pressure, Heart Rate) from nurse notes.
2. Medical History Review: Summarizes over 100 pages of attached PDF medical records to identify pre-existing conditions.
3. Diagnostic Reasoning: Analyzes the current symptoms against a complex medical knowledge base to suggest potential rare diseases.
The current prototype uses a single, ultra-large Foundation Model (FM) for all tasks. However, the system is too slow for the simple extraction task and incurs prohibitive costs when processing the large PDF history files.
As a GenAI Developer, which model coordination strategy should you implement to optimize performance and cost?

options.text: Use a Model Router pattern on Amazon Bedrock, routing each task to a purpose-fit model: lightweight for extraction, large-context for PDFs, and high-capability for reasoning.
Enable Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing to dynamically direct all three task types to the most appropriate FM based on prompt complexity scores and configured cost optimization thresholds.
Configure Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to store the 100-page PDF context across invocations and apply optimized prompt templates to reduce token overhead for all three task types.
Enable Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to distribute the three task types across multiple AWS Regions using the same ultra-large FM to reduce throttling and improve throughput.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use a Model Router pattern on Amazon Bedrock, routing each task to a purpose-fit model: lightweight for extraction, large-context for PDFs, and high-capability for reasoning.
This pattern sends each task to a model that fits the task. A small, fast model reads the blood pressure and heart rate from the nurse notes, so the simple extraction becomes quick and costs little. A model with a large context window summarizes the long PDF records, so the ultra-large model no longer reads them. A high-capability model handles only the diagnostic reasoning, where its skill is needed. The application code sends each task to its model and combines the three results. This fixes both problems: the slow extraction and the high cost of the PDF work.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.4: "Create sophisticated model coordination systems to optimize performance across multiple capabilities"
Example: "specialized FMs to perform complex tasks"

Sources:

  • GENCOST01-BP01 Right-size model selection to optimize inference costs
  • Understanding intelligent prompt routing in Amazon Bedrock
  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

INCORRECT: Enable Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing to dynamically direct all three task types to the most appropriate FM based on prompt complexity scores and configured cost optimization thresholds.
Intelligent prompt routing predicts the response quality of each model in a router for a prompt. It then sends the prompt to the model with the best mix of quality and cost for that request. A router must use exactly two models, and both must come from the same family. The startup has three different tasks and wants a purpose-fit model for each one, and those models may come from different families. A router cannot send three tasks to three chosen models, so the application needs its own routing logic.

INCORRECT: Configure Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to store the 100-page PDF context across invocations and apply optimized prompt templates to reduce token overhead for all three task types.
Prompt caching stores a long part of a prompt that many requests repeat, such as a large document, so later requests do not process it again. This lowers latency and input token cost when the same context comes back many times. It does not change which model runs each task. All three tasks still go to the same ultra-large model, so the simple extraction stays slow, and the large model still reads each new patient's records in full the first time.

INCORRECT: Enable Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to distribute the three task types across multiple AWS Regions using the same ultra-large FM to reduce throttling and improve throughput.
Cross-Region inference sends requests for one model to other AWS Regions, so the application can handle bursts of traffic with less throttling. That fits a workload that often reaches its quota in one Region. Here the problem is not throttling. All three tasks still run on the same ultra-large model, so the simple extraction stays slow and the PDF work stays expensive.

A legal technology firm is building an "AI Associate" to draft commercial contracts. A senior attorney must review and approve every draft before it is finalized. Each draft must move on as soon as it is approved, and no component may keep asking whether work or an approval is waiting.
The firm also wants to capture each attorney edit to improve the model. The review portal sends only the new text of a changed clause and the draft ID. The text before the change is in Amazon DynamoDB. Each record written to Amazon S3 must hold the text before and after the change.
Which combination of architectural patterns should the GenAI Developer implement to achieve these goals?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create an API Gateway endpoint with a Lambda integration that joins each edited clause with the original clause from DynamoDB and saves the pair to Amazon S3.
Add a Step Functions Wait state that pauses the workflow for a set review period, and then check Amazon S3 for an approval record before the next step.
Create an API Gateway endpoint with an Amazon S3 service integration that writes each edited clause and its draft ID from the request straight to the bucket.
Add a Step Functions activity task, and run a worker that calls GetActivityTask for review work and reports the attorney's decision when the review is done.
Add a Step Functions task that uses the .waitForTaskToken pattern, and have the review portal return the task token with SendTaskSuccess when the attorney approves.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an API Gateway endpoint with a Lambda integration that joins each edited clause with the original clause from DynamoDB and saves the pair to Amazon S3.
API Gateway gives the review portal an HTTPS endpoint for each edit. The Lambda function behind it uses the draft ID to read the text before the change from DynamoDB. It joins that text with the attorney's new text and writes both versions as one record to Amazon S3. The firm can later use these before and after records to improve the model. Code is needed here, because the portal sends only the new text of the changed clause.

CORRECT: Add a Step Functions task that uses the .waitForTaskToken pattern, and have the review portal return the task token with SendTaskSuccess when the attorney approves.
With the callback pattern, a Step Functions task passes a task token to another service and then pauses. The workflow waits until the token comes back in a SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure call. Here the review portal sends SendTaskSuccess with the token when the attorney approves, so the draft moves on at once. Nothing asks for work or approvals while the task waits. A human approval step is a common use of this pattern.

Exam Guide Reference:

INCORRECT: Add a Step Functions Wait state that pauses the workflow for a set review period, and then check Amazon S3 for an approval record before the next step.
A Wait state pauses a workflow for a set number of seconds or until a set time. It fits steps that must wait for a known period, such as a delay before a reminder goes out. Review times are not known here, and the draft must move on as soon as the attorney approves. A fixed wait adds delay, and a loop of checks in S3 is the kind of repeated asking that the firm does not allow.

INCORRECT: Create an API Gateway endpoint with an Amazon S3 service integration that writes each edited clause and its draft ID from the request straight to the bucket.
API Gateway can act as a proxy for Amazon S3 and write the body of a request to a bucket with no Lambda function. That fits uploads that need no change, such as a file that a user sends as it is. Here the portal sends only the new text of the clause and the draft ID. A direct write to S3 cannot read the text before the change from DynamoDB, so the record in S3 would not hold both versions.

INCORRECT: Add a Step Functions activity task, and run a worker that calls GetActivityTask for review work and reports the attorney's decision when the review is done.
An activity links a task in a state machine to a worker that runs somewhere else, for example on Amazon EC2 or in a Lambda function. The worker calls GetActivityTask to ask Step Functions for work. This fits long jobs that run on a company's own servers. Here no component may keep asking whether work is waiting, and an activity worker must do exactly that.

A developer is building a "Corporate IT Support" agent using Amazon Bedrock. The agent uses a custom tool named ResetUserPassword which requires a strictly formatted EmployeeID (e.g., "EMP-1234") and a ReasonCode.
During beta testing, the model often invokes the tool with malformed IDs (e.g., "1234" or "employee-1234"), causing the backend Identity Provider to throw unhandled exceptions that terminate the session abruptly.
According to AWS best practices for reliable tool operations, how should the developer implement the integration to resolve this issue?

options.text: Configure the tool Lambda function to catch formatting exceptions, returning a structured error mapping schema back to the agent for parameter self-correction.
Configure the tool Lambda function to return an HTTP 500 server error code directly to the agent when regex schema validation fails.
Configure the tool Lambda function with an asynchronous destination pattern to dump input syntax errors into an out-of-band Amazon SQS dead-letter queue.
Configure the tool Lambda function to invoke an upstream AWS Step Functions circuit breaker state machine to reset the active agent session.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Configure the tool Lambda function to catch formatting exceptions, returning a structured error mapping schema back to the agent for parameter self-correction.
The tool function checks that the EmployeeID has the EMP-1234 format before it calls the Identity Provider. When the check fails, the function catches the error and returns a clear error result instead of letting the exception end the session, for example "EmployeeID must look like EMP-1234". The application sends this result back to the model as the tool result, and it can mark the result as an error. The model reads which field is wrong and which format it needs, so it can call the tool again with a fixed ID.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.6: "Implement intelligent tool integrations to extend FM capabilities and to ensure reliable tool operations"
Example: "Lambda functions to implement error handling and parameter validation"

Sources:

  • Call a tool with the Converse API
  • Capturing records of Lambda asynchronous invocations

INCORRECT: Configure the tool Lambda function to return an HTTP 500 server error code directly to the agent when regex schema validation fails.
An HTTP 500 code only says that the server failed. It does not say which field was wrong or which format the field needs. The problem here is a badly formatted ID from the model, not a fault in the server. With a bare error code, the model has no detail that helps it fix the ID on the next call.

INCORRECT: Configure the tool Lambda function with an asynchronous destination pattern to dump input syntax errors into an out-of-band Amazon SQS dead-letter queue.
Lambda destinations and dead-letter queues keep records of events from asynchronous invocations that failed after all retries. They fit background jobs, where a team reviews or replays the failed events later. Here the model calls the tool and waits for the result in the same conversation. A record in an Amazon SQS queue never reaches the model, so the model cannot learn what is wrong with the ID and fix it.

INCORRECT: Configure the tool Lambda function to invoke an upstream AWS Step Functions circuit breaker state machine to reset the active agent session.
A circuit breaker stops calls to a service after repeated failures or timeouts. A Step Functions state machine can run this pattern. It fits a backend service that is down, so that callers stop sending requests to it for a time. Here the Identity Provider works. The model sends a badly formatted ID, and it can fix the ID when it learns what is wrong. A reset ends the session, and a session that ends abruptly is the problem the developer must fix.

options.text: Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for speculative decoding, so a small draft model proposes tokens, the large model checks them, and answers return faster.
Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for fast model loading, so new instances stream weights that were sharded in advance from Amazon S3 onto their GPUs.
Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for quantization, so the weights use a lower-precision data type and new instances load a smaller model onto their GPUs.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for fast model loading, so new instances stream weights that were sharded in advance from Amazon S3 onto their GPUs.
Fast model loading prepares an LLM so that SageMaker AI can load it onto an instance more quickly. The optimization job shards the model in advance, so each portion can sit on its own GPU, and it stores the weights in equal-sized chunks. When a new instance starts, SageMaker AI streams these chunks from Amazon S3 straight onto the GPUs. This skips the slow steps in the logs: the copy to disk, the load into host memory, and the split on the host. The job only divides and arranges the weights, so the approved model stays the same, and auto scaling adds serving instances sooner.

Example: "following specialized model loading strategies"

  • Inference optimization for Amazon SageMaker AI models

  • Introducing Fast Model Loader in SageMaker Inference: Accelerate autoscaling for your Large Language Models (LLMs), part 1

INCORRECT: Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for speculative decoding, so a small draft model proposes tokens, the large model checks them, and answers return faster.
Speculative decoding speeds up the way the model writes text. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large target model checks them in parallel, so answers come back sooner. That fits an endpoint where each answer is too slow. Here each answer is already fast enough once an instance is in service. The delay happens before a new instance serves any request, and speculative decoding does not change that.

INCORRECT: Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for quantization, so the weights use a lower-precision data type and new instances load a smaller model onto their GPUs.
Quantization stores the weights and activations in a less precise data type. The model needs less GPU memory and can run on less expensive GPUs. This fits a team that can accept a small change in answer quality. A quantized model might be less accurate than the source model, and the quality team will not accept any version that might answer less accurately.

INCORRECT: Run a SageMaker AI optimization job for compilation, so the model is compiled ahead of time and new instances skip compiling it when they start.
Compilation prepares the model for the chosen hardware ahead of time, so a new instance does not compile the weights just in time when it starts. That helps when compiling at startup is the slow step. Here the logs show that most of the delay is copying the model files from Amazon S3 to disk, then to host memory, and then onto the GPUs. Compilation does not remove those copy steps.

options.text: Host the Catalog Updater model on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a GPU instance, and keep a minimum instance count of 1 for the administrators.
Create Provisioned Throughput for the chatbot's model, with enough model units for the expected peak, so the chatbot has a set level of throughput during the sale.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the chatbot's model, with enough model units for the expected peak, so the chatbot has a set level of throughput during the sale.
Provisioned Throughput gives one model a higher level of throughput at a fixed cost. It comes in model units, and each unit processes a set number of input and output tokens per minute. The company sets up enough units for the expected peak of 50,000 concurrent users, and the question states that the chosen model offers Provisioned Throughput. The chatbot then has a set level of throughput during the sale, and the fixed cost applies only to the workload that needs it.

CORRECT: Convert the weekly CSV into JSONL records in Amazon S3, and run an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job that writes the product descriptions back to S3.
Batch inference processes many prompts in one job and writes the results to Amazon S3. The job runs asynchronously, which fits work where speed is not critical. The input must be a JSONL file, where each line is a record that holds the model input for one prompt. So the team first converts the weekly CSV into these records. No endpoint runs between the weekly jobs, so the six idle days add no compute cost.

Example: "Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput configurations"

INCORRECT: Host the Catalog Updater model on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a GPU instance, and keep a minimum instance count of 1 for the administrators.
A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint fits interactive work with low latency requirements, and a minimum of one instance keeps the model ready at all times. The administrators use the tool once a week and do not need fast answers. With a minimum of one GPU instance, the endpoint keeps running through the six idle days, and that idle cost is what the company wants to avoid.

INCORRECT: Serve the chatbot from a SageMaker AI asynchronous inference endpoint, which queues each request during the sale and processes the queue in the background.
SageMaker AI asynchronous inference queues incoming requests and processes them asynchronously. It fits large payloads and long processing times, and it can scale to zero instances when no requests wait. A chatbot must return each token in under a second while the customer waits. Requests that wait in a queue during the sale break that target.

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the Catalog Updater's model with a one-month commitment, so the weekly job always has a set level of throughput ready.
Provisioned Throughput gives a model a set level of throughput at a fixed cost, which fits steady, heavy traffic that uses the capacity every day. With a one-month commitment, the company cannot delete it before the term ends. The Catalog Updater runs once a week, so the company would pay for throughput through the six idle days, which is the cost it wants to avoid.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use an AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) container, and set option.tensor_parallel_degree to 8 in serving.properties, so the model is split across all eight GPUs.
The LMI container on SageMaker AI serves large models, and option.tensor_parallel_degree sets how many GPUs the model is split across. With a value of 8, the container splits the model across all eight GPUs, so each GPU holds only a part of the 140 GB of weights. The model fits in the 320 GB of the instance, the OOM error at load time goes away, and all eight GPUs work on each request.
