INCORRECT: Deploy the model as a SageMaker AI inference component that needs one GPU for each copy, and run eight copies of the model on the instance.
An inference component sets how many accelerators each copy of a model uses, and one endpoint can host several copies. That fits a model that fits on one GPU, where eight copies keep all eight GPUs busy. This model needs about 140 GB, and each GPU has 40 GB. One copy cannot fit on one GPU, so every copy would fail with the same OOM error.

INCORRECT: Run a SageMaker AI optimization job that quantizes the model to a 4-bit data type, so that the whole model fits in the memory of a single GPU.
Quantization stores the weights in a less precise data type, such as a 4-bit format. The model then needs less GPU memory and can run on fewer or less expensive GPUs, which fits a team that can accept some loss of accuracy. Here the team must keep the FP16 weights. A model on one GPU would also leave the other seven GPUs of the instance idle.

INCORRECT: Use an AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) container, and lower option.max_rolling_batch_size in serving.properties, so fewer requests share the GPU memory at one time.
The option.max_rolling_batch_size setting limits how many requests the container processes together in one continuous batch. Each request in the batch keeps its own KV cache in GPU memory, so a lower value needs less memory. That helps when the GPUs run out of memory under heavy traffic. Here the error happens at deployment, before any request arrives, because the loading script puts all the weights on one GPU. Fewer requests do not make 140 GB of weights fit in 40 GB.

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt router with Claude Sonnet and Amazon Nova Micro, so Amazon Bedrock sends each question to the model that it predicts answers better.
Turn on prompt caching for Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock, so that each request reuses the cached start of the prompt and returns sooner at a lower cost.
Send each question first to Amazon Nova Micro, and send it on to Claude Sonnet only when Nova Micro rates its own answer below a set confidence score.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Send each question first to Amazon Nova Micro, and send it on to Claude Sonnet only when Nova Micro rates its own answer below a set confidence score.
This is model cascading. A small, fast model such as Amazon Nova Micro answers each question first and returns a confidence score with its answer. Routine questions, about 70% of the traffic, end there with a low cost and a short wait. When the score falls below the threshold, the application sends the question to Claude Sonnet, so the 30% of hard questions still get deep reasoning. Cost and latency drop for most questions, and the hard questions keep the quality of the large model.

Skill 2.2.3: "Develop optimized FM deployment approaches to balance performance and resource requirements for GenAI workloads"

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt router with Claude Sonnet and Amazon Nova Micro, so Amazon Bedrock sends each question to the model that it predicts answers better.
An intelligent prompt router predicts the response quality of each of its models for a prompt. It then sends the prompt to the model with the best mix of quality and cost. It fits a team that wants Amazon Bedrock to choose between two models of one family. A router must use exactly two models from the same family. Claude Sonnet and Amazon Nova Micro come from different families, so one router cannot hold this pair.

INCORRECT: Turn on prompt caching for Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock, so that each request reuses the cached start of the prompt and returns sooner at a lower cost.
Prompt caching stores a long part of a prompt that many requests repeat, such as a large document or long instructions. Later requests reuse it, which lowers latency and input token cost. Each cache checkpoint needs a minimum number of tokens. Here the system prompt is short and users send short questions, so there is little to cache. Every routine question also still runs on the large model.

INCORRECT: Send every question to Amazon Nova Micro and retire Claude Sonnet, so that each question runs on the fastest and lowest-cost model in the application.
Moving all traffic to one small model gives the lowest cost and the shortest wait. It fits an application where every question is simple. Here 30% of the questions need the deep reasoning of the large model. Without Claude Sonnet, those questions lose the model that the company chose for deep reasoning.

options.text: The ERP calls an Amazon API Gateway REST API that streams the Lambda function's response. The first words of the Amazon Bedrock answer reach the ERP within milliseconds.
The ERP sends each note to an Amazon SQS queue and returns at once. It then checks an Amazon DynamoDB table until the Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock stores the root cause.
The ERP sends each note to an Amazon SQS queue and returns at once. A Lambda function reads the queue, calls Amazon Bedrock, and writes the root cause back through the ERP's API.
The ERP calls an AWS AppSync API that has an Amazon Bedrock resolver. The resolver calls the model synchronously and returns the root cause in the response to the mutation.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The ERP sends each note to an Amazon SQS queue and returns at once. A Lambda function reads the queue, calls Amazon Bedrock, and writes the root cause back through the ERP's API.
This design puts a queue between the ERP and the model. Sending a message to Amazon SQS does not wait for the model, so the ERP gets its reply at once and the technician can keep working. Lambda polls the queue and invokes the function with each batch of notes. The function calls the model and waits the 3 to 5 seconds that the analysis needs, and no user waits with it. When the root cause is ready, the function writes it to the issue record through the ERP's API, the way other systems already update records. The result comes to the ERP, so the ERP never has to poll for it, which it cannot do.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.1: "Create enterprise connectivity solutions to seamlessly incorporate FM capabilities into existing enterprise environments"
Example: "event-driven architectures to implement loose coupling"

Sources:

  • Using Lambda with Amazon SQS

  • Stream the integration response for your proxy integrations in API Gateway

  • AWS AppSync JavaScript resolver and function reference for Amazon Bedrock runtime

INCORRECT: The ERP calls an Amazon API Gateway REST API that streams the Lambda function's response. The first words of the Amazon Bedrock answer reach the ERP within milliseconds.
With response streaming, API Gateway sends the first part of a Lambda proxy response before the whole response is ready. This fits a chat screen that shows the answer while the model writes it. The ERP does not work that way. It reads only complete responses, and the whole analysis takes 3 to 5 seconds. So the ERP still waits far longer than 300 milliseconds, the call times out, and users stay blocked while it waits.

INCORRECT: The ERP sends each note to an Amazon SQS queue and returns at once. It then checks an Amazon DynamoDB table until the Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock stores the root cause.
A queue plus a results table that the caller checks is a common pattern when the caller can come back later, for example a web page that asks for the status every few seconds. The first half of this design fits here: the ERP sends the note and gets its reply at once. The second half does not. Checking the table again and again is polling, and the ERP cannot poll, so it has no way to read the root cause from the table.

INCORRECT: The ERP calls an AWS AppSync API that has an Amazon Bedrock resolver. The resolver calls the model synchronously and returns the root cause in the response to the mutation.
AWS AppSync can call Amazon Bedrock directly from a JavaScript resolver, with no Lambda function in between. It supports only synchronous calls, so it fits apps that can wait for a short model answer. Here the ERP waits for the resolver, and the resolver waits for the model for 3 to 5 seconds. That is far longer than the 300 milliseconds that the ERP allows, so the call times out and blocks users while it runs.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A rule on the default event bus sends each event to an EventBridge API destination whose connection stores the partner's credentials, with the partner's limit as its invocation rate and an SQS dead-letter queue.
An EventBridge API destination is an HTTPS endpoint that a rule can use as its target, so EventBridge itself calls the partner's API and the company writes no code for it. The connection of the API destination holds the partner's user name and password for basic authentication, and EventBridge stores them in a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. The invocation rate setting caps the requests per second that EventBridge sends to the endpoint, so a rate at the partner's limit keeps the company from being blocked. When the partner's API is down, EventBridge retries requests that fail with a server error or time out. An event that still fails after the last retry goes to the dead-letter queue, so no summary is lost. The partner's API needs no change, because EventBridge calls it like any other client.

INCORRECT: A rule on the default event bus invokes a Lambda function that gets the partner's credentials from AWS Secrets Manager and calls the partner's API, with reserved concurrency to limit parallel calls.
A Lambda function that gets the credentials from AWS Secrets Manager and calls the partner is a common design when each call needs custom logic, such as a change to the data before it goes out. Reserved concurrency sets how many copies of the function can run at the same time, which protects a downstream system from too many parallel calls. But the function is code that the company writes and runs to call the partner, and the company wants no code of its own there.

INCORRECT: A rule on the default event bus sends each event to an Amazon SNS topic whose HTTPS subscription has the partner's sign-in details in its URL and a delivery policy that throttles and retries.
An SNS topic with an HTTPS subscription pushes each message to a web endpoint, and the subscription URL can carry a user name and password for basic authentication. Its delivery policy can throttle deliveries to an average rate per second and retry failed ones. This fits a partner that has built its endpoint to work with SNS. SNS first sends a subscription confirmation message, and it sends nothing else until the endpoint confirms, for example by visiting the SubscribeURL. The partner will not change its API, so it never confirms, and no summary arrives.

INCORRECT: A rule on the default event bus invokes a Lambda function that gets the partner's credentials from AWS Secrets Manager and calls the partner's API, with an on-failure destination for failed events.
EventBridge invokes a Lambda function asynchronously, and an on-failure destination keeps a record of each event that fails all processing attempts, for example in an SQS queue. This is a good way to keep failed events when custom code must call an outside system. Here the function is still code that the company writes to sign in and call the partner. The company wants no code of its own that calls the partner.

The company added a job_level claim to the Entra ID token, with the value junior or senior. Junior researchers may query only the Public_Clinical_Trials knowledge base. Senior researchers may query Public_Clinical_Trials and Confidential_Molecule_Data. The front end calls the Retrieve API of Amazon Bedrock directly with the AWS SDK for JavaScript, with no API layer in between. Which TWO steps meet these requirements?

Senior researchers may query Public_Clinical_Trials and Confidential_Molecule_Data. The front end calls the Retrieve API of Amazon Bedrock directly with the AWS SDK for JavaScript, with no API layer in between. Access must follow least privilege, and the data in the two knowledge bases must stay strictly separate.
Which TWO steps meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool with Microsoft Entra ID as its OIDC provider, and set role mapping to choose the IAM role from the cognito:preferred_role claim in the token.
Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool with Microsoft Entra ID as its OIDC provider, and add role mapping rules that choose the Junior or Senior role from the job_level claim.
Add an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda authorizer that checks the job_level claim, and a Lambda function that calls Retrieve on the allowed knowledge bases.
Attach an IAM policy to each role that allows the bedrock:Retrieve action only on the Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) of the knowledge bases that the role may query.
Move all documents into one knowledge base with an access level metadata field, and have the front end add a retrieval filter that matches the job_level claim.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool with Microsoft Entra ID as its OIDC provider, and add role mapping rules that choose the Junior or Senior role from the job_level claim.
An Amazon Cognito identity pool can trust Microsoft Entra ID as an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider. The browser gives the pool the user's Entra ID token, and the pool returns temporary AWS credentials. Role mapping rules can read any claim in an OIDC token. Here one rule maps the job_level value junior to the Junior role, and another rule maps senior to the Senior role. The pool uses the IAM role of the first rule that matches, and no browser ever has long-term AWS keys.

CORRECT: Attach an IAM policy to each role that allows the bedrock:Retrieve action only on the Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) of the knowledge bases that the role may query.
The bedrock:Retrieve action takes a knowledge base as its resource, so an IAM policy can allow this action on each knowledge base separately. The ARN of a knowledge base contains the knowledge base ID, not its name. The policy of the Junior role lists only the ARN of Public_Clinical_Trials. The policy of the Senior role lists the ARNs of both knowledge bases. IAM checks each Retrieve call against the role behind the credentials. If a junior researcher edits a request in the browser to query Confidential_Molecule_Data, IAM denies the call.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.3: "Create secure access frameworks to ensure appropriate security controls"
Example: "identity federation between FM services and enterprise systems"
Example: "role-based access control for model and data access"

Sources:

  • Actions, resources, and condition keys for Amazon Bedrock

  • Using role-based access control

  • Set up permissions for a user or role to create and manage knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool with Microsoft Entra ID as its OIDC provider, and set role mapping to choose the IAM role from the cognito:preferred_role claim in the token.
With this setting, the identity pool takes the IAM role from the cognito:preferred_role claim in the token. An Amazon Cognito user pool adds this claim to its ID tokens, based on the groups that the user belongs to in the user pool. So the setting fits users who sign in through a user pool with groups. Here users sign in with Microsoft Entra ID, and the Entra ID token has a job_level claim but no cognito:preferred_role claim. The identity pool finds no role to choose in that token.

INCORRECT: Add an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda authorizer that checks the job_level claim, and a Lambda function that calls Retrieve on the allowed knowledge bases.
A Lambda authorizer reads the caller's token and returns an IAM policy that allows or denies the API call. A backend function then calls Amazon Bedrock for the user. This is a common design when a company wants its own code to check access. But this front end calls the Retrieve API directly, with no API layer in between, and this option adds that layer.

INCORRECT: Move all documents into one knowledge base with an access level metadata field, and have the front end add a retrieval filter that matches the job_level claim.
A metadata filter in a Retrieve request narrows the results to documents whose fields match. This is a good way to split one knowledge base when a backend service sets the filter. Here the front end builds each request in the browser with the AWS SDK for JavaScript, so the user can change the request. A junior researcher can remove the filter and read the confidential documents. The data also stops being strictly separate, because both kinds of documents share one knowledge base.

When the news mentions the product, traffic jumps within seconds, at times nobody can predict. Users then wait long for the first words, and each scale-out starts several minutes after the jump. The team lowered the invocations target twice. The endpoint then kept extra instances in quiet hours, and the delay during jumps hardly changed. CPU use stays low even under heavy load.
Which change to the endpoint's scaling should the team make?

A company hosts an open-weight LLM on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that runs on GPU instances. The endpoint serves one model and streams each answer, which can take up to a minute to finish. A target tracking policy on the InvocationsPerInstance metric scales the endpoint.
When the news mentions the product, traffic jumps within seconds, at times nobody can predict. Users then wait long for the first words, and each scale-out starts several minutes after the jump. The team lowered the invocations target twice. The endpoint then kept extra instances in quiet hours, and the delay during jumps hardly changed. CPU use stays low even under heavy load.
Which change to the endpoint's scaling should the team make?

options.text: Keep the target tracking policy on the InvocationsPerInstance metric, and set a lower target value, so that scale-out starts at a smaller number of invocations per instance.
Keep the target tracking policy on the InvocationsPerInstance metric, and add scheduled actions that raise the minimum instance count before busy hours and lower it afterward.
Replace the policy with a target tracking policy on the CPUUtilization metric of the endpoint instances, with a target of 50 percent average use across the instances.

Replace the policy with a target tracking policy on the SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution metric, with a target near the number of requests that one model container serves well.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Replace the policy with a target tracking policy on the SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution metric, with a target near the number of requests that one model container serves well.
This predefined metric counts the concurrent requests that a model container is handling, including the requests that wait inside the container. For a streamed answer, it keeps counting a request until the model sends the last token. So it shows the real load of an LLM, where one request can run for a minute. SageMaker AI sends this high-resolution metric every 10 seconds, while standard metrics such as InvocationsPerInstance arrive once a minute. A target tracking policy on it sees a jump sooner and starts the scale-out sooner.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.3: "Develop high-performance FM systems to maximize resource utilization and throughput for GenAI workloads"
Example: "utilization monitoring"

Sources:

  • Define a scaling policy
  • Amazon SageMaker inference launches faster auto scaling for generative AI models: up-to 6x faster scale-up detection
  • Auto scaling policy overview

INCORRECT: Keep the target tracking policy on the InvocationsPerInstance metric, and set a lower target value, so that scale-out starts at a smaller number of invocations per instance.
A lower target on InvocationsPerInstance is the first fix to try when an endpoint with short requests scales out too late. This team already tried it twice. The metric arrives once a minute and counts calls, not how long each call keeps the model busy, so it moves little when long streamed answers pile up. A lower target only made the endpoint keep extra instances in quiet hours, and the delay during jumps stayed.

INCORRECT: Keep the target tracking policy on the InvocationsPerInstance metric, and add scheduled actions that raise the minimum instance count before busy hours and lower it afterward.
Scheduled actions change capacity at set times, and they fit traffic with a known pattern, such as a busy start to each working day. Here traffic jumps when the news mentions the product, at times nobody can predict. A schedule cannot add capacity before those jumps, and the invocations policy still starts late when they come.

INCORRECT: Replace the policy with a target tracking policy on the CPUUtilization metric of the endpoint instances, with a target of 50 percent average use across the instances.
A target tracking policy can use CPUUtilization as a custom metric, and this fits a model that runs on the CPU, where CPU use rises with load. This model runs on GPU instances, and CPU use stays low even under heavy load. A policy on CPU use would see no reason to add instances when traffic jumps.

Users report that the application feels unresponsive because it takes several seconds to display the final answer for complex queries. The developer wants to improve the user experience by displaying the text progressively as it is generated.
The chatbot uses Claude Sonnet. The team must keep that model and the current answer length, because only that setup passed the quality tests.
Which solution should the developer implement to achieve the lowest perceived latency?

options.text: The backend calls InvokeModel with Claude Haiku in place of Claude Sonnet, so the full answer is ready sooner, and sends it through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
The backend calls InvokeModelWithResponseStream and sends each chunk to the browser through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API as soon as the chunk arrives.
The backend calls InvokeModel with a lower max_tokens value, so the model stops sooner, and sends the full answer through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
The backend calls InvokeModelWithResponseStream, joins the chunks into the full answer, and sends it to the browser through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The backend calls InvokeModelWithResponseStream and sends each chunk to the browser through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API as soon as the chunk arrives.
InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the answer as a stream of chunks while the model writes it. The backend sends each chunk to the browser over the open WebSocket connection, with a POST to the @connections endpoint of the API, as soon as the chunk arrives. The user sees the first words quickly and watches the rest appear, which gives the lowest perceived latency. The model and the answer length stay the same, as the quality tests require.

Exam Guide Reference:

Example: "Amazon Bedrock streaming APIs for incremental response delivery"

  • InvokeModelWithResponseStream
  • Use @connections commands in your backend service

INCORRECT: The backend calls InvokeModel with Claude Haiku in place of Claude Sonnet, so the full answer is ready sooner, and sends it through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
A faster model from the same family can shorten the time to a full answer, and this fits chatbots where the smaller model gives good enough answers. This team must keep Claude Sonnet, because only that setup passed the quality tests. The call also still waits for the full answer, so the user sees no text while the model writes.

INCORRECT: The backend calls InvokeModel with a lower max_tokens value, so the model stops sooner, and sends the full answer through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
The max_tokens value caps how many tokens the model writes before it stops, so a lower value gives a shorter answer that is ready sooner. This fits answers that run longer than users need. Here the team must keep the current answer length. The call also waits for the full answer before the browser gets any text.

INCORRECT: The backend calls InvokeModelWithResponseStream, joins the chunks into the full answer, and sends it to the browser through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
Joining the chunks before sending them fits a design where each full answer must pass a check before any user sees it. The model still streams, but the browser gets nothing until the last chunk arrives. The user waits as long as with a call that does not stream, and the developer wants the text to appear while the model writes it.

Last month, a developer turned logging off during a test, and an audit found the gap weeks later. No log file was deleted. New logs stopped because logging was off.
The account's AWS CloudTrail trail logs management events and delivers them only to an S3 bucket. The security team owns the trail and allows no changes to it.
The governance team wants the approved settings back within minutes of any change, with no person's action, and an alert about each change.
Which steps should the team take?
Select TWO.

Last month, a developer turned logging off during a test, and an audit found the gap weeks later. No log file was deleted. New logs stopped because logging was off.
The account's AWS CloudTrail trail logs management events and delivers them only to an S3 bucket. The security team owns the trail and allows no changes to it.
The governance team wants the approved settings back within minutes of any change, with no person's action, and an alert about each change.

Select TWO.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches the CloudTrail events for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, with an Amazon SNS topic target that alerts the governance team.
Turn on S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the invocation log bucket, so that no one can delete or overwrite the log files during the retention period.
Send the trail's events to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, add a metric filter for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, and add an alarm that notifies the governance team's SNS topic.

Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches the CloudTrail events for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, with a Lambda function target that puts back the approved settings.

Send the trail's events to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, add a metric filter for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, and add an alarm whose Lambda function action puts back the approved settings.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches the CloudTrail events for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, with an Amazon SNS topic target that alerts the governance team.
CloudTrail records PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration as management events, and EventBridge delivers them to the default event bus, where a rule can send them to an Amazon SNS topic. The governance team subscribes to the topic and gets a message for each change, with the details of the call, such as who made it. This meets the alert need with no change to the trail, because EventBridge receives the events from CloudTrail and no one has to read the log files.

CORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches the CloudTrail events for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, with a Lambda function target that puts back the approved settings.
CloudTrail records the calls that change the logging settings, PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration, as management events. Because the account has a trail with logging on, EventBridge receives these calls as "AWS API Call via CloudTrail" events, and it delivers them only to the default event bus. A rule there matches the two calls and invokes a Lambda function. The function reads the current settings with GetModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and puts the approved bucket and log group back when they differ. It changes nothing when they already match, so its own call does not start a loop. The settings come back within minutes, and no person has to act.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.4: "Implement continuous monitoring and advanced governance controls to support safety audits and regulatory readiness"
Example: "automated alerting and remediation workflows"

Sources:

  • AWS service events delivered via AWS CloudTrail

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

  • Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail

INCORRECT: Turn on S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the invocation log bucket, so that no one can delete or overwrite the log files during the retention period.
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode stops every user, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting a locked object version during its retention period. It fits audit logs that someone might try to delete. Here no log file was deleted. The logs stopped because logging was off, so no new files reached the bucket, and Object Lock cannot turn logging back on.

INCORRECT: Send the trail's events to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, add a metric filter for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, and add an alarm that notifies the governance team's SNS topic.
A metric filter with an alarm on a log group that receives the trail's events is a common way to alert on API calls. For this, the trail must send its events to CloudWatch Logs, which means an update to the trail that names a log group and an IAM role. The security team allows no changes to the trail, and the trail delivers only to an S3 bucket.

INCORRECT: Send the trail's events to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, add a metric filter for the Bedrock logging configuration calls, and add an alarm whose Lambda function action puts back the approved settings.
A CloudWatch alarm can invoke a Lambda function when it changes state, so a metric filter on the trail's events can start a fix within minutes. This fits an account whose trail already sends its events to CloudWatch Logs. This trail delivers only to an S3 bucket. Sending its events to a log group means an update to the trail that names a log group and an IAM role, and the security team allows no changes to the trail.

A spec is a set of documents that Kiro builds for a feature before it writes code. From the request, Kiro first writes requirements as user stories with acceptance criteria. From the approved requirements, it writes a design with the data flow, the interfaces and the database schema. Then it writes a list of tasks, and each task links to the requirements it covers. The product owner reviews the requirements and the architect reviews the design and its DynamoDB data model, so a misread rule shows up in a document, before any file changes. A steering file is a markdown file that gives Kiro lasting knowledge about the project, such as its standards, libraries and patterns. It is the right tool for rules that every task must follow, so nobody explains them again in each chat. Here Kiro did not lack context. The developer already pasted the whole request, with every detail, and Kiro still misread a rule. More context in every chat still gives the product owner and the architect no point to agree before code exists.

An agent hook is an automated trigger that runs a set action when an event happens in the project, such as when Kiro saves a file. A hook like this one catches a mistake soon after Kiro makes it. But it runs only after the code is written. The product owner and the architect must agree before any code exists, and a check after each save cannot give them that.

MCP lets Kiro talk to outside servers that give it tools and data, such as documentation or an external service. This helps when the details of a task live in a system that Kiro cannot see. Here the full request already reached Kiro, pasted into the chat, and Kiro misread a rule anyway. Reading the same details from a ticket adds no review of the plan before the code.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Have a startup script use the task role to generate a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, pass it to the tool, and replace it before it expires.
A short-term Amazon Bedrock API key is made from the credentials of an IAM principal, and it has the same permissions as that principal. Here the task role makes the key, for example with the Amazon Bedrock token generator library, so every call runs with only the permissions of that role. The tool sends the key as a bearer token in the Authorization header, and Amazon Bedrock Runtime actions such as Converse accept it. The key expires with the role session or at a set maximum time, so the script makes a new key before the old one runs out. Short-term keys are the right choice for production workloads like this one.

INCORRECT: Add the AWS SDK to the tool so that it signs each Converse request with Signature Version 4, using the credentials of the task's IAM role.
The AWS SDK signs each request with Signature Version 4, and it can use the credentials of the task role. This is the usual way to call Amazon Bedrock from code that a team owns. Here the tool comes from a vendor that does not allow changes to its code, and its connector cannot sign requests. The team cannot add the SDK to it.

INCORRECT: Put an Amazon API Gateway REST API with request validation in front of Amazon Bedrock, and have the tool call it with an API key from a usage plan.
An API Gateway REST API can validate requests, and usage plans with API keys give each client its own access and limits. This fits a company that wants its own API in front of a model for many clients. Here the platform team does not allow any new service between the tool and Amazon Bedrock. The API would also call Amazon Bedrock with its own role, not with the task's role.

INCORRECT: Create a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key with an expiration date, store it in AWS Secrets Manager, and have the task pass it to the tool at startup.
A long-term Amazon Bedrock API key lasts until its expiration date, and it is a quick way to explore Amazon Bedrock. The key belongs to an IAM user, and calls with it use the permissions of that user. The security team does not allow IAM users, and every call must use the permissions of the task role.

CORRECT: When the support system reports a closed ticket, the second function publishes it as a CloudWatch custom metric with a ModelId dimension, and the dashboard graphs it beside each model's metrics.
A custom metric is a number that an application publishes to CloudWatch, and a dimension is a name and value pair that says what the number describes. The Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics, such as InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount and InvocationLatency, carry the ModelId dimension. The second function learns about each ticket that closes with no human, together with the model of its chat, so it can publish the count with a ModelId dimension for that model. CloudWatch treats each dimension value as its own metric. The dashboard can then graph the closed tickets of each model next to that model's tokens and latency, and the graph updates during the day.

INCORRECT: When a chat ends with no handoff request, the assistant's function publishes it as a CloudWatch custom metric with a ModelId dimension, and the dashboard graphs it beside each model's metrics.
Publishing a metric at the end of a chat is the right design when the chat itself settles the outcome, for example when the assistant completes an order inside the chat. Here customers often write back after the chat ends, and a human agent then takes over the ticket. A chat that ends with no handoff request is not yet a ticket closed with no human, so this count comes out too high for both models.

INCORRECT: When the support system reports a closed ticket, the second function writes it to Amazon S3, and a nightly Amazon Athena query builds a report for each model and hour.
Amazon Athena runs standard SQL on files in Amazon S3, and a nightly query is a good way to build a report that people read the next morning. This option also counts the right event, because it uses the result that the support system reports. But the report runs once a night and sits outside the dashboard. Leaders want the count on the same dashboard, through the day, beside each model's token and latency metrics.

INCORRECT: When a chat ends with no handoff request, the assistant's function writes it to Amazon S3, and a nightly Amazon Athena query builds a report for each model and hour.
A nightly Athena report on files in Amazon S3 fits a daily summary, and a record at the end of each chat fits an outcome that the chat settles. This option fails on both points. Customers often write back and reach a human agent after the chat ends, so the end of a chat does not mean a closed ticket. The leaders also want the numbers on the dashboard during the day, not in a report the next morning.

A company's assistant answers questions from its product manuals. An AWS Lambda ingestion function embeds manual chunks with a Cohere Embed model in Amazon Bedrock and stores the vectors in Amazon OpenSearch Service. A second function embeds each user question and searches the index.
A month ago, a developer moved both functions to one shared helper that builds every embedding request. The developer copied the helper from the question function. Since then, questions about manuals added in the last month often miss the right pages. Questions about older manuals still work. The chunk size, the model and the index did not change, and every chunk is far below the model's input limit.
Which action fixes the retrieval?

options.text: In the shared helper, set input_type to search_document for manual chunks and search_query for questions, then embed again all the manuals that were added since the helper change.
In the shared helper, set input_type to search_document for manual chunks and search_query for questions, and keep the stored vectors, since the setting affects only new calls.
In the shared helper, set the truncate setting to NONE so a text over the input limit fails, then embed again all the manuals that were added since the helper change.
In the shared helper, set the truncate setting to NONE so a text over the input limit fails, and keep the stored vectors, since the setting affects only new calls.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In the shared helper, set input_type to search_document for manual chunks and search_query for questions, then embed again all the manuals that were added since the helper change.
Cohere Embed models on Amazon Bedrock need an input_type in every request, and the model adds special tokens for each type. For search, the stored documents use search_document and the questions use search_query, so the two sides match. The helper came from the question function, so for a month it has sent search_query for the manual chunks too. Those newer vectors were made as if they were questions, which is why only the newer manuals retrieve poorly. The helper must set the type for each side, and the manuals from the last month must be embedded again so their stored vectors match the older ones.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.4: "Troubleshoot retrieval system issues to identify and resolve problems that affect information retrieval effectiveness for FM augmentation"
Example: "vectorization issue resolution"

Sources:

  • Cohere Embed v3

  • Cohere Embed v4

INCORRECT: In the shared helper, set input_type to search_document for manual chunks and search_query for questions, and keep the stored vectors, since the setting affects only new calls.
This fixes every future request, and it would be enough if only the question side had used the wrong type. Here the wrong type went into the stored vectors of every manual added in the last month. Those vectors do not change when the helper changes, so the newer manuals keep retrieving poorly until the team embeds them again.

INCORRECT: In the shared helper, set the truncate setting to NONE so a text over the input limit fails, then embed again all the manuals that were added since the helper change.
With truncate set to NONE, a text longer than the model's input limit returns an error instead of being cut. This is a useful check when long chunks lose their end without any warning. Here every chunk is far below the input limit, so no text was cut, and the setting changes nothing. The new vectors would still carry the wrong input type.

INCORRECT: In the shared helper, set the truncate setting to NONE so a text over the input limit fails, and keep the stored vectors, since the setting affects only new calls.
With truncate set to NONE, a text longer than the model's input limit returns an error instead of being cut. Keeping the stored vectors fits a team that finds long questions cut without warning while the stored documents are fine. Here every chunk is far below the input limit, so no text was cut. The stored vectors of the newer manuals still carry the wrong input type, so those manuals keep retrieving poorly.

A financial services firm is building a GenAI application that allows analysts to ask natural language questions about real-time trade volume stored in a robust relational database (Amazon RDS). The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) has identified two critical risks that must be mitigated:
1. Hallucination Risk: The model must not generate fictitious trade figures. It must strictly retrieve exact data from the database.
2. Reputation Risk: The final summary generated by the model must be automatically screened to ensure it does not contain profanity, hate speech, or a specific list of banned "insider trading" slang terms.
Which development approach effectively addresses these risks using AWS native controls?

options.text: Export the trade tables to Amazon S3 each night for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and attach a guardrail with content filters and a denied topic that describes insider trading slang.
Export the trade tables to Amazon S3 each night for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and attach a guardrail with content filters, the managed profanity filter and a custom word list.
Have the model turn each question into a SQL query that runs on the Amazon RDS database, and attach a guardrail with content filters, the managed profanity filter and a custom word list.
Have the model turn each question into a SQL query that runs on the Amazon RDS database, and attach a guardrail with content filters and a denied topic that describes insider trading slang.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Have the model turn each question into a SQL query that runs on the Amazon RDS database, and attach a guardrail with content filters, the managed profanity filter and a custom word list.
In a text-to-SQL design, the model turns the analyst's question into a SQL query, and the application runs that query on the Amazon RDS database. The trade figures come from the query result, not from what the model remembers, so they match the database at the moment of the question. The guardrail then screens the summary in three ways. Content filters catch hate speech. The managed profanity filter, part of the word filters, blocks profane words, and profanity is not one of the content filter categories. A custom word list blocks the exact slang terms on the company's list.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.2: "Create content safety frameworks to prevent harmful outputs"
Example: "text-to-SQL transformations to ensure deterministic results"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter responses"

Sources:

  • Remove a specific list of words and phrases from conversations with word filters
  • Block harmful words and conversations with content filters
  • Sync your data with your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base

INCORRECT: Export the trade tables to Amazon S3 each night for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and attach a guardrail with content filters and a denied topic that describes insider trading slang.
This option puts the trade tables in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and screens the summary with content filters and a denied topic. A nightly export gives the knowledge base yesterday's trade volume, but analysts ask about real-time figures that must match the database exactly. A denied topic blocks a subject that its definition describes, not a list of exact terms. Profanity is also not one of the content filter categories, and this guardrail has no word filter, so no setting in it targets profane words.

INCORRECT: Export the trade tables to Amazon S3 each night for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and attach a guardrail with content filters, the managed profanity filter and a custom word list.
An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base can read .csv files from Amazon S3, turn them into embeddings and retrieve the closest chunks for each question. It fits documents that change slowly. The guardrail in this option is right. But the trade volume is real-time, and a nightly export holds yesterday's numbers until the next export and sync. Retrieval also returns chunks of text, not the exact result of a query on the database.

INCORRECT: Have the model turn each question into a SQL query that runs on the Amazon RDS database, and attach a guardrail with content filters and a denied topic that describes insider trading slang.
A denied topic blocks a whole subject that an application must avoid, for example investment advice in a bank's assistant. The guardrail compares prompts and answers with the topic's definition and blocks any match. The SQL part of this option is right, but the guardrail misses two needs. The company has a specific list of terms, and matching exact words and phrases is the job of a word filter, not of a topic definition. Profanity is not one of the content filter categories, and this guardrail has no managed profanity filter, so no setting in it targets profane words.

A legal technology company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to extract liability clauses from contracts that users upload. Each contract has numbered sections. Users report that the model sometimes returns clauses that do not exist in the contract. The system prompt already limits the model to the contract text, and the inference parameters are already set so that answers vary as little as possible. The application must check each extracted clause against the contract before a user sees the clause.

Which TWO actions should the company take so that the application rejects invented clauses before users see them?

Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A legal technology company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to extract liability clauses from contracts that users upload. Each contract has numbered sections. Users report that the model sometimes returns clauses that do not exist in the contract. The system prompt already limits the model to the contract text, and the inference parameters are already set so that answers vary as little as possible. The application must check each extracted clause against the contract before a user sees the clause.
Which TWO actions should the company take so that the application rejects invented clauses before users see them?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add an instruction to the system prompt that tells the model to extract clauses only from the uploaded contract and to answer "none found" when a clause is absent.
Run an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job each week with the built-in Accuracy metric on a reference set of past contracts, and review the prompt when the score falls.
Create embeddings for each extracted clause and each passage of the contract, and accept a clause only when the closest passage scores above a threshold that the team sets.
Define a JSON Schema in a tool definition with fields for the clause text and its section number, and check each clause against that section of the contract.
Lower the temperature in the inference parameters of every request, so the model chooses higher-probability words and writes fewer clauses that are not in the contract.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create embeddings for each extracted clause and each passage of the contract, and accept a clause only when the closest passage scores above a threshold that the team sets.
Semantic similarity compares the meaning of two texts. An embeddings model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, converts each extracted clause and each passage of the contract into a vector, and the application compares the vectors. A clause that the model took from the contract scores high against the passage it came from. A clause with no close passage scores low, and the application rejects that clause before a user sees it. Embeddings compare meaning, not exact words, so an invented clause that differs from a passage of the contract in only one amount can still score above the threshold. The check against the text of the section catches that case.

CORRECT: Define a JSON Schema in a tool definition with fields for the clause text and its section number, and check each clause against that section of the contract.
A tool definition includes an input schema, written as a JSON Schema. When the application asks the model to use this tool, the model returns each clause in named fields instead of free text: the clause text and the number of the section it came from. The application then opens that section of the contract and checks that the clause text is there. An invented clause has no matching text, so the application rejects it. The model can still return a field in the wrong form, so the application also validates each response against the schema.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.3: "Develop accuracy verification systems to reduce hallucinations in FM responses"
Example: "confidence scoring and semantic similarity search for verification"
Example: "JSON Schema to enforce structured outputs"

Sources:

  • Structured data response with Amazon Bedrock: Prompt Engineering and Tool Use

  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models

  • Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

INCORRECT: Add an instruction to the system prompt that tells the model to extract clauses only from the uploaded contract and to answer "none found" when a clause is absent.
An instruction that limits the model to the given text, and lets the model say that it found nothing, is a good first step against invented answers. The system prompt here already limits the model to the contract text, and users still report invented clauses. An instruction guides the model, but it does not check the result. The application must check each clause against the contract before a user sees the clause.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job each week with the built-in Accuracy metric on a reference set of past contracts, and review the prompt when the score falls.
A model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock scores a model on a prepared set of prompts, for example with the built-in Accuracy metric. This is the right tool to compare models or prompt versions before a release. The job runs on the reference set, not on live requests. So the job never checks the clause that one user is about to read.

INCORRECT: Lower the temperature in the inference parameters of every request, so the model chooses higher-probability words and writes fewer clauses that are not in the contract.
Temperature controls how the model picks its next word. A lower value makes the model choose higher-probability words, so the answers are less random. This helps when answers vary too much from one request to the next. Here the inference parameters are already set so that answers vary as little as possible, and the model still invents clauses. A high-probability answer can still describe a clause that the contract does not contain.

The knowledge base reads the bucket through its own IAM service role. The role's permissions policy allows only reads on that bucket. The role's trust policy lets the Amazon Bedrock service assume the role, with no conditions.
Other teams will soon create more knowledge bases in the same account. The security team wants Amazon Bedrock to use the HR role only when it acts for the HR knowledge base, never for another knowledge base in this account or in any other account.
Which change to the HR role should the security team make?

options.text: Attach a permissions boundary to the role that allows read actions on the salary documents bucket, so the role cannot do more than that.
Add a condition to the role's trust policy that requires an sts:ExternalId value, and have the caller that assumes the role pass that value in each request.
Add conditions to the role's trust policy that require aws:SourceAccount to match the company's account and aws:SourceArn to match any knowledge base ARN in it.
Add conditions to the role's trust policy that require aws:SourceAccount to match the company's account and aws:SourceArn to match the HR knowledge base ARN.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add conditions to the role's trust policy that require aws:SourceAccount to match the company's account and aws:SourceArn to match the HR knowledge base ARN.
A role's trust policy says who may assume the role. When Amazon Bedrock assumes a service role, it acts for one of your resources, and the aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount condition keys check which resource and which account that is. With the full ARN of the HR knowledge base, Amazon Bedrock can assume the role only when it acts for that one knowledge base. A knowledge base that another team creates, in this account or in another, has a different ARN, so the trust policy does not let Amazon Bedrock assume the HR role for it. This is the protection that Amazon Bedrock recommends against the cross-service confused deputy problem.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "IAM policies to enforce secure data access patterns"

Sources:

  • Cross-service confused deputy prevention

  • Create a service role for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

  • The confused deputy problem

INCORRECT: Attach a permissions boundary to the role that allows read actions on the salary documents bucket, so the role cannot do more than that.
A permissions boundary sets the most that a role's identity-based policies can allow. It is a good way to cap the roles that developers create for their own work. The HR role already allows only reads on one bucket, so a boundary adds no new limit. A boundary also does not change who can assume the role. The risk here is that Amazon Bedrock acts for the wrong knowledge base, and only the trust policy controls that.

INCORRECT: Add a condition to the role's trust policy that requires an sts:ExternalId value, and have the caller that assumes the role pass that value in each request.
An external ID is a value that the caller passes when it assumes a role, and the role's trust policy checks it. It protects a role that another company's AWS account assumes, for example a monitoring vendor, and that company generates the value. Here the Amazon Bedrock service assumes the role for a knowledge base, not a user in another account. For a role that an AWS service assumes, the right checks are on the source of the request: the resource and the account that the service acts for.

INCORRECT: Add conditions to the role's trust policy that require aws:SourceAccount to match the company's account and aws:SourceArn to match any knowledge base ARN in it.
This is the pattern of the example trust policy for a knowledge base service role, with a wildcard in place of the knowledge base ID. It fits a role that every knowledge base in one account may share. It keeps out other accounts, but any knowledge base in this account matches the pattern. Other teams will create knowledge bases here, and the HR role must serve only the HR knowledge base. The best practice is to replace the wildcard with the ID of the knowledge base once it exists.

1. Patient names and Social Security numbers must be identified and redacted from the prompt text before the data is sent to the Foundation Model.

options.text: Send a copy of each chat log to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and set the retention setting of that log group to 30 days.
Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with sensitive information filters that mask PII types, such as names and email addresses, in the model's responses.
Run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the chat log bucket every day, and send its findings about names and Social Security numbers to the team.
Call Amazon Comprehend from an AWS Lambda function each time a chat log is written to the data lake, and replace names and Social Security numbers with placeholders.
Add an S3 Lifecycle rule to the chat log bucket that expires objects 30 days after creation, and also expires noncurrent versions if the bucket uses versioning.
Call Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities in each user message, and replace names and Social Security numbers with placeholders before the application calls Amazon Bedrock.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with sensitive information filters that mask PII types, such as names and email addresses, in the model's responses.
A guardrail's sensitive information filters find PII types, such as names, email addresses and phone numbers, in prompts and in model responses. With the mask action, the guardrail replaces each item in the response with its type, for example {NAME}, before the answer reaches the patient. This covers PII that the model writes in its own answer, as the second requirement asks.

CORRECT: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule to the chat log bucket that expires objects 30 days after creation, and also expires noncurrent versions if the bucket uses versioning.
An S3 Lifecycle rule with an expiration action removes objects a set number of days after they are created. Each chat log is written when its session ends, so a 30-day expiration removes the log about 30 days after the session. Amazon S3 can take a short time after the expiration date to remove an object. In a bucket with versioning, expiration only adds a delete marker and keeps the old version as a noncurrent version. A noncurrent version expiration action is then needed as well, so the logs are deleted for good.

CORRECT: Call Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities in each user message, and replace names and Social Security numbers with placeholders before the application calls Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Comprehend detects PII in English or Spanish text in real time. For each entity, it returns the type, such as NAME or SSN, and the character offsets where the entity starts and ends. The application uses these offsets to replace each name and Social Security number with a placeholder, and only then sends the prompt to Amazon Bedrock. The model never receives these values, as the first requirement asks.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter outputs"
Example: "Amazon S3 Lifecycle configurations to implement data retention policies"

Sources:

  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters

  • Detecting PII entities

  • Lifecycle configuration elements

INCORRECT: Send a copy of each chat log to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and set the retention setting of that log group to 30 days.
CloudWatch Logs keeps log events in log groups, and a retention setting deletes the events in a log group after the set number of days. It fits application logs that a team only needs for a short time. But this option only sends a copy. The original raw chat logs stay in the data lake, and the third requirement asks for those logs to be deleted for good after 30 days.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the chat log bucket every day, and send its findings about names and Social Security numbers to the team.
Amazon Macie finds sensitive data in objects stored in Amazon S3, and a discovery job can run once or on a schedule. It is the right tool to learn where PII sits in a data lake. But it looks at data after it is stored, and it reports findings without changing the text. The first requirement asks to remove names and Social Security numbers before the prompt reaches the model, and a daily scan of the log bucket happens long after that.

INCORRECT: Call Amazon Comprehend from an AWS Lambda function each time a chat log is written to the data lake, and replace names and Social Security numbers with placeholders.
Amazon S3 can invoke an AWS Lambda function each time a new object is written, and the function can call Amazon Comprehend to find names and Social Security numbers in the stored text. This fits a data lake where stored records must not keep PII. But it runs after the chat, on the log. The first requirement asks to remove these values from the prompt before it reaches the model, and by the time the log is written, the model has already seen them.

Company policy says every application stack must use the company's Amazon Bedrock guardrail and a CloudWatch Logs log group with a set retention. A central team keeps one approved AWS CloudFormation template for this stack.
Audits found teams that had changed their own copy of the template. Each team must now start new stacks by itself, whenever it needs one, from the approved template only. Team roles may not create IAM roles, and the template creates one for the application.
How should the central team give the product teams these stacks?
questions.promptText:
A company has 20 product teams, each in its own AWS account in AWS Organizations, and each team builds applications with Amazon Bedrock. Company policy says every application stack must use the company's Amazon Bedrock guardrail and a CloudWatch Logs log group with a set retention. A central team keeps one approved AWS CloudFormation template for this stack.
Audits found teams that had changed their own copy of the template. Each team must now start new stacks by itself, whenever it needs one, from the approved template only. Team roles may not create IAM roles, and the template creates one for the application.
How should the central team give the product teams these stacks?

options.text: Share the template from an Amazon S3 bucket that the team accounts can read, and give team roles the IAM permissions to create the resources in the template.
Publish the template as an AWS Service Catalog product in a portfolio shared with the team accounts, and add a launch constraint that names a launch role for the product.
Push the template from the central account to each team account with CloudFormation StackSets, and turn on automatic deployment for accounts that join the organization later.
Share the template from an Amazon S3 bucket that the team accounts can read, and let team roles pass a CloudFormation service role that creates the resources in the template.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Publish the template as an AWS Service Catalog product in a portfolio shared with the team accounts, and add a launch constraint that names a launch role for the product.
AWS Service Catalog lets a central team publish approved CloudFormation templates as products in a portfolio, and end users deploy only the products they are given. The central team can share the portfolio with the team accounts, and a receiving account cannot change the shared products or their constraints. A launch constraint names the IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when a user launches, updates or ends the product. So the launch role, not the team's role, creates the application's IAM role, and team roles need only the rights to launch the product. When the constraint gives a role name, each account uses its own role with that name.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.3: "Create organizational governance systems to ensure consistent oversight of FM implementations"
Example: "comprehensive frameworks that align with organizational policies, regulatory requirements, and responsible AI principles"

Sources:

  • AWS Service Catalog Launch Constraints

  • Sharing a Portfolio

  • Managing stacks across accounts and Regions with StackSets

INCORRECT: Share the template from an Amazon S3 bucket that the team accounts can read, and give team roles the IAM permissions to create the resources in the template.
A shared bucket is a simple way to share a template, and teams with the right IAM permissions can deploy it with CloudFormation whenever they want. This works when teams may create every resource in the stack. Here team roles may not create IAM roles, and the template creates one, so these permissions break company policy. Each team would also deploy from its own copy of the template, which is the problem that the audits found.

INCORRECT: Push the template from the central account to each team account with CloudFormation StackSets, and turn on automatic deployment for accounts that join the organization later.
StackSets create, update or delete stacks in many accounts and Regions with one operation from an administrator account. With AWS Organizations, automatic deployment also adds the stack to new accounts when they join. This fits a stack that every account needs once, such as a shared baseline. Here each team starts its own new stacks, at the time it builds an application. With StackSets, the central team starts each deployment, not the product teams.

INCORRECT: Share the template from an Amazon S3 bucket that the team accounts can read, and let team roles pass a CloudFormation service role that creates the resources in the template.
A CloudFormation service role lets CloudFormation create, update or delete the stack's resources with the role's credentials. The user who starts the stack then needs permission to use CloudFormation and to pass the role (iam:PassRole), but not the rights to every resource. This fits teams that may deploy their own templates without broad rights, and it keeps IAM role creation away from team roles. But a team role that can pass the service role can use it with a template that the team chose, including a changed copy. The audits found changed copies, and each team must start stacks from the approved template only.

A company runs an internal HR assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Employees ask in English which leave they can take, and the model answers from the company's written leave policy. Every application calls the Converse API with the same shared guardrail.
An audit found that the assistant told part-time employees they could take leave that the policy gives only to full-time staff with more than one year of service.
For each answer, the compliance team needs a result that says if it follows the leave policy and names the rules behind that result. Employees must still get answers about leave. The check must run in the shared guardrail, not in code that each application team writes.
Which change meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company runs an internal HR assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Employees ask in English which leave they can take, and the model answers from the company's written leave policy. Every application calls the Converse API with the same shared guardrail.
An audit found that the assistant told part-time employees they could take leave that the policy gives only to full-time staff with more than one year of service.
For each answer, the compliance team needs a result that says if it follows the leave policy and names the rules behind that result. Employees must still get answers about leave. The check must run in the shared guardrail, not in code that each application team writes.
Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a contextual grounding check to the shared guardrail with the leave policy document as the grounding source, so the guardrail scores each answer against it.
Add a Lambda function after each Converse call that sends the answer and the leave policy to a second model, which judges if the answer follows the policy.
Add an Automated Reasoning policy that is built from the leave policy document to the shared guardrail, so the guardrail checks each answer against its rules.
Add a denied topic for leave eligibility to the shared guardrail, so the guardrail blocks the questions and the answers about who can take each type of leave.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an Automated Reasoning policy that is built from the leave policy document to the shared guardrail, so the guardrail checks each answer against its rules.
An Automated Reasoning policy holds rules and variables that Amazon Bedrock extracts from a source document, here the written leave policy. When the guardrail uses the policy, it translates each question and answer into logic and checks the claims against the rules. Each answer gets a finding, such as VALID or INVALID. A VALID finding lists the rules that support the answer, and an INVALID finding lists the rules that the answer breaks, for example the rule that gives this leave only to full-time staff. That is the result the compliance team asked for. Automated Reasoning checks only report findings and do not block content, so employees still get answers about leave. The check runs in the shared guardrail, and the questions are in English, which these checks require.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.3: "Develop policy-compliant AI systems to ensure adherence to responsible AI practices"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails based on policy requirements"

Sources:

  • What are Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails?

  • Automated Reasoning checks concepts

  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses

INCORRECT: Add a contextual grounding check to the shared guardrail with the leave policy document as the grounding source, so the guardrail scores each answer against it.
A contextual grounding check compares each answer with a grounding source and with the user's question. It returns a grounding score and a relevance score, and it blocks answers that score below the threshold that you set. It is a good choice for summaries and for question answering over text that the application sends with each request. Here the compliance team needs a result that names the policy rules behind it. A score does not name any rule, so the team cannot see which part of the policy an answer breaks. The check also does not support chatbot use cases.

INCORRECT: Add a Lambda function after each Converse call that sends the answer and the leave policy to a second model, which judges if the answer follows the policy.
A second model that judges each answer against a reference text is a common way to check answers, and a Lambda function can call it after each model call. It fits when each team can add the check to its own application. Here the check must run in the shared guardrail, not in code that each application team writes. This design adds a function and a second model call to every application.

INCORRECT: Add a denied topic for leave eligibility to the shared guardrail, so the guardrail blocks the questions and the answers about who can take each type of leave.
A denied topic blocks prompts and answers about a subject that the application must not discuss, such as investment advice in a bank assistant. Here employees must still get answers about leave, and leave eligibility is the main thing they ask about. This topic would block those questions. It also does not check if an answer follows the policy.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A media analytics company processes full movie scripts using an Amazon Bedrock model (Claude Sonnet) to generate psychological profiles of main characters. Each script goes to the model once, in one request for all main characters. The application is highly effective, but the cost per analysis is exceeding the budget due to the massive number of input tokens required for full scripts. The data science team determines that while character dialogue is essential for the analysis, the extensive scene descriptions and technical camera directions are irrelevant to the character profiling task.
Which implementation strategy should the team use to reduce token costs while maintaining the effectiveness of the application?
questions.promptText:
A media analytics company processes full movie scripts using an Amazon Bedrock model (Claude Sonnet) to generate psychological profiles of main characters. Each script goes to the model once, in one request for all main characters. The application is highly effective, but the cost per analysis is exceeding the budget due to the massive number of input tokens required for full scripts. The data science team determines that while character dialogue is essential for the analysis, the extensive scene descriptions and technical camera directions are irrelevant to the character profiling task.
Which implementation strategy should the team use to reduce token costs while maintaining the effectiveness of the application?

options.text: Cache each full script as a prompt prefix in Amazon Bedrock, and have later requests with the same script read it from the cache at a lower input rate.
Set a lower maxTokens value in each request to Claude Sonnet, so that the model writes shorter profiles and each analysis uses fewer output tokens.
Add an instruction to the prompt for Claude Sonnet that asks for shorter profiles, so that the model writes less and each analysis uses fewer output tokens.
Add a pre-processing step that uses parsing logic or a lightweight model to remove scene descriptions and camera directions, and send only the dialogue to Claude Sonnet.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a pre-processing step that uses parsing logic or a lightweight model to remove scene descriptions and camera directions, and send only the dialogue to Claude Sonnet.
This is context pruning. The team knows which part of each script the task needs: the dialogue. A parser, or a small low-cost model, removes the scene descriptions and camera directions before the main model call. Claude Sonnet then reads far fewer input tokens, and the question says that the input tokens of full scripts cause the high cost. The dialogue reaches the model in full, so the text that the analysis needs does not change, and the profiles keep their quality.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.1: "Develop token efficiency systems to reduce FM costs while maintaining effectiveness"
Example: "context pruning"

Sources:

  • GENCOST03-BP01 Optimize prompt token length
  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

INCORRECT: Cache each full script as a prompt prefix in Amazon Bedrock, and have later requests with the same script read it from the cache at a lower input rate.
Prompt caching keeps a long prompt prefix, such as a document, so that later requests that start with the same prefix do not process it again. Tokens read from the cache cost less than normal input tokens. It fits users who ask several questions about the same document before the cache expires. Here each script goes to the model once, in one request for all main characters. No later request repeats the script, so no request ever reads it from the cache.

INCORRECT: Set a lower maxTokens value in each request to Claude Sonnet, so that the model writes shorter profiles and each analysis uses fewer output tokens.
The maxTokens value caps the number of tokens that the model can generate in one response. Teams lower it when long answers make up most of the cost. In this company the cost comes from the input side: the full scripts, with their scene descriptions and camera directions. The model still reads every one of those tokens, and a cap that is too tight can stop a profile before it ends.

INCORRECT: Add an instruction to the prompt for Claude Sonnet that asks for shorter profiles, so that the model writes less and each analysis uses fewer output tokens.
An instruction that asks the model to be brief is a simple way to get shorter answers, and shorter answers cost less when output tokens make up most of the cost. Here the cost comes from the input tokens of the full scripts. The instruction makes the prompt a little longer, and every scene description and camera direction stays in it. So the input cost does not go down.
