The summary must appear as one complete block when the page opens, because it sits in a product comparison table. Most products get only a few views each day, and every view must show the summary with no wait. The quality team approved summaries from Claude Sonnet only.
Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online retailer shows an AI summary of customer reviews on each of its 30,000 product pages. Today, each page calls Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock when it loads, and shoppers wait several seconds for the summary. The store adds new reviews once a day, in one load at night.
The summary must appear as one complete block when the page opens, because it sits in a product comparison table. Most products get only a few views each day, and every view must show the summary with no wait. The quality team approved summaries from Claude Sonnet only.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Generate each product summary with Claude Sonnet when the page loads, and stream the text into the page with ConverseStream while the model writes it.
Generate each product summary with Claude Sonnet on the first page view, store it in Amazon ElastiCache with a time to live, and read it on later views.
Generate each product summary with Claude Haiku when the page loads, so a fast and smaller model writes the complete summary for the page sooner.
Generate each product summary with Claude Sonnet after the nightly review load, store it in Amazon DynamoDB, and read the stored summary when the page loads.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Generate each product summary with Claude Sonnet after the nightly review load, store it in Amazon DynamoDB, and read the stored summary when the page loads.
This design computes each summary before any shopper asks for it. The input of each summary is known, and it changes only once a day, when the new reviews arrive. So a job can run the model for every product right after the nightly load and store each summary in DynamoDB. When a page loads, the application reads a stored item and makes no model call. The summary is complete at once, and every view is fast, even the first view of a product that day. The summaries still come from Claude Sonnet, the model that the quality team approved.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.1: "Create responsive AI systems to address latency-cost tradeoffs and improve the user experience with FMs"
Example: "pre-computation to perform predictable queries"

Sources:

  • Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock

  • ConverseStream (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Caching strategies for Memcached (Amazon ElastiCache)

INCORRECT: Generate each product summary with Claude Sonnet when the page loads, and stream the text into the page with ConverseStream while the model writes it.
ConverseStream returns the model's answer in a stream, so the page can show the text while the model writes it. Streaming is a good way to cut the wait in a chat, where users read an answer as it grows. Here the summary must appear as one complete block in a comparison table. With streaming, the complete summary still takes as long as the model needs to write it, so shoppers still wait.

INCORRECT: Generate each product summary with Claude Sonnet on the first page view, store it in Amazon ElastiCache with a time to live, and read it on later views.
Loading a result into a cache on the first request, with a time to live, is a common pattern for data that many users read again and again. The first request is a cache miss, so it still waits for the model. Here most products get only a few views each day, and the reviews change every night, so many views would be the first view of a new summary. Those shoppers would still wait several seconds.

INCORRECT: Generate each product summary with Claude Haiku when the page loads, so a fast and smaller model writes the complete summary for the page sooner.
Claude Haiku is a fast and cost-effective model, and a smaller model is a real choice for time-sensitive requests when its answers are good enough for the task. Here the quality team approved summaries from Claude Sonnet only. This design also still calls a model at every page view, so shoppers still wait for it.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A market research firm processes 50,000 customer feedback surveys every night to extract sentiment and key themes. The feedback text is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The current implementation uses a fleet of AWS Lambda functions triggered by S3 events to call the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API for each file. However, this approach frequently results in ThrottlingException errors, high operational overhead for managing retries, and suboptimal throughput.
Which architecture change should the developer implement to maximize throughput and resource efficiency for this workload?
questions.promptText:
A market research firm processes 50,000 customer feedback surveys every night to extract sentiment and key themes. The feedback text is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The current implementation uses a fleet of AWS Lambda functions triggered by S3 events to call the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API for each file. However, this approach frequently results in ThrottlingException errors, high operational overhead for managing retries, and suboptimal throughput.
Which architecture change should the developer implement to maximize throughput and resource efficiency for this workload?

options.text: Replace the Lambda-based architecture with Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference. Aggregate the survey data into JSONL files stored in S3, and submit a CreateModelInvocationJob request to process the entire dataset asynchronously.

Create Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for the model with a 1-month commitment. Configure the Lambda functions to target the Provisioned Model ARN to ensure guaranteed capacity during the nightly processing window.

Replace the per-file Lambda triggers with an Amazon SQS queue ingesting the S3 event notifications. Configure a Lambda consumer with a batch size of 100 and reserved concurrency of 50, processing surveys in controlled parallel bursts against the On-Demand InvokeModel API throughout the night.

Implement a "prompt packing" strategy within the Lambda functions to concatenate 10 surveys into a single prompt. Use the InvokeModel API to process these packed prompts, thereby reducing the total number of API calls by 90%.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Replace the Lambda-based architecture with Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference. Aggregate the survey data into JSONL files stored in S3, and submit a CreateModelInvocationJob request to process the entire dataset asynchronously.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference takes many prompts from JSONL files in Amazon S3 as one job, which the firm starts with CreateModelInvocationJob, and it writes the responses back to S3. The job runs asynchronously, so the firm no longer sends thousands of separate InvokeModel calls from Lambda functions, and it no longer handles the throttling and the retries of each call. The nightly surveys do not need an answer right away, which is the kind of work that batch inference is made for. For supported models, batch inference is also priced lower than on-demand calls.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.3: "Implement FM throughput optimization to address the specific throughput challenges of GenAI workloads"
Example: "batch inference strategies"

Sources:

  • Process multiple prompts with batch inference
  • Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Create Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for the model with a 1-month commitment. Configure the Lambda functions to target the Provisioned Model ARN to ensure guaranteed capacity during the nightly processing window.
Provisioned Throughput gives a model a fixed, higher level of throughput, and AWS bills it every hour until you delete it. It fits a workload that uses that throughput through most of the day. This option takes it with a 1-month commitment, so the firm cannot delete it before the month ends and pays for every hour of the month. The surveys need the capacity for only a few hours each night.

INCORRECT: Replace the per-file Lambda triggers with an Amazon SQS queue ingesting the S3 event notifications. Configure a Lambda consumer with a batch size of 100 and reserved concurrency of 50, processing surveys in controlled parallel bursts against the On-Demand InvokeModel API throughout the night.
An SQS queue in front of a Lambda function with a concurrency limit is a real way to smooth bursts and stop throttling. But the firm still sends 50,000 separate on-demand calls, and it still sets the concurrency and handles the failed calls itself. Batch inference takes the whole set as one job and needs no concurrency settings in the firm's code. For supported models, it is also priced lower than the same calls on demand, which fits a nightly job that does not need answers right away.

INCORRECT: Implement a "prompt packing" strategy within the Lambda functions to concatenate 10 surveys into a single prompt. Use the InvokeModel API to process these packed prompts, thereby reducing the total number of API calls by 90%.
Packing several surveys into one prompt cuts the number of calls. But each call gets longer, and the Lambda code must split the model's answer back into ten results, one for each survey. The functions still call InvokeModel on demand, so their tokens still count against the same on-demand quotas, and the firm still handles throttling and retries in its own code. Batch inference takes the whole set as one job and adds no new parsing step.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A travel agency operates a GenAI-powered trip planner that uses Amazon Bedrock. Users frequently submit slightly different variations of the same requests, such as "Plan a 3-day trip to Paris" and "I need a 3-day itinerary for Paris." These requests currently trigger distinct, full model invocations, resulting in unnecessary costs and latency.
The developer needs to implement a caching mechanism that recognizes these variations as the same intent and serves a previously generated response.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A travel agency operates a GenAI-powered trip planner that uses Amazon Bedrock. Users frequently submit slightly different variations of the same requests, such as "Plan a 3-day trip to Paris" and "I need a 3-day itinerary for Paris." These requests currently trigger distinct, full model invocations, resulting in unnecessary costs and latency.
The developer needs to implement a caching mechanism that recognizes these variations as the same intent and serves a previously generated response.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Implement semantic caching using a vector database (e.g., Amazon OpenSearch Service). Generate embeddings for incoming user queries and search the cache for vectors with a high cosine similarity. Serve the associated cached response if a match is found.

Implement a normalized-key response cache using Amazon ElastiCache. Lowercase each incoming query and strip stop words, then use the processed string as the cache key. Serve the cached response only when the normalized key matches a previous request exactly.
Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching to cache the system instructions and few-shot examples at the beginning of the prompt context, reducing the processing time for the static portions of the input.
Implement deterministic request hashing by calculating a SHA-256 hash of the user's input prompt. Store the hash and response in Amazon DynamoDB and perform a look-up before invoking the model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Implement semantic caching using a vector database (e.g., Amazon OpenSearch Service). Generate embeddings for incoming user queries and search the cache for vectors with a high cosine similarity. Serve the associated cached response if a match is found.
Semantic caching compares the meaning of requests, not their words. The application turns each query into an embedding and searches the cache for earlier queries with a similar embedding. When the closest match scores above a similarity threshold that the team sets, the application returns the stored response and does not call the model. "Plan a 3-day trip to Paris" and "I need a 3-day itinerary for Paris" use different words but have close embeddings, so the second request gets the stored answer, with no model cost and no wait for a new answer. Amazon OpenSearch Service is one store for the cached embeddings, and other stores with vector search, such as Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, also work. The threshold needs tuning: a higher value gives fewer wrong matches but fewer cache hits, and a value that is too low returns answers to questions that users did not ask.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.4: "Create intelligent caching systems to reduce costs and improve response times by avoiding unnecessary FM invocations"
Example: "semantic caching"

Sources:

  • AGENTCOST02-BP03 Use intelligent caching to reduce redundant model invocations
  • Using Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for semantic caching
  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

INCORRECT: Implement a normalized-key response cache using Amazon ElastiCache. Lowercase each incoming query and strip stop words, then use the processed string as the cache key. Serve the cached response only when the normalized key matches a previous request exactly.
Normalizing a query removes differences in capital letters and filler words, and an exact key lookup in Amazon ElastiCache is fast. This fits requests that repeat with small surface changes, such as the same text typed in capital letters. It does not make two different phrasings the same. The example queries become "plan 3-day trip paris" and "need 3-day itinerary paris", which are still two different keys, so the second request misses the cache and calls the model again. ElastiCache itself can hold a semantic cache when it compares embeddings with vector search. This option fails because it compares exact strings.

INCORRECT: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching to cache the system instructions and few-shot examples at the beginning of the prompt context, reducing the processing time for the static portions of the input.
Prompt caching stores the start of a prompt, such as long system instructions and few-shot examples. Later requests that repeat exactly the same start read it from the cache and do not process it again. This lowers input token cost and the time before the answer starts, so it fits a long system prompt or a large document that many requests reuse. It does not return an earlier answer. The model still writes a new answer for every trip request, so each variation of the Paris request still pays for a full model call. The cached part also expires after a short time without use.

INCORRECT: Implement deterministic request hashing by calculating a SHA-256 hash of the user's input prompt. Store the hash and response in Amazon DynamoDB and perform a look-up before invoking the model.
Deterministic request hashing turns each prompt into a fixed key, here with SHA-256, and stores the response in DynamoDB under that key. A hash matches only when the text is exactly the same. If one character changes, the hash is completely different. This pattern fits requests that repeat word for word, for example a fixed template with no free text. Here users write the same request in different words, so the two Paris requests get two different hashes, and the second request misses the cache and calls the model again.

A company runs a RAG application on Amazon Bedrock. It stores document chunks and their embeddings in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL table with the pgvector extension, and the table has an HNSW index. The application logs the time of each step of every request.
After last week's code release, the retrieval step went from well under a second to several seconds. The time the model takes to write each answer did not change, and the table size and the traffic did not change. The database now works much harder: its processor use and its disk reads went up sharply after the release.
Which step will show the team the cause of the slow retrieval?

options.text: Use OpenTelemetry tracing with AWS X-Ray to compare how long each call in a request takes before and after the release.
Use CloudWatch Database Insights in Advanced mode to compare the execution plans of the top similarity search query before and after the release.
Use CloudWatch graphs of the CPUUtilization and ReadIOPS metrics of the Aurora DB instances to compare their load before and after the release.
Use Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs in CloudWatch Logs Insights to compare the size of the prompts and responses before and after the release.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use CloudWatch Database Insights in Advanced mode to compare the execution plans of the top similarity search query before and after the release.
CloudWatch Database Insights shows which SQL statements add the most load to an Aurora database. In Advanced mode, it also captures the execution plans of the top SQL statements on Aurora PostgreSQL, and it lets the team compare the plans of one statement over time. An execution plan shows how the database reads the data, for example with an index scan or with a sequential scan of the whole table. Here the table, the traffic and the model did not change, and only the code did, so the team needs to see how the database now runs the similarity search query. One way a release causes this with pgvector: an index works only when the query uses the distance operator that matches the operator class of the index. If the new code uses another distance operator, the plan shows a sequential scan of every row instead of the HNSW index, which also explains the extra processor use and disk reads.

INCORRECT: Use OpenTelemetry tracing with AWS X-Ray to compare how long each call in a request takes before and after the release.
OpenTelemetry tracing with AWS X-Ray shows how long each downstream call in a request takes, so it finds the slow step when a team cannot see it. Here the application already logs the time of each step, and the team knows that the retrieval step is slow. A trace would show the same slow database call again. It would not show why the database needs more time inside that call.

INCORRECT: Use CloudWatch graphs of the CPUUtilization and ReadIOPS metrics of the Aurora DB instances to compare their load before and after the release.
CPUUtilization and ReadIOPS are metrics of each Aurora DB instance. They show how busy each instance is: how much of its processor it uses and how many disk reads it makes each second. Graphs and alarms on them fit capacity planning, for example to see when the instances need more capacity as traffic grows. Here the team already knows that processor use and disk reads went up after the release while the traffic stayed the same. These graphs would show that rise again, but not which query causes it or why.

INCORRECT: Use Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs in CloudWatch Logs Insights to compare the size of the prompts and responses before and after the release.
Model invocation logging records the request and the response of each model call, with their token counts, and CloudWatch Logs Insights can compare them over time. This is the right tool when answers get slower because prompts grew, for example when retrieval sends more chunks to the model. Here the time the model takes to write each answer did not change. The slow step is retrieval, which runs in the database before the model call.

A support platform sends each customer email to a model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. The model returns a category label and a one-line reason. Each request sets the largest output size that the model allows, copied from a code sample, but the model invocation logs show that every answer is short.

CloudWatch shows that the tokens sent and received each minute stay far below the tokens-per-minute quota, and the calls per minute stay below their quota. Policy says every request must stay in the application's Region, and a cut label breaks the routing.
Which change stops the throttling within these rules?
questions.promptText:
A support platform sends each customer email to a model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. The model returns a category label and a one-line reason. Each request sets the largest output size that the model allows, copied from a code sample, but the model invocation logs show that every answer is short.
At busy hours, many calls fail with ThrottlingException. CloudWatch shows that the tokens sent and received each minute stay far below the tokens-per-minute quota, and the calls per minute stay below their quota. Policy says every request must stay in the application's Region, and a cut label breaks the routing.
Which change stops the throttling within these rules?

options.text: Set maxTokens just above the largest output token count in the model invocation logs, so each request holds back less of the token quota when it starts.
Send each request through a geographic cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can process it in one of several Regions in the same geography.
Request a higher requests-per-minute quota for the model through Service Quotas, so that more calls can start in each minute before Amazon Bedrock throttles the extra calls.
Send each request through a global cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can process it in one of the supported commercial Regions worldwide.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set maxTokens just above the largest output token count in the model invocation logs, so each request holds back less of the token quota when it starts.
Amazon Bedrock counts tokens against the tokens-per-minute quota at two points. When a request starts, it deducts the input tokens plus the maximum output tokens of the request (maxTokens), and it throttles the request if this goes over the quota. When the request ends, it counts the tokens that the request really used and gives the rest back to the quota. Here every request holds back the largest output size that the model allows, while the real answers are short. The quota fills up at the start of each request, so calls fail while the real token use stays far below the quota. The model invocation logs show the output token count of each answer. A maxTokens value just above the largest one holds back far fewer tokens and still leaves room for every complete label.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.5: "Create efficient resource allocation systems specifically for FM workloads"
Example: "capacity planning for token processing requirements"

Sources:

  • How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock

  • InferenceConfiguration (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference

INCORRECT: Send each request through a geographic cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can process it in one of several Regions in the same geography.
A geographic cross-Region inference profile lets Amazon Bedrock process each request in a Region of one geography, such as US or EU, which helps with traffic bursts. It fits a team whose requests may leave the source Region as long as they stay in that geography. Here policy says every request must stay in the application's Region, so a cross-Region profile breaks the policy.

INCORRECT: Request a higher requests-per-minute quota for the model through Service Quotas, so that more calls can start in each minute before Amazon Bedrock throttles the extra calls.
The requests-per-minute quota caps how many inference requests the account can send to the model in one minute. When calls fail because they reach that cap, a higher quota through Service Quotas is a real fix, where AWS marks the quota as adjustable. Here CloudWatch shows that the calls per minute stay below their quota, so this cap does not throttle the calls. The throttling comes from the tokens that each request holds back when it starts, and a higher request quota leaves that cause in place.

INCORRECT: Send each request through a global cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can process it in one of the supported commercial Regions worldwide.
A global cross-Region inference profile lets Amazon Bedrock process requests in supported commercial Regions worldwide, not only in one geography. It spreads requests across more Regions than a geographic profile, and it fits a team with no rule about where its requests run. This team has a strict rule: every request must stay in the application's Region. Requests that run in other Regions of the world break that rule.

A healthcare startup runs a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application on 50 million medical journal abstracts in Amazon OpenSearch Service. Each query runs an exact k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) search, which compares the query with every vector in the index. As the data grew, the search time rose above 4 seconds, and requests from the chat front end now time out. Most questions are not limited to one specialty, so they use no metadata filter. The cluster budget cannot grow, and tests with fewer vector dimensions lowered relevance on medical terms. The data nodes have enough free memory for any type of k-NN index on these vectors.

How can the startup reduce the search time and keep high relevance?
questions.promptText:
A healthcare startup runs a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application on 50 million medical journal abstracts in Amazon OpenSearch Service. Each query runs an exact k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) search, which compares the query with every vector in the index. As the data grew, the search time rose above 4 seconds, and requests from the chat front end now time out. Most questions are not limited to one specialty, so they use no metadata filter. The cluster budget cannot grow, and tests with fewer vector dimensions lowered relevance on medical terms. The data nodes have enough free memory for any type of k-NN index on these vectors.
How can the startup reduce the search time and keep high relevance?

options.text: Add a metadata filter on the medical specialty before the exact k-NN search, so that each query scores only the vectors of one specialty.
Move the data nodes to larger memory-optimized instance types, so that the exact k-NN search keeps every vector in memory while it scores them.
Reduce the embeddings to far fewer dimensions before a full re-index, so that the exact k-NN search does less work for each vector that it scores.
Re-index the embeddings into a k-NN index that uses the HNSW method, so that each query runs an approximate nearest neighbor search over the vectors.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Re-index the embeddings into a k-NN index that uses the HNSW method, so that each query runs an approximate nearest neighbor search over the vectors.
An exact k-NN search compares the query with every vector, so the search time grows with the size of the index. HNSW is an approximate nearest neighbor algorithm. At indexing time, HNSW builds a graph that connects vectors that are close to each other, and each query searches only part of this graph. This makes approximate k-NN the best choice for large indexes that need low latency. The results are close to the exact results, though not always the same. The HNSW graphs need memory, and the data nodes have enough free memory for any k-NN index on these vectors. The startup re-indexes the existing vectors and needs no new embeddings.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.2: "Enhance retrieval performance to improve the relevance and speed of retrieved information for FM context augmentation"
Example: "index optimization"

Sources:

  • Amazon OpenSearch Service's vector database capabilities explained

  • Supported instance types in Amazon OpenSearch Service

INCORRECT: Add a metadata filter on the medical specialty before the exact k-NN search, so that each query scores only the vectors of one specialty.
Exact k-NN with a filter first is a good pattern when each query targets a small part of the data, because the search then scores only the vectors that pass the filter. Here most questions are not limited to one specialty, so they use no metadata filter. Those queries would still score all 50 million vectors, and their search time would not change.

INCORRECT: Move the data nodes to larger memory-optimized instance types, so that the exact k-NN search keeps every vector in memory while it scores them.
Vector search needs memory, and larger memory-optimized instances are the right step when a cluster does not have enough memory. Here the cluster budget cannot grow. Larger nodes also do not change how an exact search works. The search still compares every query with every vector, so the search time keeps growing with the data.

INCORRECT: Reduce the embeddings to far fewer dimensions before a full re-index, so that the exact k-NN search does less work for each vector that it scores.
Fewer dimensions make each vector smaller, so each distance calculation needs less memory and less work. This fits a task where vectors with fewer dimensions still give enough relevance. Here the tests with fewer dimensions lowered relevance on medical terms. The search would also still be exact and would still score every vector.

questions.promptHtml:
A news agency uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. The vector index contains embeddings of news articles. To ensure content freshness, thousands of articles are updated, replaced, or deleted every day. No article changes overnight, and every change must be searchable within one second.
After several weeks of operation, the retrieval latency has increased significantly, causing timeouts in the GenAI application. Amazon CloudWatch metrics show a high number of DeletedDocuments and an increasing segment count in the OpenSearch cluster, despite the total number of active articles remaining constant. CPU utilization stays low.
Which operational management system should the developer implement to resolve the performance degradation and maintain reliability?
questions.promptText:
A news agency uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. The vector index contains embeddings of news articles. To ensure content freshness, thousands of articles are updated, replaced, or deleted every day. No article changes overnight, and every change must be searchable within one second.
After several weeks of operation, the retrieval latency has increased significantly, causing timeouts in the GenAI application. Amazon CloudWatch metrics show a high number of DeletedDocuments and an increasing segment count in the OpenSearch cluster, despite the total number of active articles remaining constant. CPU utilization stays low.
Which operational management system should the developer implement to resolve the performance degradation and maintain reliability?

options.text: An EventBridge Scheduler schedule runs a Lambda function each morning, so the function sets the replica count of the vector index to two for the busy hours.
An EventBridge Scheduler schedule runs a Lambda function each night, so the function calls the force merge API on the vector index of the OpenSearch domain.
An EventBridge Scheduler schedule runs a Lambda function each night, so the function raises the refresh_interval of the vector index to 30 seconds for the next day.
A change to the domain configuration adds data nodes, so each node holds fewer shards of the vector index and runs fewer searches at a time.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An EventBridge Scheduler schedule runs a Lambda function each night, so the function calls the force merge API on the vector index of the OpenSearch domain.
In OpenSearch, an update or a delete does not remove the old document from disk at once. OpenSearch marks the document as deleted and removes it from disk only when it merges segments. The more segments a node holds, the longer each search takes. That is what the metrics show here: the DeletedDocuments count is high and the segment count grows, while the number of live articles stays the same. The force merge API merges the segments of an index and removes its deleted documents. AWS advises force merge on indices that get no writes, and this index gets no changes overnight. So an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts an AWS Lambda function each night, and the function calls the force merge API on the vector index. The cleanup becomes a routine that runs with no person involved.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.5: "Create vector store operational management systems to ensure optimal vector store operation and reliability for FM augmentation"
Example: "automated index optimization routines"

Sources:

  • How do I troubleshoot search latency spikes in my Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster?
  • Monitoring OpenSearch cluster metrics with Amazon CloudWatch
  • What is Amazon EventBridge Scheduler?

INCORRECT: An EventBridge Scheduler schedule runs a Lambda function each morning, so the function sets the replica count of the vector index to two for the busy hours.
A replica shard is a full copy of a primary shard. More replicas during the busy hours help when many searches arrive at the same time and the nodes run short of CPU, because more nodes can answer them. Here CPU utilization stays low, so the nodes are not busy. Each replica also holds the same many segments and the same deleted documents, so a search on it is as slow as a search on the primary.

INCORRECT: An EventBridge Scheduler schedule runs a Lambda function each night, so the function raises the refresh_interval of the vector index to 30 seconds for the next day.
A refresh makes recent changes visible to search, and each refresh can create a new small segment. The default interval is one second. Teams often raise it to 30 seconds or more during heavy writing, because fewer refreshes create fewer segments. This use case does not allow it: every change must be searchable within one second. A longer interval would also leave the deleted documents that are already in the index where they are.

INCORRECT: A change to the domain configuration adds data nodes, so each node holds fewer shards of the vector index and runs fewer searches at a time.
Adding data nodes is the right fix when a cluster runs short of CPU or memory, because each node then carries less of the work. Here CPU utilization stays low, so the cluster has capacity to spare. The problem is inside the index. A shard that moves to a new node keeps the same deleted documents and the same many segments, so its searches stay slow.

The data science team previously relied on ROUGE-N scores, but these metrics failed to capture these semantic errors. A financial services firm has developed a Generative AI application using Amazon Bedrock to summarize lengthy earnings call transcripts. During beta testing, analysts reported that while the summaries read smoothly, they occasionally contain figures that do not exist in the source transcript (hallucinations) or fail to address the specific financial metrics requested by the user. The data science team previously relied on ROUGE-N scores, but these metrics failed to capture these semantic errors. The team must score summaries of new transcripts, and no reference summaries exist for them.
Which evaluation strategy should the developer implement to accurately assess the quality of the model's outputs regarding these specific issues?

options.text: Run an automatic Amazon Bedrock evaluation job for text summarization, and score each summary with the Robustness metric on changed copies of each transcript.
Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and score each summary with the built-in Logical coherence and Professional style and tone metrics.
Run an automatic Amazon Bedrock evaluation job for text summarization, and score each summary with the Accuracy metric against the reference summaries.
Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and score each summary with the built-in Faithfulness and Relevance metrics.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and score each summary with the built-in Faithfulness and Relevance metrics.
In a model evaluation job with a judge model, a second model grades each response against a metric. The built-in Faithfulness metric checks whether the response contains information that is not in the prompt. Here the prompt holds the transcript, so a figure in the summary that is not in the transcript lowers the score. The built-in Relevance metric measures how relevant the answer is to the prompt, so a summary that skips the financial metrics the user asked for scores low. Neither metric needs a reference summary, so the team can score the new transcripts. Both metrics judge meaning, which word overlap scores such as ROUGE-N cannot do.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.1: "Develop comprehensive assessment frameworks to evaluate the quality and effectiveness of FM outputs beyond traditional ML evaluation approaches"
Example: "metrics for relevance, factual accuracy, consistency, and fluency"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand model performance
  • Text summarization for model evaluation in Amazon Bedrock
  • Custom prompt dataset (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)

INCORRECT: Run an automatic Amazon Bedrock evaluation job for text summarization, and score each summary with the Robustness metric on changed copies of each transcript.
The Robustness metric changes each prompt a little, for example with typos, lower case text or numbers written as words, and measures how much the response changes. It suits a team that needs summaries to stay stable when the input is messy. It needs a reference summary for each prompt, and no reference summaries exist for the new transcripts that the team must score. The analysts also reported invented figures and missing metrics, not unstable summaries.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and score each summary with the built-in Logical coherence and Professional style and tone metrics.
Logical coherence looks for gaps and contradictions inside a response. Professional style and tone grades whether the style, format and tone suit a business setting. These metrics fit when summaries read badly or sound wrong for their readers. Here the analysts said the summaries read smoothly. The real problems are invented figures and missing metrics, and neither metric compares the summary with the transcript or with the user's request.

INCORRECT: Run an automatic Amazon Bedrock evaluation job for text summarization, and score each summary with the Accuracy metric against the reference summaries.
In an automatic job for text summarization, the Accuracy metric is a BERTScore: it compares the meaning of each summary with a reference summary that a person wrote. This works well when every test transcript has a reference summary. Here the team must score summaries of new transcripts, and no reference summaries exist for them. A close match to a reference would also not prove that each figure in the summary comes from the transcript.

Which TWO actions should the team take to choose the model?
Select TWO.

options.text: Put two of the candidate models behind an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt router, so each request goes to the model with the best predicted quality and cost.
Run a load test with production-like prompts against each candidate model, and compare the InvocationLatency metric of each model in Amazon CloudWatch.
Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model for each candidate model, on the same prompts and approved descriptions, and compare the Correctness scores.
Send a copy of live product page requests to each candidate model, keep the descriptions hidden from shoppers, and compare each model's token cost.
Send a small share of live product page requests to each candidate model, and compare the add-to-cart rate of each model's descriptions.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model for each candidate model, on the same prompts and approved descriptions, and compare the Correctness scores.
A model evaluation job with a judge model grades the responses of one generator model, so the team runs one job for each candidate. Each job uses the same prompt dataset: the product features as prompts and the approved descriptions as the ground truth. The built-in Correctness metric grades each generated description against that ground truth. Same prompts, same judge and same metric give a fair comparison of text quality, before any shopper sees a description.

CORRECT: Send a small share of live product page requests to each candidate model, and compare the add-to-cart rate of each model's descriptions.
An A/B test sends a small share of live traffic to each candidate and measures the result. The add-to-cart rate is a business outcome, so the team can measure it only when shoppers see the descriptions. Here each candidate model writes the descriptions for a small share of product page requests. The team then compares the add-to-cart rate of each model, which shows the business value that offline scores cannot show.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.2: "Create systematic model evaluation systems to identify optimal configurations"
Example: "A/B testing and canary testing of FMs"

Sources:

  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge

  • Use metrics to understand model performance

  • Understanding intelligent prompt routing in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Put two of the candidate models behind an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt router, so each request goes to the model with the best predicted quality and cost.
An intelligent prompt router predicts the response quality of each model for each request. The router then sends the request to the model with the best mix of quality and cost. A router uses two models from the same model family, and it fits an application that can keep using both. Here the Provisioned Throughput commitment is for one model only, so the team must choose a single model, and a router keeps two in use.

INCORRECT: Run a load test with production-like prompts against each candidate model, and compare the InvocationLatency metric of each model in Amazon CloudWatch.
InvocationLatency is the time from when a request is sent to when the last token arrives. Comparing it under load is the right test when the team must pick the fastest model. Here all three models already meet the latency target of the product pages, so latency does not decide the choice. The metric also says nothing about text quality or the add-to-cart rate.

INCORRECT: Send a copy of live product page requests to each candidate model, keep the descriptions hidden from shoppers, and compare each model's token cost.
This is a shadow test: each candidate model receives a copy of live requests, but its output never reaches shoppers. It is a safe choice when outputs must not reach users before a review. Here the team must measure the add-to-cart rate, and a shopper cannot react to a description that no one shows. The test gives token cost, but no add-to-cart data and no quality score.

CORRECT: Each week, a Lambda function scores a sample of last week's logged prompts and answers in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and alarms on a drop.
Model invocation logging already keeps every prompt and answer in Amazon S3, so last week's real traffic is ready to use. Each week, an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts an AWS Lambda function.

The function takes a sample of the log records and writes them into a prompt dataset, with each stored answer in the response field. Amazon Bedrock evaluation jobs can grade responses that the team brings: the job skips the model call, and a judge model grades the stored answers.

INCORRECT: Each night, an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts the AWS CodePipeline pipeline, so that the release check scores the answers to the 300 test questions even when no release happens.
A scheduled run of the release check tests the application even in weeks with no release, so it catches a quality change that does not come from the team's own code, such as a change on the model side. But the 300 questions were written before the new product line launched, and none of them ask about it. The nightly score would stay high while real users ask about the new products and get weak answers.

Alarms on client and server errors show when model calls fail, for example after a permission change or a request in a wrong format, and every production application needs them. Here every model call succeeds. The problem is weaker answers that arrive with no error, so these two metrics stay normal while user ratings fall.

INCORRECT: The team writes new test questions about the new product line and adds them to the 300 questions that the AWS CodePipeline release check scores.
Test questions about the new product line make the release gate stronger, and the team should add them before the next release. But the gate runs only when a release starts, and no release happened in the last six weeks. The drop came with no change to the application, so a release check does not see it. The next new product line would also need new questions again before the gate could see a problem there.

An engineering firm uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store to query a library of technical specifications. When engineers ask for specific values (e.g., "What is the maximum torque for bolt X-99?"), the system answers "The manual discusses bolt X-99 assembly procedures" but fails to provide the exact number.

options.text: Raise the number of results in the retrieval configuration of the query from five to twenty, so the chunk with the torque value reaches the model.
Set the knowledge base query to the hybrid search type, so the part number and the word torque also count as keyword matches in the search.
Give each manual a document type attribute in its metadata file, and filter the knowledge base query to technical specification documents.
Add an Amazon Bedrock reranker model to the knowledge base query, so the most relevant retrieved chunks move to the top of the results.
Re-create the data source with fixed-size chunks of a smaller maximum token count and some overlap, and then sync the manuals again.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the knowledge base query to the hybrid search type, so the part number and the word torque also count as keyword matches in the search.
A knowledge base query can use the semantic search type or the hybrid search type. Semantic search compares vector embeddings only, so text with a similar general meaning, such as the assembly steps for the same bolt, can rank above the short line that holds the value. Hybrid search also searches the raw text. An exact part number like X-99 and the word torque then count as keyword matches, and the chunk with the value moves up. Hybrid search needs a vector store with a filterable text field for the chunk text. The standard setup of an OpenSearch Serverless vector store marks that field as filterable, so this knowledge base can use hybrid search.

CORRECT: Re-create the data source with fixed-size chunks of a smaller maximum token count and some overlap, and then sync the manuals again.
With fixed-size chunking, the team sets the maximum number of tokens in a chunk and an overlap between chunks. A large chunk mixes the torque value with a lot of general assembly text, so its embedding mostly stands for the general text. A smaller chunk gives the value an embedding that is much closer to a question about it, and the overlap keeps the value next to its label. The chunking settings of an existing data source cannot change, so the team re-creates the data source with the new settings and syncs the manuals again.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.4: "Troubleshoot retrieval system issues to identify and resolve problems that affect information retrieval effectiveness for FM augmentation"
Example: "chunking and preprocessing remediation"

Sources:

  • Configure and customize queries and response generation
  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases
  • Modify a data source for your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base

INCORRECT: Raise the number of results in the retrieval configuration of the query from five to twenty, so the chunk with the torque value reaches the model.
The number of results sets how many chunks a query returns. Raising it helps when the right chunk ranks just below the cut. Here a test that returned many more chunks still missed the torque value, so a larger number only adds more assembly text to the prompt.

INCORRECT: Give each manual a document type attribute in its metadata file, and filter the knowledge base query to technical specification documents.
A metadata file gives every chunk of a document the same attributes, and a filter then limits the search to documents with a matching value. That works when the wrong chunks come from other kinds of documents. Here the torque tables and the assembly steps sit in the same manual, so all their chunks carry the same document type, and the filter keeps both.

INCORRECT: Add an Amazon Bedrock reranker model to the knowledge base query, so the most relevant retrieved chunks move to the top of the results.
A reranker model scores the chunks that the search returned and puts the most relevant ones first. It fits when the right chunk is among the results but sits too low. A reranker cannot add a chunk that the search never returned, and here the torque chunk is missing even from much larger result sets.

questions.promptHtml:
A legal technology startup has built a RAG application with a model on Amazon Bedrock and an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store to analyze commercial contracts. The ingestion pipeline uses a fixed-size chunking strategy (500 tokens) to split the PDF documents. Clauses run from one line to several pages, and one question can need clauses from many contracts.
The application provides incorrect answers regarding "Liability" clauses. The root cause analysis reveals that the fixed-size chunks often cut through the middle of these paragraphs, separating the condition from the consequence across two retrieved segments. This context fragmentation prevents the model from "seeing" the full clause logic.
Which remediation strategy represents a dynamic chunking approach to resolve this content handling issue?
questions.promptText:
A legal technology startup has built a RAG application with a model on Amazon Bedrock and an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store to analyze commercial contracts. The ingestion pipeline uses a fixed-size chunking strategy (500 tokens) to split the PDF documents. Clauses run from one line to several pages, and one question can need clauses from many contracts.
The application provides incorrect answers regarding "Liability" clauses. The root cause analysis reveals that the fixed-size chunks often cut through the middle of these paragraphs, separating the condition from the consequence across two retrieved segments. This context fragmentation prevents the model from "seeing" the full clause logic.
Which remediation strategy represents a dynamic chunking approach to resolve this content handling issue?

options.text: Send each whole contract to a model with a larger context window in a single prompt, and remove the chunking and retrieval steps.
Keep fixed-size chunking, but raise the chunk size from 500 to 2,000 tokens and add a 20 percent overlap between neighboring chunks.
Switch to hierarchical chunking with a set maximum token size for parent and child chunks, and return the parent chunk of each matched child to the model.
Change the splitter to find headings, paragraph breaks and list items, and end each chunk at one of them, so chunk sizes vary with the text.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change the splitter to find headings, paragraph breaks and list items, and end each chunk at one of them, so chunk sizes vary with the text.
A structure-aware splitter reads the layout of each contract, such as headings, paragraph breaks and list items, and ends each chunk at one of these boundaries. The chunk size then follows the text: a one-line clause gets a small chunk, and a chunk never ends in the middle of a paragraph. This is dynamic chunking. The liability paragraph keeps its condition and its consequence in the same chunk, so the model sees the whole rule when that chunk is retrieved.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.1: "Resolve content handling issues to ensure that necessary information is processed completely in FM interactions"
Example: "dynamic chunking strategies"

Sources:

  • Accelerate performance using a custom chunking mechanism with Amazon Bedrock
  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Send each whole contract to a model with a larger context window in a single prompt, and remove the chunking and retrieval steps.
A model with a large context window can read one whole document with no chunking at all. That fits questions about a single document that fits in the window. Here one question can need clauses from many contracts, so the application must still find the right clauses across the whole collection. Removing retrieval removes the step that does this.

INCORRECT: Keep fixed-size chunking, but raise the chunk size from 500 to 2,000 tokens and add a 20 percent overlap between neighboring chunks.
A larger chunk keeps more text together, and overlap repeats some text at the edge of neighboring chunks. That can reduce bad cuts when sections have about the same length. Clauses here run from one line to several pages, so a 2,000-token cut still falls inside some clauses, and one chunk mixes many short clauses. The size is still fixed.

INCORRECT: Switch to hierarchical chunking with a set maximum token size for parent and child chunks, and return the parent chunk of each matched child to the model.
Hierarchical chunking builds large parent chunks and small child chunks, each with a maximum token size. During retrieval, it finds the matching child chunks and returns their parent chunks, so the model gets more context around a precise match. This helps when a short match needs the text around it. But the parent size is still a token count, not a clause boundary. Clauses here run from one line to several pages, so a parent can still end in the middle of a liability paragraph. The sizes are set in advance, so this is not a dynamic approach.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs an insurance claims agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. AgentCore observability records each run, with every model response and every tool call and its input. Before each tool call, the model states its reason.
In testing, the claim records end in the right state, and the final answers are right. Still, reviewers found runs where the agent approved a claim after it checked the wrong policy clause. Faulty runs make about as many tool calls as good runs, and most claims have several valid tool orders.
The team wants a repeatable score for every test run that finds these weak steps.
Which approach gives the team this score?
questions.promptText:
A company runs an insurance claims agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. AgentCore observability records each run, with every model response and every tool call and its input. Before each tool call, the model states its reason.
In testing, the claim records end in the right state, and the final answers are right. Still, reviewers found runs where the agent approved a claim after it checked the wrong policy clause. Faulty runs make about as many tool calls as good runs, and most claims have several valid tool orders.
The team wants a repeatable score for every test run that finds these weak steps.
Which approach gives the team this score?

options.text: Export the tool call count of each test run from the traces, publish it as a CloudWatch custom metric, and alarm when it rises above the usual count.
Export the final answer of each test run from the traces, and score it in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model and the built-in Correctness metric.
Export the steps of each test run from the traces, with each tool, input and stated reason, and score them in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model and a custom metric.
Export the tool call order of each test run from the traces, and fail the run when it differs from the one expected order that the test scenario stores.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Export the steps of each test run from the traces, with each tool, input and stated reason, and score them in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model and a custom metric.
The weak step sits in the middle of a run, so the team must score the steps, not only the result. AgentCore observability stores the traces in CloudWatch Logs, with the model calls and responses and each tool call with its input. For each test run, the team exports the steps, with the tool, the input and the reason the model gave, and puts them in the response field of a prompt dataset. An Amazon Bedrock evaluation job can grade responses that the team brings, and a custom metric holds the team's own instructions and rating scale for the judge model. Here the instructions ask whether each step used the right tool and the right policy clause for a sound reason. The same rubric and the same judge run on every test run, so the scores stay comparable from one release to the next.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.7: "Develop agent performance frameworks to ensure that agents perform tasks correctly and efficiently"
Example: "reasoning quality assessment in multi-step workflows"

Sources:

  • Create a model evaluation job using custom metrics

  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge

  • View observability data for your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents

INCORRECT: Export the tool call count of each test run from the traces, publish it as a CloudWatch custom metric, and alarm when it rises above the usual count.
A tool call count finds runs that loop or call tools far more often than usual, which is a clear sign of waste in an agent. Here faulty runs make about as many tool calls as good runs, because checking the wrong clause adds no calls. The count stays normal, and the alarm never fires.

INCORRECT: Export the final answer of each test run from the traces, and score it in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model and the built-in Correctness metric.
Grading the final answer with a judge model fits when the answers themselves go wrong, and Correctness measures if a response is correct. Here the final answers are already right, even in the runs where the agent checked the wrong clause. The score stays high and misses the weak step.

INCORRECT: Export the tool call order of each test run from the traces, and fail the run when it differs from the one expected order that the test scenario stores.
Comparing each run with one expected tool order is a simple, fixed check, and it works well for tasks that have only one valid path. Here most claims have several valid tool orders, so the check fails good runs that take another valid order. It also ignores the input and the reason of each step, so a run that follows the expected order but reads the wrong clause still passes.

A startup is testing a RAG chatbot built with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Beta testers report that the chatbot often ignores the specific technical constraints in their queries because the retrieval step fills the context window with loosely related marketing content instead of the necessary technical specifications.
The developer needs to create a systematic evaluation to quantify how much "noise" (irrelevant information) is being retrieved compared to the user's query. The team has no reference answers for its test questions.
Which metric should the developer select in an Amazon Bedrock RAG Evaluation job to measure this specific aspect of retrieval quality?
questions.promptText:
A startup is testing a RAG chatbot built with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Beta testers report that the chatbot often ignores the specific technical constraints in their queries because the retrieval step fills the context window with loosely related marketing content instead of the necessary technical specifications.
The developer needs to create a systematic evaluation to quantify how much "noise" (irrelevant information) is being retrieved compared to the user's query. The team has no reference answers for its test questions.
Which metric should the developer select in an Amazon Bedrock RAG Evaluation job to measure this specific aspect of retrieval quality?

options.text: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job, and select the Citation precision metric for the generated answer of each test question.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job, and select the Context relevance metric for the retrieved texts of each test question.
Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job, and select the Faithfulness metric for the generated answer of each test question.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job, and select the Context coverage metric for the retrieved texts of each test question.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job, and select the Context relevance metric for the retrieved texts of each test question.
A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job tests only the retrieval step of a knowledge base, with no generated answer. Its Context relevance metric measures how relevant the retrieved texts are to each question. When a technical question brings back loosely related marketing text, the score drops, so the score shows how much noise the retrieval step adds. The metric needs no reference answers, which suits a team that has none.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.6: "Implement retrieval quality testing to evaluate and optimize information retrieval components for FM augmentation"
Example: "relevance scoring"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand RAG system performance

INCORRECT: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job, and select the Citation precision metric for the generated answer of each test question.
Citation precision measures how many of the passages an answer cites were cited correctly. It helps when answers point users to the wrong sources. It grades the citations in the answer, not how relevant the retrieved texts are to the question, so it does not measure the noise that the retrieval step adds.

INCORRECT: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job, and select the Faithfulness metric for the generated answer of each test question.
Faithfulness measures how well the generated answers avoid hallucination with respect to the retrieved texts. It fits when the model adds facts that the retrieved texts do not contain. It grades the answer, not the retrieval. An answer can stay faithful to marketing text that the knowledge base should never have returned, so the score can stay high while the noise remains.

INCORRECT: Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job, and select the Context coverage metric for the retrieved texts of each test question.
Context coverage is the other retrieve-only metric. It measures how much of the information in the ground truth texts the retrieved texts cover, so it finds retrieval that misses facts. It needs a ground truth for each question in the prompt dataset, and this team has no reference answers.
