A company runs a document summarizer in AWS Lambda. The function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock through a US geographic cross-Region inference profile, which can send each request to one of several US Regions. The model can also be called directly in each of those Regions. Today the function's IAM role allows bedrock:InvokeModel on all resources.
A security review asks for least privilege. The role must use only this model and only through this inference profile, and it must not call the model directly. Every request that the profile routes must still succeed.
Which set of IAM policy statements should the team attach to the role?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a document summarizer in AWS Lambda. The function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock through a US geographic cross-Region inference profile, which can send each request to one of several US Regions. The model can also be called directly in each of those Regions. Today the function's IAM role allows bedrock:InvokeModel on all resources.
A security review asks for least privilege. The role must use only this model and only through this inference profile, and it must not call the model directly. Every request that the profile routes must still succeed.
Which set of IAM policy statements should the team attach to the role?

options.text: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in every Region that the profile can route to, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition that names the profile.
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in the function's own Region, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition that names the profile.
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in every Region that the profile can route to, with no condition on the statement for the model.
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in the function's own Region, with no condition on the statement for the model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in every Region that the profile can route to, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition that names the profile.
A geographic cross-Region inference profile sends each request to the model in one of the Regions on its list. So the role needs permission on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in the source Region and in every destination Region of the profile. The bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition on the model statement allows a call to the model only when the call comes through the named profile. A direct call to the model ARN does not come through the profile, so the condition blocks it. The role can use no other model and no other profile.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.3: "Create secure access frameworks to ensure appropriate security controls"
Example: "least privilege API access to FMs"

Sources:

  • Prerequisites for inference profiles

  • Geographic cross-Region inference

  • Set up a model invocation resource using inference profiles

INCORRECT: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in the function's own Region, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition that names the profile.
Permission on the model in one Region fits an application inference profile that a team creates from a foundation model in one Region, because that profile sends requests to that Region. This profile is a US geographic profile that can send a request to any of several US Regions. When it routes a request to another Region, the role has no permission on the model there, and that request fails.

INCORRECT: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in every Region that the profile can route to, with no condition on the statement for the model.
Permission on the profile and on the model in every Region, with no condition, fits a role that must also call the model directly, for example a test tool that compares Regions. It lets every routed request succeed. But the review says that this role must not call the model directly. With no condition, the role can call the model ARN in any of these Regions on its own.

INCORRECT: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile ARN, and on the model ARN in the function's own Region, with no condition on the statement for the model.
This policy fits an application inference profile made from a model in one Region, for a role that may also call that model directly. It fails here in two ways. The US geographic profile can route a request to another Region, where the role has no permission on the model. With no condition, the role can also call the model directly.

questions.promptHtml:
A retailer runs a shopping assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon API Gateway sends each customer message to an AWS Lambda function, which calls the Converse API with a guardrail that has content filters. The model also reads customer reviews of products.
Last week, some answers held links to outside websites that a review had planted, and product codes that do not exist. The outside links were different each time. The valid product codes live in an Amazon DynamoDB table that changes every day. No answer with an outside link or an unknown code may reach a customer, but answers with valid codes must. The team keeps the guardrail as one layer.
Which additional control should the team add?
questions.promptText:
A retailer runs a shopping assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon API Gateway sends each customer message to an AWS Lambda function, which calls the Converse API with a guardrail that has content filters. The model also reads customer reviews of products.
Last week, some answers held links to outside websites that a review had planted, and product codes that do not exist. The outside links were different each time. The valid product codes live in an Amazon DynamoDB table that changes every day. No answer with an outside link or an unknown code may reach a customer, but answers with valid codes must. The team keeps the guardrail as one layer.
Which additional control should the team add?

options.text: Have the Lambda function check each link and product code in the answer against the company domain and the DynamoDB table, and return a safe reply if one fails.
Add a custom word filter to the guardrail that lists the outside domains from last week's answers, and set the Block action on model responses.
Add a regular expression for the product code format to the sensitive information filters of the guardrail, and set the Block action on model responses.
Stream the model invocation logs through a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to a function that compares each response with the catalog and alerts the team about unknown links or codes.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Have the Lambda function check each link and product code in the answer against the company domain and the DynamoDB table, and return a safe reply if one fails.
The Lambda function already sits between the model and the customer, so it can check each answer after the model writes it and before API Gateway returns it. The function finds every link and every product code in the answer. It accepts a link only on the company's own domain, and a code only when the code exists in the DynamoDB table, so the check always uses the current list of products. When a check fails, the function sends a safe reply in place of the answer. This adds a layer to the guardrail: the guardrail filters harmful content, and the function checks facts that only the company's own data can confirm.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.4: "Create defense-in-depth safety systems to provide comprehensive protection against FM misuse"
Example: "Lambda functions to perform post-processing validation"

Sources:

  • Designing serverless AI architectures

  • Remove a specific list of words and phrases from conversations with word filters

  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters

INCORRECT: Add a custom word filter to the guardrail that lists the outside domains from last week's answers, and set the Block action on model responses.
A custom word filter blocks exact words and phrases from a list, which works well for a fixed set of terms, such as the names of banned products. It can hold only what the team already knows. The outside links were different each time, so next week's links will not be on the list, and those answers will still reach customers.

INCORRECT: Add a regular expression for the product code format to the sensitive information filters of the guardrail, and set the Block action on model responses.
A regular expression in the sensitive information filters finds values that follow a pattern, such as a booking ID, and blocks or masks them. That fits a value that must never leave the system. A pattern cannot tell a valid product code from an unknown code in the same format, and the guardrail cannot read the DynamoDB table. With the Block action, every answer that holds any product code is blocked, including the answers with valid codes that customers must still receive.

INCORRECT: Stream the model invocation logs through a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to a function that compares each response with the catalog and alerts the team about unknown links or codes.
A subscription filter sends a real-time feed of log events to a Lambda function, which suits alerts and later review, and the function can compare each response with the catalog. A log entry exists only after the model has answered, and nothing in this design holds the answer back while the log is checked. The function can raise an alert, but it cannot stop the answer. The question says no answer with an outside link or an unknown code may reach a customer.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare company is deploying a medical documentation assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The assistant helps clinicians generate patient reports. The company wants to identify prompts that contain potential Protected Health Information (PHI) or requests for medical diagnoses to analyze usage patterns and improve training materials. However, the assistant must continue processing all requests without blocking any clinician workflows, as blocking could delay critical patient care.
The solution must log all detected policy violations for weekly review by the compliance team and trigger immediate alerts only for high-severity violations. Only a request for a medical diagnosis counts as a high-severity violation.
Which solution meets ALL these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A healthcare company is deploying a medical documentation assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The assistant helps clinicians generate patient reports. The company wants to identify prompts that contain potential Protected Health Information (PHI) or requests for medical diagnoses to analyze usage patterns and improve training materials. However, the assistant must continue processing all requests without blocking any clinician workflows, as blocking could delay critical patient care.
The solution must log all detected policy violations for weekly review by the compliance team and trigger immediate alerts only for high-severity violations. Only a request for a medical diagnosis counts as a high-severity violation.
Which solution meets ALL these requirements?

options.text: Set the sensitive information filter and the denied topic for diagnoses to detect mode, log each guardrail trace to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for denied topic findings.
Set the sensitive information filter and the denied topic for diagnoses to detect mode, log each guardrail trace to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for all findings.
Set the sensitive information filter to detect mode and the denied topic for diagnoses to block, log each guardrail trace to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for blocked requests.
Call Amazon Comprehend to detect PII in each prompt before the model call, log each finding to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for high-score findings.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the sensitive information filter and the denied topic for diagnoses to detect mode, log each guardrail trace to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for denied topic findings.
Each guardrail policy has an action for prompts and an action for responses. Detect mode, the NONE action in the API, takes no action on the content but returns what the guardrail found in the trace. So every request still reaches the model, and clinicians get their reports with no delay. When the application calls the model with the guardrail and turns the trace on, the response holds an assessment for each policy, such as the topic policy and the sensitive information policy. The application writes each trace to a log group in CloudWatch Logs, so the compliance team can review every finding each week. A metric filter turns log events into a CloudWatch metric that an alarm can watch. A filter that matches only findings of the denied topic for diagnoses counts the high-severity requests, and its alarm sends an alert at once. Prompts with PHI stay in the logs for the weekly review and raise no alert.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.4: "Implement continuous monitoring and advanced governance controls to support safety audits and regulatory readiness"
Example: "automated detection for misuse, drift, and policy violations"

Sources:

  • Options for handling harmful content detected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

  • Include a guardrail with the Converse API

  • Creating metrics from log events using filters

INCORRECT: Set the sensitive information filter and the denied topic for diagnoses to detect mode, log each guardrail trace to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for all findings.
This design detects and logs the same things as the right one. Only the alarm is different. A metric filter that counts every finding fits a team that wants an alert for each detection. Here, clinical notes often hold patient details, and a prompt with PHI is not a high-severity violation. The alarm would fire for those prompts too, but the company wants immediate alerts only for requests for a diagnosis.

INCORRECT: Set the sensitive information filter to detect mode and the denied topic for diagnoses to block, log each guardrail trace to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for blocked requests.
The block action stops content that matches the policy and replaces it with the blocked message that the team sets. It fits a company that must refuse requests for a diagnosis. Here the assistant must not block any clinician workflow. A blocked request returns no report, and that can delay patient care.

INCORRECT: Call Amazon Comprehend to detect PII in each prompt before the model call, log each finding to CloudWatch Logs, and alarm on a metric filter for high-score findings.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection finds entities such as a name or an address in a text, with a score for each entity. A check like this before the model call fits an application that must find personal data in prompts. But it finds types of personal data, not what a request asks for. A request for a diagnosis may hold no personal data at all. The check does not find the high-severity requests, so the alarm cannot fire for them.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A retail company labels the sentiment of each customer review on its website. Today an AWS Lambda function sends each review with a prompt to Claude Sonnet in Amazon Bedrock. It stores one label for the whole review in Amazon DynamoDB: positive, negative, neutral or mixed. The reviews are short and written in English, and millions arrive each day. The model cost is now higher than the value of the feature.
Each model update forced the team to rewrite and test the prompt again, so the team wants no prompt to maintain for this task. The team also has no labeled reviews to train a model with.
Which change should the team make to the Lambda function?
questions.promptText:
A retail company labels the sentiment of each customer review on its website. Today an AWS Lambda function sends each review with a prompt to Claude Sonnet in Amazon Bedrock. It stores one label for the whole review in Amazon DynamoDB: positive, negative, neutral or mixed. The reviews are short and written in English, and millions arrive each day. The model cost is now higher than the value of the feature.
Each model update forced the team to rewrite and test the prompt again, so the team wants no prompt to maintain for this task. The team also has no labeled reviews to train a model with.
Which change should the team make to the Lambda function?

options.text: Send each review to the Amazon Comprehend DetectSentiment operation, and store the sentiment label that it returns in DynamoDB.
Send each review to the Amazon Comprehend DetectTargetedSentiment operation, and store the sentiment that it returns for each product or feature in DynamoDB.
Train an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier on the four labels, send each review to its endpoint, and store the returned label in DynamoDB.
Send each review with the same prompt to a smaller, lower-cost model in Amazon Bedrock, and store the label that it returns in DynamoDB.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Send each review to the Amazon Comprehend DetectSentiment operation, and store the sentiment label that it returns in DynamoDB.
Amazon Comprehend uses a pre-trained model to find insights in text, such as its sentiment, so the team does not provide any training data. DetectSentiment returns the most likely sentiment of the text, positive, negative, neutral or mixed, and a score for each of the four. These are the same four labels that the store keeps today. The Lambda function sends each short review in one API call, with no prompt to write and no model to host. The task is narrow and runs millions of times each day, so a pre-trained model built for this one task replaces the large foundation model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.3: "Develop optimized FM deployment approaches to balance performance and resource requirements for GenAI workloads"
Example: "smaller pre-trained models for specific tasks"

Sources:

  • Sentiment (Amazon Comprehend Developer Guide)
  • What is Amazon Comprehend?
  • Targeted sentiment (Amazon Comprehend Developer Guide)

INCORRECT: Send each review to the Amazon Comprehend DetectTargetedSentiment operation, and store the sentiment that it returns for each product or feature in DynamoDB.
Targeted sentiment finds the entities that a text names, such as a product, a feature or a person, and gives a sentiment for each mention. It fits a team that wants to know which parts of a product get good or bad feedback. This store keeps one label for the whole review. A review that praises the battery and criticizes the screen would get two sentiments, not one label.

INCORRECT: Train an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier on the four labels, send each review to its endpoint, and store the returned label in DynamoDB.
A custom classifier learns classes that the team defines, for example the department that should answer each customer email. It fits labels that the pre-trained features do not offer. To train one, the team must gather example documents for each class. This team has no labeled reviews, and the four labels it needs are the ones that sentiment analysis already returns.

INCORRECT: Send each review with the same prompt to a smaller, lower-cost model in Amazon Bedrock, and store the label that it returns in DynamoDB.
A smaller model in Amazon Bedrock can handle a simple task, and it fits a team that wants to keep the flexibility of a prompt, for example to add new labels later. But the model still needs the prompt to know the task and the labels. The team would still rewrite and test that prompt after model updates, and that is the work it wants to stop.

questions.promptHtml:
A research company builds a literature review system with Strands Agents and models in Amazon Bedrock. Four specialist agents do the work: one searches academic databases, one extracts key findings from the papers, one writes the summary report, and one checks every citation in the report. An editor agent fixes reports with citation problems. Each agent has its own prompt and model, and the team updates each agent on its own.

How should the team connect the agents?
questions.promptText:
A research company builds a literature review system with Strands Agents and models in Amazon Bedrock. Four specialist agents do the work: one searches academic databases, one extracts key findings from the papers, one writes the summary report, and one checks every citation in the report. An editor agent fixes reports with citation problems. Each agent has its own prompt and model, and the team updates each agent on its own.
Auditors require that every review runs the steps in the same order. The citation check must run on every report, and the team does not want a model to decide which step runs next.
How should the team connect the agents?

options.text: Build a Strands Agents graph with each agent as a node, edges that fix the order, and a condition that sends a failed check to the editor agent.
Build a Strands Agents swarm in which all the agents share one context and hand the work to each other in the order that the agents choose.
Build an orchestrator agent in Strands Agents that calls each specialist agent and the editor agent as tools, and that decides when each one runs.
Build one agent in Strands Agents with all the tools and one system prompt that lists every step in order, with the citation rules and the editor step at the end.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Build a Strands Agents graph with each agent as a node, edges that fix the order, and a condition that sends a failed check to the editor agent.
A graph in Strands Agents connects agents through directed links that the team defines. Each agent is a node, and the edges say which agent works next, so every review runs the steps in the same order. A graph also supports conditional routing: a report that fails the citation check goes to the editor agent, and a report that passes goes on. The order follows rules that the team writes into the graph, so no model decides the next step and no step is skipped. This is the pattern for approval chains and quality gates. Each node keeps its own prompt and model, so the team can still update one agent without changes to the others.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.5: "Develop advanced GenAI applications to implement sophisticated AI capabilities"
Example: "Strands Agents and AWS Agent Squad for AWS native orchestration"

Sources:

  • Introducing Strands Agents 1.0: Production-Ready Multi-Agent Orchestration Made Simple

  • Multi-Agent collaboration patterns with Strands Agents and Amazon Nova

INCORRECT: Build a Strands Agents swarm in which all the agents share one context and hand the work to each other in the order that the agents choose.
A swarm is a team of peer agents that share memory and build on each other's work. No central controller sets the order. The agents decide among themselves who works next. This fits brainstorming and open problems, where the best path is not known in advance. The auditors require the same order in every review, and a swarm does not give a fixed order.

INCORRECT: Build an orchestrator agent in Strands Agents that calls each specialist agent and the editor agent as tools, and that decides when each one runs.
With agents as tools, an orchestrator agent calls specialist agents as its tools and combines their answers. It fits requests that break into different tasks, where the specialists that a request needs change from one request to the next. But the orchestrator is itself a model, and it decides which specialist to call and when. The team does not want a model to choose the next step, and the citation check must run every time.

INCORRECT: Build one agent in Strands Agents with all the tools and one system prompt that lists every step in order, with the citation rules and the editor step at the end.
One agent with all the tools is the simplest design, and it fits a small task that one prompt can describe. Here each specialist has its own prompt and model, and the team updates each one on its own. A single agent has one prompt and one model for every step. The model also reads the order from its prompt, so a model still decides what happens next.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
An online store lets users pick any two products and see a written comparison. An AWS Lambda function builds each request from a prompt template, the records of the two products in Amazon DynamoDB and fixed inference settings, and then calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. Popular pairs come up thousands of times each day, and every request for the same pair is the same, word for word.
Most of the cost and the wait come from the long text that the model writes. Two pairs that differ in one product must never share a comparison. After each update of the prompt template, users must see comparisons from the new template.
Which caching design meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
An online store lets users pick any two products and see a written comparison. An AWS Lambda function builds each request from a prompt template, the records of the two products in Amazon DynamoDB and fixed inference settings, and then calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. Popular pairs come up thousands of times each day, and every request for the same pair is the same, word for word.
Most of the cost and the wait come from the long text that the model writes. Two pairs that differ in one product must never share a comparison. After each update of the prompt template, users must see comparisons from the new template.
Which caching design meets these needs?

options.text: Before each model call, hash the full request, with the template version and both product records, and return the stored comparison when ElastiCache holds that hash.
Before each model call, hash the IDs of the two products that the user picked, and return the stored comparison when ElastiCache holds that hash.
Before each model call, embed the names of the two products, and return a stored comparison when ElastiCache holds one above the similarity threshold that the team sets.
Before each model call, put a cache checkpoint after the template and the product records, so that Amazon Bedrock reads that input from its cache.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Before each model call, hash the full request, with the template version and both product records, and return the stored comparison when ElastiCache holds that hash.
Request-response caching stores each request with its result. When the same request comes again, the application returns the stored answer and does not call the model at all. It fits identical requests, with the same prompt and the same settings, that give the same answer. Here the function builds each request in the same way, so a popular pair produces the same request every time. A hash turns that full request into a short key of fixed length. Because the template version and both product records are part of the hashed request, two pairs that differ in one product get different keys, and a new template gives new keys. Users then get comparisons from the new template, while each repeated request skips the long text generation.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.4: "Create intelligent caching systems to reduce costs and improve response times by avoiding unnecessary FM invocations"
Example: "deterministic request hashing"

Sources:

  • Optimize LLM response costs and latency with effective caching

  • Best practices (Amazon ElastiCache semantic caching)

  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

INCORRECT: Before each model call, hash the IDs of the two products that the user picked, and return the stored comparison when ElastiCache holds that hash.
A key built from the product IDs alone is short and simple. It fits an answer that depends only on those IDs and never on how the answer is produced. Here the answer also depends on the prompt template. After the team updates the template, the same pair still gives the same key, so users keep getting the comparison from the old template until the entry expires.

INCORRECT: Before each model call, embed the names of the two products, and return a stored comparison when ElastiCache holds one above the similarity threshold that the team sets.
This is a semantic cache. It compares the meaning of a new request with stored requests and returns a stored answer when the similarity is above a threshold. It fits users who ask the same question in different words. The threshold trades more cache hits against a higher risk of a wrong answer. Two pairs that differ in one product can have very similar names, so the cache can return the comparison of a different pair, which the store must never do.

INCORRECT: Before each model call, put a cache checkpoint after the template and the product records, so that Amazon Bedrock reads that input from its cache.
Prompt caching reuses a repeated part of the input, the prefix up to the checkpoint. It lowers the cost of input tokens and the time the model needs to read a long, repeated prompt. The model still writes the whole comparison on every call. Most of the cost and the wait come from that written text, so this change leaves most of both in place.

questions.promptHtml:
An AWS Lambda function summarizes support documents with the Converse API in Amazon Bedrock. When a call fails, the function waits two seconds and tries again, up to three times. After the last failed try, the function writes "summary failed" and the document ID to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

The failed documents form two groups. Documents in the first group fail only during the morning peak and succeed later. Documents in the second group fail on every try at any hour. A test call for one of these documents returned a ValidationException.

The team needs to see why each document failed, and the function must stop sending calls that cannot succeed.

How should the function handle failed calls?
questions.promptText:
An AWS Lambda function summarizes support documents with the Converse API in Amazon Bedrock. When a call fails, the function waits two seconds and tries again, up to three times. After the last failed try, the function writes "summary failed" and the document ID to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
The failed documents form two groups. Documents in the first group fail only during the morning peak and succeed later. Documents in the second group fail on every try at any hour. A test call for one of these documents returned a ValidationException.
The team needs to see why each document failed, and the function must stop sending calls that cannot succeed.
How should the function handle failed calls?

options.text: Add CloudWatch alarms that watch the InvocationThrottles and InvocationClientErrors metrics of the model, and notify the team through an Amazon SNS topic when either count rises.
Log the error code and message of each failed call, retry throttling and other temporary errors with backoff, and send ValidationException failures to a review queue.
Request a higher tokens-per-minute quota for the model through Service Quotas, and send the failed documents again once the higher quota applies to the account.
Add a CloudWatch dashboard that graphs the InvocationThrottles and InvocationClientErrors metrics of the model, and have the team review it after each morning peak.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Log the error code and message of each failed call, retry throttling and other temporary errors with backoff, and send ValidationException failures to a review queue.
Each failed call returns an error code and a message, and the log now keeps both, so the team knows why each document failed. A ThrottlingException means that requests went over the account quotas, which fits the documents that fail only during the morning peak. Retries with exponential backoff and random jitter wait longer after each failure, so these calls can succeed after the peak. A ValidationException means that the input does not meet the constraints of Amazon Bedrock, and the test call showed this error for the second group. A retry sends the same input and fails again. So the function sends these failures to a review queue and stops sending calls that cannot succeed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.2: "Diagnose and resolve FM integration issues to identify and fix API integration problems specific to GenAI services"
Example: "error logging"

Sources:

  • Troubleshooting Amazon Bedrock API Error Codes

  • Retry behavior (AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide)

  • Monitor bedrock-runtime inference using CloudWatch metrics

INCORRECT: Add CloudWatch alarms that watch the InvocationThrottles and InvocationClientErrors metrics of the model, and notify the team through an Amazon SNS topic when either count rises.
These alarms watch the counts of throttled calls and of calls with client errors, and an SNS topic tells the team when a count goes up. This fits a team that wants to hear quickly when errors rise. But a metric is only a number. It does not say which document failed or what the error message was, and the team needs to see why each document failed. The function also keeps sending the calls that fail on every try.

INCORRECT: Request a higher tokens-per-minute quota for the model through Service Quotas, and send the failed documents again once the higher quota applies to the account.
A higher tokens-per-minute quota fits a workload that goes over its quota at busy times, and it can help the documents that fail only during the morning peak. The second group fails at any hour, also when traffic is low, so the quota does not cause those failures. When the team sends those documents again, the calls fail in the same way. The function also still writes only a general failure line, so the team does not learn why each document failed.

INCORRECT: Add a CloudWatch dashboard that graphs the InvocationThrottles and InvocationClientErrors metrics of the model, and have the team review it after each morning peak.
A dashboard shows the throttle and client error counts as graphs, which helps a team see trends over days, such as a peak that grows each week. It fits a regular review of service health. The graphs still show numbers only, with no document IDs and no error messages, so the team cannot learn why each document failed. Nothing in this change stops the function from sending calls that cannot succeed.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A media company is building an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base containing thousands of news articles, opinion pieces, and investigative reports. Journalists complain that when they query the AI assistant, the retrieved content often feels fragmented. Answers include incomplete thoughts, cut-off explanations, or context that seems to start mid-topic.
The articles have minimal structural hierarchy (just headline and body text) and often blend multiple related topics in a flowing narrative style. Larger fixed-size chunks with more overlap did not help. Answers must quote only the relevant part of an article.
The solution must ensure that retrieved chunks contain complete, coherent ideas that maintain the natural flow of the original writing.
Which chunking strategy should be used?
questions.promptText:
A media company is building an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base containing thousands of news articles, opinion pieces, and investigative reports. Journalists complain that when they query the AI assistant, the retrieved content often feels fragmented. Answers include incomplete thoughts, cut-off explanations, or context that seems to start mid-topic.
The articles have minimal structural hierarchy (just headline and body text) and often blend multiple related topics in a flowing narrative style. Larger fixed-size chunks with more overlap did not help. Answers must quote only the relevant part of an article.
The solution must ensure that retrieved chunks contain complete, coherent ideas that maintain the natural flow of the original writing.
Which chunking strategy should be used?

options.text: Use semantic chunking, which compares the embeddings of nearby sentences and starts a new chunk where the meaning changes more than a set threshold.
Use hierarchical chunking, which matches a search to small child chunks and then gives the model the larger parent chunk that holds each match.
Use fixed-size chunking with a larger maximum number of tokens in each chunk and a higher overlap percentage between neighboring chunks.
Use no chunking, so that each article is stored as a single chunk and each search returns the whole article to the model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use semantic chunking, which compares the embeddings of nearby sentences and starts a new chunk where the meaning changes more than a set threshold.
Semantic chunking divides text into meaningful chunks. For each sentence, it builds an embedding together with the sentences around it, and it measures how different neighboring sentences are. The breakpoint percentile threshold sets how different two sentences must be before a new chunk starts. A maximum token count limits each chunk, and the chunker keeps sentences whole. So a chunk ends where an article moves to a new topic, not at a fixed count of tokens, unless the topic runs longer than the maximum. For flowing articles with no headings, each chunk then holds one complete idea, and the answer can quote just that part. Semantic chunking has an extra cost, because it uses a foundation model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.1: "Develop effective document segmentation approaches to optimize retrieval performance for FM context augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock chunking capabilities"

Sources:

  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Use hierarchical chunking, which matches a search to small child chunks and then gives the model the larger parent chunk that holds each match.
Hierarchical chunking builds nested child and parent chunks. A search first finds child chunks, and then the knowledge base replaces them with their parent chunks, which give the model more context. This fits documents where a small, exact match needs the text around it, such as one clause of a long contract. But the team sets both chunk sizes as a maximum number of tokens. The boundaries still fall at a count of tokens, not where a topic ends, so a parent chunk can hold the end of one topic and the start of the next.

INCORRECT: Use fixed-size chunking with a larger maximum number of tokens in each chunk and a higher overlap percentage between neighboring chunks.
Fixed-size chunking splits text by a maximum number of tokens, with an overlap percentage between chunks. It fits text where ideas have a similar length, and bigger chunks can then hold whole ideas. The team already tried larger chunks with more overlap, and the problem stayed. A chunk still ends at a count of tokens, and overlap only repeats some text in the next chunk.

INCORRECT: Use no chunking, so that each article is stored as a single chunk and each search returns the whole article to the model.
With no chunking, each document is one chunk. It fits content that the team splits into small files before ingestion, one topic in each file. These articles blend several topics in one file, and answers must quote only the relevant part of an article. A whole article gives the model every topic at once.

questions.promptHtml:
A financial analyst uses an internal GenAI tool to extract data from quarterly earnings PDFs into a standardized JSON format. The tool uses the Converse API in Amazon Bedrock. The application is reporting frequent ValidationError exceptions in the backend. Upon investigation, the developer notices that for certain complex PDFs, the model either omits required fields or outputs the data as a Markdown table instead of JSON, despite the system prompt instructions. The same PDFs fail the same way on every run, and failed calls finish as fast as the others. The budget allows one model call for each PDF.
Which troubleshooting and remediation workflow should the developer implement to resolve these prompt maintenance issues and prevent recurrence?
questions.promptText:
A financial analyst uses an internal GenAI tool to extract data from quarterly earnings PDFs into a standardized JSON format. The tool uses the Converse API in Amazon Bedrock. The application is reporting frequent ValidationError exceptions in the backend. Upon investigation, the developer notices that for certain complex PDFs, the model either omits required fields or outputs the data as a Markdown table instead of JSON, despite the system prompt instructions. The same PDFs fail the same way on every run, and failed calls finish as fast as the others. The budget allows one model call for each PDF.
Which troubleshooting and remediation workflow should the developer implement to resolve these prompt maintenance issues and prevent recurrence?

options.text: Turn on model invocation logging, find the failed requests with CloudWatch Logs Insights, test the prompt on those PDFs, add JSON examples, and validate each output against the schema.
Turn on AWS X-Ray tracing for the tool, find the slowest model calls in the traces, test those PDFs again, and move the extraction to a faster, smaller model.
Log each failed output to CloudWatch Logs, set the temperature to zero in every call, test the failed PDFs again, and compare the new outputs with the old ones.
Log each failed output to CloudWatch Logs, send each one back to the model with the validation error, and ask the model to rewrite the output as valid JSON.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging, find the failed requests with CloudWatch Logs Insights, test the prompt on those PDFs, add JSON examples, and validate each output against the schema.
Model invocation logging records the full request and response of each Converse call and can send them to CloudWatch Logs. With CloudWatch Logs Insights, the developer searches that log data for the failed requests and sees which PDFs lead to the wrong format, for example the ones with complex tables. Those PDFs become a test set for the prompt template. Examples of the correct JSON in the prompt show the model the exact output it must produce. Examples in a prompt can help the model with complex tasks, such as these PDFs. The test set then checks each new version of the prompt before release. Validation against the schema catches an output with a missing field or the wrong format before the backend processes it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.5: "Troubleshoot prompt maintenance issues to continuously improve the performance of FM interactions"
Example: "template testing and CloudWatch Logs to diagnose prompt confusion"

Sources:

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Analyzing log data with CloudWatch Logs Insights
  • Design a prompt

INCORRECT: Turn on AWS X-Ray tracing for the tool, find the slowest model calls in the traces, test those PDFs again, and move the extraction to a faster, smaller model.
AWS X-Ray collects data about the requests of an application and the calls it makes to other services, and it shows where the time goes. This helps when calls run slowly or time out. Here the failed calls finish as fast as the others, so time is not the problem. The model answers quickly, but in the wrong format. A faster model with the same prompt gets the same instructions that already fail on these PDFs.

INCORRECT: Log each failed output to CloudWatch Logs, set the temperature to zero in every call, test the failed PDFs again, and compare the new outputs with the old ones.
A lower temperature makes the model choose higher-probability outputs, so its answers vary less from one call to the next. It helps when the same input gives a different format on different runs. Here the same PDFs fail in the same way on every run, so the output is already stable. The most likely output for these PDFs is the wrong format, and only a change to the prompt changes that.

INCORRECT: Log each failed output to CloudWatch Logs, send each one back to the model with the validation error, and ask the model to rewrite the output as valid JSON.
A second call that sends the output back with the error is a common way to repair a broken format. It fits when an extra call for some documents is acceptable. The budget allows one model call for each PDF, and every failed PDF would need two. The prompt also stays the same, so the same PDFs keep failing on the first call.
